The sound of firecrackers filling the air is not far away as Deepavali draws closer. But the excitement of bursting firecrackers comes with a word of caution from ophthalmologists as they warn that a moment of carelessness can cause eye injuries ranging from minor abrasions to severe ocular trauma.
M. Elangovan, director, Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital (RIO-GOH), Chennai, said that there are different types of crackers. “Bursting types (explosive crackers) will produce irregular, small and forcible particles in all directions and are the most dangerous. These particles can travel at such a velocity that they could hit or penetrate any soft surface. Then, there is direct heat injury caused by crackers such as sparklers that can cause scar formations in the cornea or conjunctiva due to the heat generated. Sudden and close exposure to bright light-emitting crackers can also cause bleaching or temporary blackout due to the impact on the rod and cone cells in the retina,” he explained.

Breast cancer begins long before the lump: why diet and lifestyle matter
While genetic predisposition is one factor, a majority of breast cancers develop in women with no family history: metabolic health and physical inactivity play a role too, and it is important for women to know about these factors
Students seen taking part in a ‘Pink Umbrella’ walk to create awareness on breast cancer. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
Last month, celebrated as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, reminded us, as it does every year, about the importance of mammograms, early diagnosis, and advances in treatment. These messages save lives and deserve continued attention. However, there is another conversation that often receives far less attention: the role of food, physical activity, obesity, diabetes, physical activity, and metabolic health in breast cancer.
In my oncology clinic, patients are often surprised when I bring up these topics. They say, “Doctor, I knew breast cancer was related to family history. I didn’t know that lifestyle diseases such as diabetes and obesity had anything to do with it.”

A cancer medicine supplied to a retailer for ₹2,700 carries a maximum retail price (MRP) of ₹27,000. Who accounts for this tenfold difference? This was among the examples highlighted by the Supreme Court in September 2026, when it questioned the gap between the prices paid for medicines and what patients ultimately pay.
Subsequently, on October 17, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) announced a 30% cap on trade margins for 137 anti-cancer drugs, effective from November 9. This intervention could reduce prices substantially for some products. It also raises a broader question: how does India decide what medicines should cost?

Those of us missing the John Wick universe can take heart, because Chad Stahelski—who created that franchise—is coming back early next year with a new dystopian action film. It’s called Karōshi (a Japanese term that means “death overwork”), and Lionsgate released a killer trailer that puts this film at the top of my list of “must see” movies of 2027.
Dying from working too hard is a very real phenomenon, not just in Japan and much of Asia, but also in Sweden, where some 700 workers die each year from overwork. The physical cause is usually stress-related heart attacks or strokes, as well as suicide (karōjisatsu in Japan). Writer/director Takashi Doscher has transported that concept to a grim, futuristic corporate Manhattan, specifically a company called Ikigai Technologies. Per the official premise:
Karōshi is an action-thriller set in a near-future Manhattan, where corporate loyalty and cultural tradition have reshaped everyday life. When a mysterious outsider infiltrates a powerful company after a worker’s death, he exposes the violent system hidden beneath its polished surface.
Teo Yoo (Past Lives) stars as the aptly named Hiro, who is clearly out for vengeance against the offending corporation. The cast also includes Takehiro Hira, so memorable in the 2024 miniseries Shōgun, as well as Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu.

Neither Charlie Collier, who had a four-year run leading Roku‘s ad and platform business, nor Tubi CEO Anjali Sud will join Fox Corp. after its acquisition of Roku.
The exec departures were among several organizational updates shared by Anthony Wood and Paul Cheesebrough, Co-Chairs of Fox Digital Platforms. After Friday morning’s close of Fox’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku, which Wood founded, the digital division has been set up as home to Roku, Tubi, Red Seat Ventures and other properties.
Sud, who presided over Tubi’s rise to the top of the free, ad-supported streaming sector, is taking on a role outside of the company, the memo said. She will stay on to help with the transition to Pete Distad, the former Apple exec who spearheaded the launch of flagship streamer Fox One and will now add Tubi as well as Roku subsidiary Frndly TV to his portfolio.
Watch on Deadline
“She and her team have helped take Tubi from a challenger brand to a free streaming force,” Wood and Cheesbrough wrote of Sud. “We want to thank her for her extraordinary contributions and wish her every success in her next endeavor.”
Collier became President of Roku Media in 2022 after a run as CEO of Fox Entertainment. He previously had overseen cable network AMC.
Mustafa Ozgen will succeed Wood as CEO of Roku. The streaming provider’s open platform, which Wood and Cheesbrough said is “central to its success with viewers and content partners,” will stay intact.
Ozgen will continue to lead Roku’s device, product and technology organization. In addition, he will now oversee Fox ad tech platform AdRise, the Roku Channel, streaming services partnerships, Roku Subscriptions, subscription service Howdy, Roku Pay, and Roku brand and creative operations.
Also exiting with Collier and Sud are Chris Handman, SVP and General Counsel at Roku, and Robyn Peterson, EVP of AdRise.
Other new appointments include Mike Bidgoli, who has been promoted to president of Tubi, reporting to Distad; Frndly TV co-founder and CEO Andy Karofsky, who will also join Distad’s group; and Lisa Holme, head of content for The Roku Channel. Holme will report to Distad and work closely with Adam Lewinson and the Tubi content team.
Ad sales across the portfolio will continue to report to Jeff Collins, President of Advertising Sales at Fox.
“We won’t have every answer on Day 1,” Wood and Cheesbrough wrote. “We’ll share decisions as they’re made, be clear about what’s still open, and keep moving. Our priorities remain the same: build great products, serve our viewers and partners, and support each other.”
The memo noted that town halls are planned in San Jose and San Francisco on Monday; the Fox lot and Santa Monica on Tuesday; Austin Wednesday and New York Thursday. International town halls will follow, the company said.

Since at least the 1920s, a persistent rumor has alleged Albert Einstein once failed math during his schooling years prior to becoming a famous theoretical physicist.
"Albert Einstein failed math," a 1997 newspaper article flatly claimed. Many other newspapers have promoted the rumor over past decades. The claim has also appeared on TV shows, for example "The Big Bang Theory" and "Tiny Toon Adventures."
Over and over again, our digging revealed examples of the claim on social media platforms, including Facebook (archived), Reddit (archived) and X (archived).
A study of historical records found this claim to be false, however, and that Einstein had, by himself, mastered integral and differential calculus and analytical geometry by age 14.
How did the myth get started? It's possible it stemmed from people misinterpreting his grades after a school he attended briefly reversed the meaning of the numbers in its grading scale, giving the false impression that Einstein failed some of the courses that in reality, he passed with flying colors. It may also have stemmed from misunderstandings about the time that during his teenage years, Einstein failed an entrance examination to Zurich Polytechnic in Switzerland. It's true that he failed the exam but also true that he excelled in the sections about math and physics.
Whereas in the past many less-reliable books and newspapers promoted the false claim, in the present day books and newspapers — and websites — widely dismiss the idea of Einstein failing math as nothing more than a popular myth.
Early findings, grade-scale reversal
To investigate this topic, Snopes primarily searched the newspaper archives on Newspapers.com, book archives on Google Books and other sources, in particular those covering the period of Einstein's life between 1879 and 1955.
In the earliest record of the claim, dating from 1928, an article in the Brooklyn Daily Eagle reported Einstein had, at a young age, failed math while attending a university in Berlin. The headline of author Meyer Weisgal's article read, "Einstein, Though at Home With Relativity, Flunked As Mathematics Student."
In 1929, amid the other trivia and jokes in a miscellany column in The Evansville Journal came the line, "Einstein failed in mathematics when he was graduated in Berlin. Math teachers, play that on your ukuleles."
That same year, H. Wieleitner, then principal of Luitpold Gymnasium, reportedly wrote to a Munich newspaper to refute a Berlin magazine's claim that Einstein had once been a very poor student. The New York Times included these details in 1984 in an article promoting Princeton University Press' upcoming release of "The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein" (pages C1, bottom right of page, and C9, bottom left of page).
The gist of the report was that Einstein's school had briefly reversed its numeric grading scale, allegedly, leading to some confusion among researchers studying Einstein's early years.
The Times printed a picture of Einstein's grades from a semester at a school in Aargau, Switzerland. Originally, the numeral 6 was the highest possible grade and 1 was the lowest. When the scale was reversed for a short period of time, Einstein received the then-top score of 1 for mathematics. The school later changed its scale back.
The Times cited John Stachel, the editor of Princeton's Einstein papers project, when reporting:
Although some Einstein biographers have disputed the widely held belief that Einstein was a poor student, the papers at Princeton lay this to rest, once and for all. According to Dr. Stachel, those who saw Einstein's academic records may have been misled by a reversal in the grading system of his school in Aargau, Switzerland.
A 'master' of math at age 14
In 1931, a review of author Anton Reiser's 1930 biography, "Albert Einstein: A Biographical Portrait," shed light on the emergence of Einstein's early genius in the 1890s. Page 37 reads:
At fourteen the boy was already master of the higher mathematics which the secondary school, based on humanistic principles, did not teach. Integral and differential calculus, analytical geometry—he mastered them all by himself. His mathematical knowledge was already so great that he amazed both teachers and fellow-students. The talent manifested was that of genius. To the teachers, it was not always pleasing. Many questions the boy asked embarrassed them to the point of silence.
Pages 44 and 45 discuss Einstein's truly failing an entrance examination in Zurich, Switzerland, at a school now named ETH Zurich. However, Reiser explained Einstein's failure had nothing to do with mathematics and physics, in which he shined so brightly it "astounded his professors" (emphasis ours):
At the age of sixteen Albert applied for admission to the Polytechnic Academy at Zurich. He wanted to pass his entrance examination as an alternative to the required graduation certificate, to which his premature departure from the Munich gymnasium and his lack of further schooling did not entitle him. His courage was indeed considerable. Almost a year had passed since he had received any instruction, and now he had come to this strange city to get his matriculation certificate. Unfortunately, his success corresponded with the gloomy probabilities.
This first examination, which Albert Einstein needed to pass, ended in complete failure. To begin with, his knowledge of languages and descriptive natural science was unusually poor. True, he shone all the more in mathematics and physics, and astounded his professors. It was suggested that he attend certain lectures on these subjects.
Einstein reportedly addressed rumor in 1935
In 1935, a man named Rabbi Harry Cohen reportedly showed Einstein a clipping of Robert Ripley's "Believe It or Not" column headlined "Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics."
Author Denis Brian's 1996 biography, "Einstein: A Life," documented Einstein's exchange with Cohen in which the physicist said he had mastered differential and integral calculus by age 15:
Cohen showed Einstein a newspaper feature titled "Believe It Or Not!" by Robert Ripley, which read, "Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics," and asked if it was true. "The story has been completely distorted," he replied, with a laugh. "When I applied for admission to the Polytechnic School in Zurich at sixteen I was not completely prepared in French and botany. I never failed in mathematics. Before I was fifteen I had mastered differential and integral calculus."
Those words — "greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics" — first appeared in newspapers as early as 1930 in an article about an oil industry trade show, not as a "Believe It or Not" column.
In 1931, a Ripley reader looking to win a prize in a contest of "Believe It or Nots" submitted the same purported fact as "Einstein, the great German mathematician and originator of his theory of relativity, failed in math while going to college."
Then, as early as 1932, Ripley's column featured a section with the title "Einstein Failed In Mathematics." It read:
"Albert Einstein, the greatest of living mathematicians, author of the Theory of Relativity, failed in the entrance examinations of the Federal Polytechnic College of Zurich. He was then sixteen years old. The man who was to be ranked with Newton and Copernicus had to do plenty of 'cramming,' and submit to a second examination before he was admitted."
Nearly 100 years later, in 2024, Ripley's corrected the record on its website by accurately reporting the facts about the grade-scale reversal at Einstein's school, along with information about his entrance exam failure.
"How did the whole story come about, then?" Ripley's writer Chris Littlechild wrote. "In the same way many other misconceptions come about: a combination of hearsay, exaggeration, and half-truths."
For further reading, we previously reported about how Einstein truly married one of his cousins.

Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones from classrooms as part of a federal government effort to limit children's and teenagers' use of electronic devices, following similar measures taken by over a hundred countries in the last decade.
The initiative, spearheaded by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, has been supported by experts who see it as an opportunity to reduce young Mexicans' exposure to technology and the resulting attention deficit, stress and anxiety.
Mexican authorities are also preparing to implement regulations this month that will require digital platforms to remove posts containing hate speech, abuse, sexual violence, harassment, cyberbullying and other illegal content.
However, the cellphone ban, which will take effect on November 3, is already facing resistance in some parts of the country. Some parents fear being unable to communicate with their children amid ongoing violence, from which children and adolescents are not spared.
According to the civil society coalition Network for Children's Rights in Mexico (REDIM), in the first half of this year, one in 10 Mexicans between the ages of 0 and 17 were victims of crimes involving organised crime.
“I don't think parents will accept not giving their children a means of digital communication, especially when those children … are spending so much time at home instead of at school,” said Francisco Ortiz, state representative of the National Union of Parents in Sinaloa, accusing the government of ignoring parents and approving regulations that “go against parental authority, against the rights of parents.”
The decree issued by Sheinbaum prohibits the use of cellphones and electronic devices inside elementary and middle schools throughout the school day, and only allows their use for educational purposes under the guidance of teachers or for personal emergencies, disability and health needs. Students can take their phones with them on the way to school.
Benigno Gomez, a father from Reynosa in the northern state of Tamaulipas, said that while he understood the educational authorities' need to reduce students' time on cellphones, he found it “a little difficult” that they weren't allowed to have a cellphone to deal with a potential risk situation.
Mexican authorities have not commented on these concerns and have instead focused on the harm caused by cellphones.
During a recent address to the Chamber of Deputies, Mexico's Secretary of Public Education, Mario Delgado, stated that the Sheinbaum administration seeks to “prevent addiction to digital platforms and the disorders they cause in minors.”
Parents seek reassurance
Just as the sun was beginning to rise, the residents of Escuinapa, the capital of the municipality of the same name located in southern Sinaloa, awoke on the morning of October 22 to alarming news. A bus that regularly travels through the small town -- which relies on mango and shrimp production -- was shot at by a man on a motorcycle.
More than a dozen high school students were on board. A video recorded by one of the passengers circulated on social media, showing children on the floor and others hiding among the seats while one teenager asks another, “Do you have any credit (on your cellphone)?”
In the attack, only the bus driver was injured, suffering cuts from shards of glass shattered by the gunfire.
Upon learning of the shooting, one Escuinapa resident immediately called her teenage daughter, who had left early for high school in a car driven by her aunt.
“Just hearing my daughter's voice and knowing she was OK calmed me down,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of the criminals plaguing her community -- admitting that she didn't hesitate to interrupt her daughter's class to check on her.
The mother expressed doubts that parents will comply with the cellphone ban, fearing that violence could now reach schools in Escuinapa, and insisted that “the safety of our children comes first.”
In defence of the regulation
For Israel Sanchez, president of the National Union of Parents, the Mexican government's decision represents progress after years of struggle by the civil organisation, which brings together hundreds of parents from public and private schools, mostly Catholic.
Sanchez argued that authorities must undertake an awareness campaign for parents and provide training for teachers to achieve the effective implementation of the regulation.
Lucía Magis-Weinberg, a neurodevelopmental researcher at the University of Washington who has studied the effects of technology on children and adolescents for years, said Mexico is joining the international movement to regulate cellphones at a very opportune moment.
Magis-Weinberg acknowledged the benefits of technology for socialisation and accessing information but said it is “a double-edged sword.”
Regulations are needed to avoid cognitive damage, digital conflicts, and the risks of platforms that “are designed to maintain, to maximise our attention.”
The ban on cellphones in schools is already in place in 114 countries, according to UNESCO data. In Europe, restrictions have gained increasing traction, especially in France, where the ban was extended to secondary schools in August. Controls have also been implemented in some countries in Latin America, such as Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Costa Rica. In the United States, bans are only maintained in some states.

The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.
Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.
Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.
Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”
A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.
Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.
After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.
A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.
Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.
Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).
Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.
Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu, where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.
After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).
He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

The 16 Best Subscription Boxes for Kids
Featured in this article
Rather than give your kid a big, expensive present once or twice a year, why not surprise them with subscription boxes for kids once a month? I have an 8-year-old and a 10-year-old, and they are thrilled when a package arrives in the mail that isn’t bills, replacement chargers from Amazon, or Garnet Hill catalogs.
Subscription boxes for kids can be useful educational supplements for homeschool or remote learning. Most are consumable, so your kid can have a treat that won't be left to molder in a corner of a playroom until they're 25. They're also handy to have around the house if you can’t send your sniffly kid to school or a big indoor birthday party. As a bonus, they’re usually affordable. I tested some of the subscriptions on this list, like the Lovevery Reading Skill Set 3-box set ($160), and I bought others for my kids and their friends. These are our favorites. Be sure to check out our other buying guides for kids, including the Best Strollers, the Best Kids Bikes, and the Best STEM Toys.
Updated November 2025: We refreshed information on all the crates, added new pictures, and added the Lovevery reading skill set box, CrunchLabs Creative Kits, Bookroo, and Enlightened Generation. We also updated links and prices.
- Best Box for All Ages KiwiCo Kiwi Crate We subscribed to Kiwi Crate's monthly subscription for so long that the company sent us a cautious email asking whether it was OK that we were getting repeat boxes. I now check in every year to discover that yes, the company's boxes are still amazing. Each box comes with a single, delightful, themed activity that's appropriate for a kid aged anywhere from a few months old to 18 years. A recent Delivery Bot ($24) aimed for 9+ years entertained my 8-year-old son for an afternoon. I can't extoll the virtues of this crate enough. The instructions are clear enough for young kids to follow. The pieces are easy for little fingers to manipulate (he did need some adult help adjusting the wheels), and the final project is always delightful: a little remote-controlled delivery bot that you can put things in and drive your sister and mother (literally) crazy! Kiwi Crate offers various gift boxes for all ages, from toddlers under 2 to teenagers. You can also select one-off boxes for specific interests, such as music, mazes, holiday crafts, and robots, or different themes, like Atlas Crates for geography or Doodle Crates for drawing. Kiwi is noted for its careful curation—the projects are fun and age-appropriate, but it doesn't break my kids' hearts when they inevitably lose or destroy them. If you're looking for just one crate, get this one and no one in your house will be disappointed.
- Best Clothing Box Stitch Fix Kids Clothes Box As my kids have gotten older, shopping for their clothes has become more and more difficult. One child has sensory issues. He hates stiff or tight fabrics, clothes that are too fuzzy, certain colors, and all jackets. The other is a budding fashionista who is on a running team and dances and needs workout clothes, baggy jeans, or whatever else happens to not be in her closet at the moment. Whenever I find a sweatshirt they will wear, Target immediately discontinues it and my cycle of living hell continues. Stitch Fix will cure what ails you, and you can start or stop your subscription as needed. You enter your child's age and size; color preferences and patterns to avoid; themes that they like; features to avoid (no crop tops); activities they like; and most importantly, budgets for every category. Stitch Fix sends you a box and you and your child keep what you like and send back the rest. I recently re-tested the box with my now-10-year-old, and both of us liked the new picks. I was able to easily get an assortment of athletic clothing for her, as well as a cloud sweater she adores. This is an easy way to update wardrobes for kids who grow out of everything instantaneously and are really hard to shop for. ★ Alternative: I also tried a box from Kidpik (starts at $100) for my now-8-year-old. Kidpik's selection is so appealing and stylish that my husband asked if the clothes came in his size. The clothes are much sturdier than the Stitch Fix selections. However, the selection is much smaller, and my son rejected half the clothes that Kidpik sent. Stitch Fix's extensive style quiz ensures that there's at least a fighting chance that your child will like any given garment.
- Best Puzzles Highlights Puzzlemania Book Club Subscription My kids are 8 and 10, and they are obsessed with puzzles of all kinds. This is great because they are at the age when they need to practice reading, and there are only so many times you can force them to reenact The Lord of the Rings trilogy. The classic children's publisher Highlights also offers a few different reading and activity boxes, in addition to the iconic magazine. My kids and I tried the I Can Read book club ($14/month) and the Puzzlemania subscription ($4/month). Puzzlemania was delightful. Each puzzle book is 32 pages and has a wide variety of puzzles, including sticker puzzles, word searches, Mad Libs–style storytelling, and riddles. We spent several afternoons filling in sticker puzzle pieces and playing the Highlights version of Sudoku. They both loved this puzzle pack so much that I bought the Highlights Great Big Book of Really Hard Puzzles ($13), which I'm anticipating will keep them occupied for at least one weekend trip or two.
- Best Science Box CrunchLabs Hack Pack This is coming with a big disclaimer: CrunchLabs, the company founded by former NASA engineer and YouTuber Mark Rober, says that its Hack Pack is for people over 14 years old. However, my 8-year-old put it together with minimal help in an afternoon, although it did take him much longer than the 60-minute estimated time for a teenager. ("Why are you so worried, Mama?" he admonished me when I showed skepticism. "The drawings show you exactly what to do.") Each box has a robot to assemble that illustrates a STEM principle, complete with a battery and an Arduino microcontroller. You can also unlock a video, but the drawings in the included manual were clear and big enough that we could put it together without the help of the internet. Our box had the infrared turret to illustrate the principle of infrared communication. My 8-year-old was thrilled, hiding it and using the infrared remote to ambush his sister with a barrage of foam darts. You can also unlock a web-based coding console to hack the robot by locking out other users. It's expensive, but the price-per-payoff valuation is worth it—the STEM principle it illustrated was interesting, the build process was engaging without being frustrating, and the project itself was very fun. ★ Alternatives: I love Mark Rober, so this is obviously the best box, but there are a ton of different science boxes. Kiwi Crate has a dedicated science crate. For much younger kids, Little Passports has an Early Explorers box ($25/month) aimed at children as young as 3. Science Expeditions is aimed at children over the age of 8; the projects are a little bizarre, like extracting the DNA from a strawberry. Neither my child nor I knew what we were supposed to do with this. Finally, a lot of people like Steve Spangler's Science Club STEM kits ($35), which are huge and come with multiple projects. These are fairly simple, like a marshmallow masher that you could Google yourself and make with stuff you probably have at home. However, I thought it was worth it to have the lesson and objects bundled so I didn't have to drink and empty a plastic soda bottle myself.
- Best Craft Kit CrunchLabs Creative Kit CrunchLabs is great, but it is aimed at older kids—my son needed a bit of help. The newly launched Creative Kit is aimed at 6- to 10-year-olds, so it's for a slightly younger demographic. I'm shocked at how well-thought-out these kits are. CrunchLabs sent the Ice Cream Stand and the Architect's Treehouse. The morning after both of the crates were assembled, both begged to get more. Even after my 8-year-old son had put together the tiny ice cream stand, he continued to play with it all afternoon. It comes with delightful little accessories, like moldable ice cream in different “flavors” (colors), little toppings, and tiny cones and cups. (I was just offered a tiny scoop of “Super Strawberry Smash.”) Unlike most tie-dye or pinwheel kits, the Creative Kit encourages play long after the craft has been completed. My 10-year-old likes these better than the Kiwi Crates because “it's like building a tiny town!”
- Best Reading Support Box Lovevery Reading Skills Support Box Now, my third-grader is a voracious reader. But it took him a few years and some hurdles to get to this point. In that time, the Reading Skill Set ($155) by Lovevery was invaluable. These books and games are a complete homeschool reading curriculum aimed at kindergarten through the second grade, but we used them as supplementary materials. Each set comes with three separate components: lovely, sturdy games; a few books; and parent course materials to explain both. The set was particularly crucial for my son during the second grade years. I particularly liked that the skill set addressed common errors and advanced vowel rules. It is really hard to remember what the letter “e” does in a word! My son found the board game to be very fun, like Chutes & Ladders but for word play. It was almost a disappointment when we realized, at the end of the summer, that he could actually read perfectly.
- Best Book Club Literati Book Club If you and your family are struggling to find reading material for your required 20 minutes of reading per day for school (that's not Wings of Fire over and over again), I highly recommend a book subscription. We paid for a Literati subscription until its curation system worked against them. Literati offers book clubs that take newborn children up to their teens. Literati will send your child five books each month. Return any books you don't like and pay Amazon's list price for the rest. Every book was a hit, and each kid had to have every book in every box. For the sake of my wallet and our already-groaning bookshelves, I had to stop the subscription. You can gift a subscription or a one-time, age-appropriate theme box with a card, personalized stickers, and artwork. It's a great way to expose your children (and yourself!) to wonderful new works of art or literature without dragging them to a bookstore. ★ Alternatives: Having to send back books your kid loves is a trap. If you want to just get and keep a book subscription, Bookroo ($20) is what you want; my son's first box just arrived with The Map Trap, of Andrew “Frindle” Clements fame, and he loves it. Also, if you or your child is bilingual, you might want to consider Curio ($58/quarterly), which currently offers themed books and audio reading guides in different age ranges for Spanish, Chinese, and French.
- Best Snack Box Universal Yums Snack Box This is the best box. And kids need to snack every day anyway, so you might as well read and learn while you're at it. My kids tear into the Universal Yums snack box like a very small pack of very tiny wolves. My colleague Louryn Strampe recommends it in her Best Snack Boxes guide and Best Subscriptions guide. You can choose a small, medium, or large box, and it includes an informative booklet, games, and trivia. Food is a great way to learn about geography and different cultures. Every month, my kids and I open the box, look at a globe, and do a lot of Googling. We have liked several foreign candies enough to start ordering them separately on Amazon. Even when the snacks aren't a hit—I got the salted truffle French fries all to myself—my kids always try them and ask a lot of questions about why a country is called the Kingdom of Butterflies and when we can visit.
- Best Coding Box Lingo Subscription Box Lingo was founded by Aisha Bowe, a former NASA scientist, and is intended to bring STEM skills to children who may have been underexposed. That description does not precisely apply to my 7-year-old, but he nevertheless enjoyed this kit. We tried In the Driver's Seat ($75), which teaches you how to build a backup sensor for a car. Mileage will vary, and the kit is technically aged for sixth to 12th graders. However, my son and I found it easy to follow along once we figured out how to log in to the Lingo portal and access all the videos on his iPad. We followed the video instructions in the portal to learn how to build circuits on a breadboard using lights and resistors, and program to turn the lights on and off. I particularly like that it doesn't purport to teach children coding via puzzle pieces or blocks but uses an actual circuit board and a real programming environment. Lingo also offers teacher support if you get stuck. However, I should note that while the kit contains all the hardware components you need to build the sensor, you will need your own iPad or laptop to access the videos and instructions.
- Best for Preschoolers Lovevery Play Kit We first received a Lovevery kit when my son was 2 years old. Now he’s 8, and I still find the company’s sturdy, Montessori-inspired toys in use around our house. Lovevery (pronounced “love-every”) promotes what it calls stage-based learning. At each stage of development, babies need different (beautiful, colorful, durable) toys to help them develop different parts of their brain. It’s pretty cute to term every stage with a different focus, like The Inspector or The Explorer, although I have to admit that I’m not so sure my son enjoyed experimenting with gravity that much more at 10 months than at a year old (he still dropped things on the floor is what I’m saying). My much older daughter also enjoyed arranging giant, gorgeous felt flowers just as much as my son did. If you’re a special person in a little one’s life and want to send them attractive and sturdy toys to pass down to others, this is the best toy subscription to get. ★ Alternative: Is your toddler going through a specific (very annoying) phase, and you need some help? Lovevery also offers parent course packs (starting at $50) to address needs like potty training or getting a new sibling. The course pack offers access to the Lovevery app, video content, toys, and books.
- Best for Babies Lalo’s Play Boxes are made for the littlest people in our lives. There are 10 different boxes of toys that are designed for different months within the first two years of a kiddo’s life, starting at the zero-to-12-month infant stage. It’s available both as a subscription or a one-off purchase of a specific developmental window, such as three to four months or 16 to 18 months, and you can add it to a registry on Babylist. The toys are beautifully made with nontoxic materials. Most of the toys I tested with my son were made of wood, like the wooden blocks he likes to knock over from the 19 to 21 month box and the drum he plays from the 13 to 15 month set. Each box comes with a little Play Guide to describe how the toy is meant to be used and to stimulate their age group. I also liked when the booklet gave tips on how to use the toys when my son got older, too. I tried out two different Lalo Play Boxes and was happy to see that my son was usually interested in at least three of the items consistently, which is pretty great for a toddler! I’m honestly jealous of how pretty some of the toys are, and regularly resist the temptation to steal the cute Stacking Rocket for my bedside table. —Nena Farrell
- Best for Artists SketchBox Art supplies—drawing, painting, pastels—are the delight of my family's life. SketchBox is a monthly box, and each month has a theme that's put together by an artist. My daughter's charcoal box was assembled by mixed media artist Nikoli Shaver and included a graphite starter kit, a small pack of media-appropriate paper, an eraser, charcoal pencils, and more. This box has an amazing value—the Nitram starter kit alone costs $16, and my 10-year-old spent several days sketching, tapping, and blending. If you're unsure of where to start with watercolor or oil pastels and find wandering Blick's aisles to be intimidating, these boxes are a great place to start. You can get a basic box for $25 or a premium one for $35, which has a higher-quality selection plus a piece of art to inspire you. ★ Alternatives: Art subscriptions are a great way to buy an assortment of materials so that you don't find yourself with 400 extra pipe cleaners on your hands. The Kids Art Box ($38) is aimed at children 3 to 7 years old. It's expensive, but five activities are quite a lot, even though I did have to hunt through my house for supplementary materials like extra paintbrushes and jars. Finally, one of my favorite boxes is the Zollie (starting at $40) craft kits. These boxes are not subscription-based, but you can order up to five kits at once. Each kit has everything you need to complete several small fiber-art projects, like embroidering flowers or knitting washcloths. My 10-year-old spent several happy afternoons looking up the QR code, watching the videos, and teaching herself how to do slip stitches and French knots.
- Best Baking Kit Bake Eat Love Baking Kit Cooking and baking subscription boxes are some of the best subscription boxes I've tried. Feeding kids every day is a chore, and I welcome any way to get some variety. Bake Eat Love is the first kit I was just as excited to try as my kids. That said, the Bake Eat Love boxes are probably best suited for an older age group, with slightly more sophisticated palates. We tried the sampler box with tiramisu cupcakes. While I love the light, fluffy texture of tiramisu and the innovative recipe, my son was perturbed to find that a cupcake he assumed was chocolate tasted more like Mommy's coffee. The kit does include a few prepackaged ingredients, but as with most cooking and baking sets, you do have to have a basic set of cooking utensils and a few ingredients that might require an extra shopping trip, like mascarpone. ★ Alternatives: I have gifted several Raddish Kids cooking club subscriptions ($24) to several nieces and nephews. The recipes are extremely easy for little kids to follow (my children particularly loved making pretzels), and the included tiny utensils are adorable and perfect for tiny hands (and for moms who just like using tiny things). We also tried Eat2Explore ($30), which was founded by a graduate of the French Culinary Institute. Each box features fun tools, nonperishable seasonings, recipe cards, and educational booklets from different countries. The salmon teriyaki was not the right pick for a child who has described fish as smelling like “stinky garbage,” but he did love using the included chopsticks. This is a fun, relatively affordable way to try to expand a kid's picky palate.
- Best Sticker Club Stickii Club My kids' appetite for stickers is endless. I find them constantly, on the mirrors in our house, on their school planners and water bottles, and occasionally stuck to the back of my chair or in the car. Stickers are also an accessible way of supporting independent artists. Maybe you can't buy a painting or a T-shirt, but a sticker only costs a few dollars and you can display it everywhere. For $12 a month, Stickii Club offers three different sticker styles—Cute, Vintage, or Pop—along with a storage sleeve and three stationery items, like a notepad, card, or stamp. The club works with independent artists and illustrators (no AI-generated art yet) to produce sheets of original designs. We tried the Pop subscription. These stickers are marvelous. There's a huge variety in the sheets sent. Some are vinyl, some are transparent, but all are high quality and intricately detailed. The artist is also noted on each corner so we can look them up ourselves. My kids were delighted and traded them with each other like currency. I am now investing in Stickii folios (from $18) in the hopes that I can keep these just a little bit more organized (and sticking a few on my laptop while I'm at it). ★ Alternative: You can't pick the style of box with a Pipsticks Kids Club sticker pack ($20), but with such a big selection, there are bound to be stickers that your child or children will love. It includes 15 sheets of Pipstickers, collectible stickers, a postcard, an activity book, and more. I have two kids who love stickers, and even we found the classic pack to be a bit much; Pipsticks also has a petite pack option for $14.

The story so far: The Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report of 2021, released by the Office of the Registrar General of India recently, showed that India has maintained its Total Fertility Rate (TFR) at 2.0 — the same as reported in 2020. While the national average for TFR has remained the same, there is a wide regional variation in TFR data for States and Union Territories (UTs) reported independently.
The highest TFR was recorded in Bihar at 3.0 and the lowest was reported for West Bengal and Delhi at 1.4. The data went on to reveal that in the decade between 2009-11 and 2019-21, TFR has been on an overall decline, in States, and nationally, albeit at different rates.

A voter going to the polls Tuesday night was more likely than not to use information from their favorite influencer than traditional news when casting their vote. According to a recent YouGov survey, nearly 65 percent of 2,000 adults surveyed say they receive their political information from digital creators.
Given that that statistic jumps to 77 percent when you isolate Gen Z, it’s unlikely to change anytime soon. On the heels of a historic Democratic wave capturing the House and Senate Tuesday, Kat Abughazaleh, who ran for an Illinois House seat earlier this year as a Democrat, and Republican strategist CJ Pearson talked about the future of influencers and algorithms at the WIRED World Fair in Miami on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has been particularly aggressive in welcoming right-wing creators into the White House. Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt opened formal press briefings to digital creators last year and hosted influencer-specific briefings during her tenure. (Leavitt’s move garnered hefty criticism for favoring softball questions, especially as the administration cracked down on the presence of more traditional media in press briefings.)
Pearson, who previously served on the RNC’s Youth Advisory Council, has been directly involved in these efforts, and points out that multiple federal agencies are now copying the White House’s playbook. He said that it’s simply the cost of getting people’s attention in the digital age.
“It’s a very chronically online administration,” he said. “With how short people’s attention spans are, you have to make [things] interesting.” Not all of the White House’s efforts have been received smoothly on the right: Pearson believes the administration’s decision to distribute portions of the Epstein files to 15 right-wing creators last year was “a misstep.”
For Abughazaleh, a former Media Matters reporter, the administration’s embrace of the internet signals something far more nefarious. Abughazaleh brought up the Department of Education’s recent use of the “Malfoid” meme—a gender-bent Harry Potter fascist figurehead—which, she said, was being promoted for a too-online audience of “incels.” And the White House’s embrace of “AI slop and brutality,” seen in ads about ICE actions, was turning “cruelty into content” rather than informing people, she says.
“They’re trying to ruin your attention span,” she said.
Abughazaleh and Pearson are pretty far apart on the political spectrum. The WIRED forum included some testy exchanges, including whether or not ICE facilities can be called “concentration camps”—a term Abughazaleh, who was arrested for protesting outside an ICE facility last year, used consistently. (The charges were dropped after allegations of misconduct by prosecutors before a grand jury.) They also skirmished over Pearson’s claim that Elon Musk had turned X into a “bastion of free speech.”
But both agreed that reliance on algorithms is increasingly creating echo chambers with young Americans of both parties.
“Algorithms show us what you want to see,” Pearson said, mentioning that his friends on the left will sometimes send him articles on political topics he simply hasn’t seen before. “The deeper question is, is that good for society or for democracy?”
On this, Abughazaleh agrees. “We have no shared reality,” she added.

2026 అక్టోబర్ చివరలో జరిగిన ఇజ్రాయెల్ ఎన్నికల్లో ప్రధానమంత్రి బెంజమిన్ నెతన్యాహు పార్టీ, దాని మిత్రపక్షాలు మొత్తం 53 సీట్లు గెలుచుకున్నాయి. అయితే, ప్రభుత్వాన్ని ఏర్పాటు చేయడానికి అవసరమైన 61 సీట్లను సాధించలేకపోయాయి. ప్రతిపక్ష పార్టీలు 48 సీట్లు గెలుచుకోగా, అరబ్ పార్టీలకు 19 సీట్లు వచ్చాయి. ఎన్నికల తర్వాత, కొత్త ప్రభుత్వాన్ని ఎవరు ఏర్పాటు చేయగలరో నిర్ణయించేందుకు అధ్యక్షుడు ఐజాక్ హెర్జోగ్ వివిధ పార్టీల నాయకులతో చర్చలు ప్రారంభించారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు అందరూ కలిసి నమాజ్ చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదనలో నిజమెంతుందో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు అందరూ కలిసి నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫ్యాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో జోర్డాన్ రాజధాని అమ్మాన్లోని జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటులో 2026 నవంబర్ 3న ఎంపీలు మధ్యాహ్నం (దుహర్) నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలను చూపిస్తుంది. ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు నమాజ్ చేసినట్లు ఎలాంటి వార్తలు లేవు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
మొదట, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటు (క్నెసెట్)లో ఇటీవల ఇలాంటి ఘటన ఏదైనా జరిగిందా అని వెతికితే, ఈ ఘటన జరిగినట్టు ఎలాంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు మాకు లభించలేదు. అంతేకాకుండా, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటు అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్ ప్రకారం, కొత్తగా ఎన్నికైన క్నెసెట్ తొలి సమావేశం 10 నవంబర్ 2026న జరగనుంది. ఈ సమావేశంలో కొత్తగా ఎన్నికైన ఎంపీలు ప్రమాణ స్వీకారం చేయడంతో పాటు, పార్లమెంటు స్పీకర్ను ఎన్నుకోనున్నారు.
తర్వాత, వైరల్ వీడియో యొక్క కీ ఫ్రేమ్లను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, అవే దృశ్యాలతో కూడిన వీడియోలు BBC News Arabic (ఇక్కడ), జోర్డాన్కు చెందిన మీడియా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ప్రచురించినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ కథనాల ప్రకారం, 3 నవంబర్ 2026న జోర్డాన్ రాజధాని అమ్మాన్లోని ప్రతినిధుల సభ (జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటు) లో ఎంపీలు మధ్యాహ్నం (దుహర్) నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు ఇవి.
ఈ కథనాల ప్రకారం, పార్లమెంటు శాశ్వత బ్యూరో సభ్యులను ఎన్నుకునేందుకు నిర్ణయించిన సమావేశానికి ముందు ఎంపీ డా. అహ్మద్ అల్-రఖబ్ నమాజ్కు నాయకత్వం వహించారు. కొన్ని మీడియా సంస్థలు ప్రచురించిన పూర్తి వీడియోలో ఆయన నమాజ్కు నాయకత్వం వహిస్తున్న దృశ్యాలను కూడా చూడవచ్చు.
అంతేకాకుండా, వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న జోర్డాన్ జాతీయ చిహ్నం (ఇక్కడ ), అలాగే జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటు లోపలి భాగానికి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు (ఇక్కడ) కూడా ఈ వీడియో జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటుకు చెందినదేనని స్పష్టం చేస్తున్నాయి.
చివరిగా, జోర్డాన్ పార్లమెంటులో ఎంపీలు నమాజ్ చేస్తున్న వీడియోను, ఇజ్రాయెల్ పార్లమెంటులో ముస్లిం ఎంపీలు నమాజ్ చేస్తున్నారని తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Google's eyewear partners can't keep a lid on its smart glasses plans
Gentle Monster shared that its “Intelligent Eyewear” will be available to pre-order on November 12.
Gentle Monster has announced its version of Google's Android XR smart glasses will launch in December, and its website says pre-orders open on November 12, the same date Warby Parker appeared to accidentally share on Thursday. Both eyewear brands, along with Samsung, are Google's partners on the project, which is set up to be both a competitor to Meta's smart glasses and a revival (of a sort) of Google Glass. Google itself has yet to confirm either date.
The Korean brand paired its announcement with a teaser of a short film directed by Jonathan Glazer, best known for Under the Skin and The Zone of Interest, and starring Joaquin Phoenix, who famously played a man who falls in love with an AI in Her. Gentle Monster says a full version of the short will be available in mid-November. The teaser suggests it'll skew much more toward experimental film than a straightforward commercial.

Google's Android XR platform is designed to power everything from the mixed reality experience on the Samsung Galaxy XR to the augmented reality one offered on the Xreal Aura. If you've been coveting one of Rocco’s smart designer minifridges, you might be interested to know the brand's biggest sale of 2026 starts today, featuring the brand-new Rocco Essential for under $1,000 and the OG Classic in this year’s new Beige colorway, as well as white and two rare blue colors, for $1,495—as low as the Classic ever gets.
Today also marks the rerelease of the Classic's Icy Blue and Royal Blue, two rarely seen colors that Rocco says are not coming back after this year.
The Essential
The Essential was just released in August and just began shipping in September; I'm currently testing it now. It's only been about a week and a half, but early impressions are positive. It has the same smart sight system as the Classic, but the biggest difference is obviously the look. Vintage-inspired fluted glass and rounded edges are out; sleek minimalism is in. The tinted dark glass door takes up the entire front, with a color-matched metal handle you can swap out for midcentury-inspired oak for an extra $95.
It's only got one temperature zone as opposed to the Classic's two, but my favorite part so far has been the interior—instead of the Classic's old-fashioned wire racks, the Essential sports smooth-glide drawers lined with a rubbery material and grip strips. This makes it much more accommodating to oddly shaped drinks, and prevents cans (it can hold up to 77) from rolling around every time you open your Rocco. It also gets colder than the Classic model—down to 34 degrees Fahrenheit instead of 37. My main frustration so far is that the sight system has been a little spotty and slow to recognize when drinks have been removed, but I'm having that problem with the Classic as well, so it's not specific to this model. All colors (Cream, Sage, Graphite) of the Essential are currently discounted.
The Classic
The handsome, vintage-inspired model is the one that started it all. Its thick steel body comes in a range of fun colors, the fluted glass refracts potentially drink-damaging light, and it comes with a color-matched metal tray so it can double as a bar cart. It's got two isolated temperature zones for red and white wine (or extra-crispy Cokes), plus five full-sized racks and one half-rack—enough for 88 cans or 27 bottles of wine. The wire racks don't pull out as smoothly as the Essential's rubber-lined drawers, but this is otherwise a top-of-the-line beverage cooler with an impressive 10-year warranty.
You can also control the interior lights from your phone. The sight system, however, is buggy—my Classic is currently displaying a rack of Dr. Pepper and Stella Artois bottles I had left over from a party in July (they were consumed not long after that), so I would not recommend buying one of these for the sight system alone. (Note this sale is on the Beige, White, Royal Blue, and Icy Blue Classic only.)
Back in Blue
I’m partial to the Classic’s forest green, but even I've got to admit the blue hues look pretty good. They sold out almost immediately around this time last year, so if you've been wanting one and you see this, I wouldn't wait to add it to your cart.

No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race
In Mississippi's too-close-to-call U.S. Senate race, every ballot matters.
But no one can say for sure how many ballots there are left to count.
The razor-thin margin between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom is shining a light on an election process in Mississippi that is among the slowest and most decentralized in the country.
"Mississippi is not a model of election administration," said Michael Morse, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies voting.
As of midday Friday, fewer than 2,000 votes separated the two Senate candidates. But information about exactly how many ballots were outstanding was hard to come by.
Loading...
The Colom campaign said late Tuesday it was aware of more than 15,000 provisional ballots, which require verification before they're counted. And the chair of the state Republican Party said Thursday he thought there were 20,000 outstanding ballots, including potential absentee votes that can legally be received by officials until Nov. 10 if they were postmarked by Election Day.
Mississippi's top voting official, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson, said counties run their own elections, and even his office didn't know how many provisionals were left to count. He said Thursday nearly 7,000 of them had been processed, with "roughly 80% of them being accepted."
"Until we have the certified results, the individual counties will be the best source of the latest and most up-to-date information," Watson said in a statement. There are 82 counties in Mississippi, and they are not required to transmit election results to the state until next week.
Morse said he was shocked by the lack of good information available for such a high-profile race.
"Right now I would love to know a lot of things about the process and I am struggling to figure out what is unfolding here," Morse said. "I cannot tell you basic things."
Mississippi has a relatively high rate of provisional ballots
What is becoming clear is that the rate of provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi, may end up being among the highest in the country this election cycle. Those ballots are cast by people whose eligibility is questionable, according to local officials, so those votes are segregated and officials decide on a case-by-case basis whether they will be counted.
If the Colom campaign's estimate of 15,000 affidavit ballots holds true, that would represent roughly 1.5% of the total ballots cast in the Senate race, according to unofficial results.
In the last midterm year, 2022, just four states had a provisional ballot rate higher than that, according to federal data. And Mississippi looks to have a provisional rate close to double of that in North Carolina this year, based on the preliminary data in both states.
One potential reason is an in-the-weeds detail on how Mississippi does voter registration.
In most states, when voters don't cast ballots over a certain number of election cycles, or local officials come across data that indicates a voter has moved or is ineligible for some other reason, they move that voter to what's known as "inactive" status. But the voter is still able to vote normally for a period of a few years, mandated by federal law, before they either confirm their eligibility or are eventually removed.
Mississippi is one of the few states that makes those "inactive" voters have to vote provisionally. That means those voters need to fill out another form and their information needs to be reviewed after the fact by local officials before their votes are counted.
It's unclear at this point why so many voters had questionable eligibility when they showed up to vote, although the local outlet Mississippi Today has reported extensively on the state's experimental use of credit data to cull voter lists.
Morse said that list maintenance technique is garnering attention, but it's not the whole story.
"It's pairing the experiment with credit data, which could introduce some unreliability, with an undermining of the typical procedural process [in many other states], where a voter [marked "inactive"] could cast a regular ballot for at least the next two federal general elections," Morse said.
Watson, the Republican secretary of state, has already come out in defense of the state's registration process.
"The extra few minutes it may take to vote via affidavit ballot are well worth the election integrity added by having cleaner voter rolls!" Watson wrote Tuesday in a post on X.
But Kathy Boockvar, the former Democratic secretary of state of Pennsylvania, told NPR that while many people who have to vote with a provisional ballot are likely to be ultimately deemed eligible, the process doesn't breed trust from those who have to interact with it.
"It feels like you have to go talk to the teacher or something in the back room," Boockvar said. "It's a little bit of a suspicious-seeming thing because somebody who's going through it generally thinks that they're eligible to vote and feels like they're being asked to do something other than that."
Boockvar added that the fact that information has been so hard to come by is a sign Mississippi hasn't been in the limelight like traditional battleground states before.
"We all have to be prepared whether we expect it or not," Boockvar said. "Transparency and good data is one of the best solutions we have to combating all the suspicion and distrust."

Tonbo Imaging swung to a consolidated net profit of ₹23.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, with operating revenue jumping over 20X YoY to ₹183.3 Cr.
Revenue growth outpaced the increase in expenses, helping the defence tech company return to profitability after losses in both the year-ago and preceding quarters.
Sequentially, Tonbo returned to the black from a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. Operating revenue rose 409% from ₹36 Cr.
Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging swung to a consolidated net profit of ₹23.5 Cr in the September quarter of FY27 from a net loss of ₹9.6 Cr in the year-ago period, supported by a sharp jump in operating revenue.
The Bengaluru-based company’s revenue from operations surged 1,963.3% YoY to ₹183.3 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹8.9 Cr in Q2 FY26.
Sequentially, Tonbo returned to the black from a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. Operating revenue rose 409% from ₹36 Cr in the preceding quarter.
Tonbo’s total expenses rose 610.5% to ₹153.7 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹21.6 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Despite the increase in spending, the revenue surge helped Tonbo post a profit before tax of ₹31.4 Cr against a pre-tax loss of ₹10.7 Cr in Q2 FY26.
Other income declined to ₹1.9 Cr from ₹2 Cr a year ago, taking total income to ₹185.2 Cr. (The story will be updated soon)

A lawyer representing LIV Golf announced the decision to shut down operations in a bankruptcy court hearing Thursday in New Jersey.
“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan. Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximising wind-down in their business,” said Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn.
LIV Golf lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after having spent more than $5 billion since 2022, which led to its filing for bankruptcy in September. A few months after the start of the Iran war, PIF changed its investment strategy in April and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.

Quick Answer
You can run AI models locally on Android and iPhone using Google AI Edge Gallery or PocketPal AI, and on Mac and Windows using LM Studio or Ollama. Simply install the app, download a compatible AI model, and start using it offline. Your data stays on your device, with no cloud access required after setup.
While many think AI is a bubble that is going to burst one day, it might be true, or it might not be at all. Only time will tell. But we should all accept that AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with our devices and do work.
For me, my life revolves around AI: I hand off some of my work to it and do things that once weren’t possible.
AI models are rapidly evolving. If you don’t know what an AI model is, it powers the apps and interfaces you interact with. For instance, the ChatGPT app uses GPT models, and the Claude app is powered by Claude models, which run behind the scenes.
While AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with devices and making work easier, handing your sensitive data to it has remained a major privacy concern.But thanks to rapid AI model development, many capable, powerful AI models enough to run locally on your device, without your data leaving your device
Companies like Google and Meta offer free AI models that can run locally on most consumer devices, including your mobile phone. Apps like Google’s AI Edge Gallery and PocketPal AI also make it easy to discover and run AI models locally without technical expertise.
If you have a capable computer with decent RAM, you can also run AI models locally to use them for writing your email, summarising PDFs, data analysis, coding, using their vision capabilities, and much more.
However, setting up an AI model locally involves downloading the app, choosing the model yourself, and understanding its capabilities first.
To help you out, I have created this detailed, comprehensive guide to set up and run local AI models on your device on Android, iPhone, Mac, or even on Windows.
I wrote this guide with beginners in mind, so every step is comprehensive and easy to follow. If you have questions, comment below. I am happy to help you. Most of these models can run locally on many consumer applications, but before that, don’t forget to check our prerequisites because that’s where your journey starts.
Table of Contents
Pre-Requirements To Run AI Models Locally on Device
Your device’s RAM determines whether it can run AI models.
Technically, a model loads into your RAM to run. As a general rule of thumb, a model needs about as much free RAM as its download size.
So, more RAM leaves room to run large AI models. A minimum of 6 GB of RAM is required to run decent, capable AI models locally on your device
Similarly, you need enough storage to download and store models locally. A model can generally range from 2 GB to 20 GB or even more, depending on its size and capabilities.
Finally, you need an internet connection and enough data to download the model so you can run it offline.
As I said before, these models can range from 2 GB to 20 GB. So it requires an internet connection to download the model and store it locally on your device.
Of course, Other minimum specifications, such as a capable Processor, Operating system, and platform, also matter but not as much as RAM does.
How to check how much RAM your device has
On Android:
Go to About Device to see how much RAM your smartphone has. To do that: Open Settings on your device, tap on the search bar at the top, and search for “About Device”. On some phones, scroll down and tap “About Device”. Look at the RAM specifications.
On some phones, you will see extra visible RAM after the plus sign, for example, 16GB + 12GB. However, only the first number is the real memory.
iPhone:
Apple generally doesn’t disclose the RAM used in iPhones. However, iPhone 15 Pro and newer devices generally have at least 8GB, while older iPhones have less than 6GB, which can run 1 billion to 2 billion models. You can check how much RAM your iPhone has from here.
Mac:
To check how much RAM on your MacBook: From the home screen, click on the Apple icon in the top left corner screen and tap on About This Mac. From here, you can check chip and memory options. Apple MacBooks running on Apple Silicon are especially good for running local AI models since the graphics chip shares all the memory.
Windows:
On Windows, you can go to Settings > System > About. From there, check the installed RAM, graphics card, and system type (x86 or ARM-based), which determines which applications you can download to run AI models locally.
Once your device meets the minimum RAM requirement, follow these steps to set it up to run AI models locally. Use the table of contents above to go to the device you want to set up. This guide covers Android, iPhone, Mac, and Windows.
How to Run AI Models Locally on Any Device
Android:
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on Android with Google AI Edge Gallery
You can run Google’s family of Open-weight AI models locally for free on your Android device using Google’s own AI Edge Gallery app (Free).
Gemma 4 is Google’s latest open-weight model. It comes in five model sizes. Gemma 4 E2B and Gemma 4 E4B are suitable for running on Android devices. 2B requires at least 8GB of RAM, and 4B requires at least 12GB of RAM.
Gemma 4 also supports vision capabilities, so it is not just text; you can also use it to understand images.
How to install and run the latest Google Gemma 4 models locally on your Android phone
Step 1: Download Google AI Edge Gallery from the Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI Chat.
Step 3: Under the recommended models, tap Download below. To download the model you want. Gemma 4 E2B is 2.6 GB and best for starters, while Gemma 4 E4B is 3.7 GB and smarter, but your phone needs at least 8 GB of RAM to run it locally.
Step 3: Once the model is downloaded, tap Try it.
Step 4: Type your prompt in the Type prompt box and tap the send button.
Step 5: Like the other AI apps, the model replies to your prompt. You can also see how fast the model runs, measured in tokens per second, and how much RAM it uses. On my Android phone, the Gemma 4 E2B model ran at about 30 tokens per second, and my model comes with 16 GB of RAM.
Method 2: Run any open model on Android with PocketPal AI
PocketPal is a popular free and open-source app for running AI models locally on Android.
Unlike Google’s AI Edge Gallery, it supports a wide variety of third-party models, including Google’s Gemma, Meta’s Llama, Microsoft’s Phi, Qwen, and more. It also supports GGUF models, including compressed versions.
How do I use the PocketPal app to run AI models locally on my device?
Step 1: Download and install the PocketPal app from the Google Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and, during onboarding, tap Download Model.
Step 3: Pick any available model to download and tap Download,
or tap the plus option to find more. To get a new model, tap the plus icon, select Hugging Face, then tap Choose and add from Hugging Face.
Step 4: From here, you can search for any model. In this case, I searched for the Qwen3 1.7B parameter model and tapped the download icon to download it locally.
Step 5: Once done, open the Models tab and select the model to load it. Now go to the chat interface and enter the prompt, and the model uses the model that you have loaded, in this case, the Qwen3 1.7 billion parameter model, to answer your queries. You can also see how much time it takes to run this model on your device.
iPhone
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on iPhone with Google AI Edge Gallery
Google’s AI Edge Gallery is also available on iPhone and supports the latest Gemma 4 family of open-weight models, similar to Android. You can download and use E2B (around 2.6 GB) and the E4B model (around 3.7 GB).
Apple doesn’t disclose the RAM used on iPhones. However, the latest iPhone models, including the iPhone 15 Pro and later, support up to 8 GB of RAM, which can run these models faster and more reliably. However, older iPhones may struggle with slow responses, battery drain, and overheating, so keep that in mind.
Step 1: Download the Google AI Edge Gallery app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI chat
Step 3: Now download the compatible AI model. In this case, I’m downloading Gemma 4 E2B, which is about 2.59 GB. Click on the download icon under the model.
Step 4: Wait for the model to download, then tap Try It, enter the prompt, and wait for a reply. If you want to use the vision capabilities, tap on the plus icon and upload an image
Method 2: Run open models on iPhone with PocketPal AI
Similar to Google’s AI Edge Gallery app, the PocketPal app is also available on iPhone. It also gives access to some of the popular Hugging Face model library and other third-party models, including models from Meta, Cohere, and more. It also supports Google Gemma 4 models.
Step 1: Install the PocketPal AI app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app, tap Download Model, select a model, and tap Download. In this case, I am downloading the Qwen3 1.7B model.
Step 3: Once downloaded, tap the Load option at the top, enter the prompt, and wait for the reply
Mac
Method 1: Run AI models on a Mac with LM Studio
You can use LM Studio on Mac to run AI models locally.
It supports a wide range of models, including models from Google Gemma, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, and more. Like the mobile app, you can install LM Studio on your Mac, download a model, and start chatting. It also supports GGUF and Apple-optimized MLX models.
Depending on the model, you can have text conversations, image analysis, and more. You can also use it as a local API for other apps.
However, LM Studio is only available on Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
How to install and run AI models locally using LM Studio on Mac
Step 1: First, go to lmstudio.ai/download and download the LM Studio app for Mac. Select the compatible version and drag and drop LM Studio into Applications to install it.
Step 2: Open LM Studio on the Mac, click on the model search in the sidebar, and search for the model; for example, in this case, I searched for the Gemma 4 E4B model

Method 2: Run AI models on a Mac with Ollama
You can also run AI models on your Mac using Ollama. It is a free, lightweight tool by Meta that lets you run local AI models in the terminal with one command. It also works with many local apps that support local AI.
Step 1: To run Ollama locally on your device, go to ollama.com/download and click on the Download manually option. You can also directly paste the command into the terminal if you are a developer.

Step 4: Next, to run ollama run llama3, copy the ollama run llama3 command, open Terminal, and paste it. Wait for the model to download completely. A bomb threat email sent to the Bombay High Court also threatened the Bombay Stock Exchange, Mahalaxmi Racecourse and actor Amitabh Bachchan's residence, Jalsa, triggering a security alert in Mumbai, NDTV reported.
Police and security agencies are investigating the email to identify the sender.
Amitabh Bachchan had received a similar threat email earlier on October 23. The message, which was also sent to Mumbai Mayor Ritu Tawde and Deputy Mayor Sanjay Ghadi, warned of a grenade attack at a school on October 31 and threatened to target the actor’s Juhu residence between October 31 and November 27.
The email, which referred to Khalistan, also threatened an attack during singer Diljit Dosanjh’s November 27 concert in the Mahalaxmi Racecourse area.
Following the threat, the 84-year-old actor changed his customary Sunday interaction with fans outside his residence. Bachchan greeted the gathering from behind a transparent bulletproof enclosure installed on an elevated platform.
