As Democrats blew away their Republican rivals in an unprecedented midterm sweep Tuesday, the Make America Health Again movement also got bowled over, raising questions about the fate of the motley movement.
MAHA—which has centered around anti-vaccine activist and current Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—saw many of its favored candidates and allies lose, while vocal adversaries of Kennedy won. And the coalition was splintering under stress even before the voting started; in recent months, supporters have accused Kennedy and the Trump administration of inaction and betrayals in their two years in power.
Now hobbled in Washington, shedding supporters, and showing little to no influence in voting booths, is MAHA on its deathbed? Or will it be reborn—possibly into a new group? Could it be assimilated into a blue platform—after sloughing off the more repulsive, conspiratorial aspects of Kennedy’s ideology? These are the questions circling in the aftermath of Tuesday’s bloodbath.
In a social media poll Wednesday afternoon, Mary Talley Bowden—a dejected MAHA activist, anti-vaccine advocate, and doctor reprimanded for prescribing ivermectin to treat COVID-19—polled her followers about what should come next. She offered three options: Start a third party, join the Democrats, or overthrow the GOP. As of publication time, joining Democrats trailed at just 3 percent of the votes. The remaining votes were roughly split between overthrowing the GOP—whatever that means—and forming a third party, which had a small lead at 49 percent.
Cracking coalition
That MAHA could fade out entirely or fracture into negligible shards seems like a very real possibility. Its collection of disparate groups and varied agenda items has always made its cohesiveness seem tenuous. A Politico poll in June revealed that people who identified as MAHA had different ideas of what the movement’s priorities are (or should be), as well as different political leanings, and sometimes opposing ideologies.
Some within the movement embrace (or at least accept) Kennedy’s fringe beliefs, such as his zealous anti-vaccine views, his rejection of germ theory, and his false claim that 5G is damaging our brains and causing cancer. Some also believe, like Kennedy, in chemtrails and want all mRNA vaccines banned. There are members who support his plan to ban water fluoridation and also seem fine with his false claim that Lyme disease was created by the US military as a military weapon.
Others, meanwhile, have been attracted to MAHA by the more reasonable, non-absurd issues Kennedy touts. Those include improving the quality of Americans’ food and diets, reducing their exposure to environmental contaminants, and limiting the influence of industry and corporate interests on Americans’ health, particularly limiting the sway of pharmaceutical and chemical companies.
With various priorities, Kennedy and MAHA leaders have spent the past two years finding ways to disappoint their members. Some like Bowdon are angered that Kennedy has yet to ban mRNA vaccines. In February, Kennedy sparked particularly intense backlash among supporters for embracing Trump’s decision to increase domestic production of the pesticide glyphosate—a pesticide many in the MAHA movement wanted banned. Kennedy further fueled feelings of betrayal in September by appearing at a MAHA-branded summit that had hefty corporate sponsorships, including from behemoths such as Walmart, Anthropic, OpenAI, Grail, and UnitedHealth.
“MAHA was supposed to expose the revolving door between money, industry and government, not build its own,” Robert Malone, a fringe scientist and previous Kennedy ally, wrote in a scathing response to the summit.
Signs of dying
Going into the midterms on Tuesday, the number of disenchanted MAHA members had mounted. In October, Tiffany Cianci, a former Kennedy supporter, published a MAHA scorecard, which lists 42 promises that Kennedy and leaders made to the MAHA members and then largely broke. The scorecard reports 37 promises broken, five partially fulfilled, and zero kept. One of the “partially kept” promises was removing synthetic dyes from foods, particularly children’s foods. Kennedy announced an effort to do that—with much ballyhoo—but later admitted that the FDA did not ban or even have an agreement with food companies to remove the dyes. Instead, Kennedy said he has an “understanding” with food companies. The dyes remain in foods.
In a press release, Cianci wrote that the scorecard revealed “an abysmal string of broken commitments and betrayals.” It also contained a direct quote from her, saying: “I believed deeply in the promise that MAHA represented, particularly the possibility of confronting chronic disease and building a healthier future for America’s children. But belief was never supposed to mean blind loyalty.”
The press release included quotes from several other prominent MAHA leaders, all expressing disappointment with Kennedy and the Trump administration. Later in October, Calley Means, a top ally and senior advisor to Kennedy, resigned from his position, reportedly “disillusioned” and frustrated by delays in food policy changes sought by MAHA.
Another prominent figure to fall out with Kennedy was Vani Hari, an online influencer who goes by “food babe” and has previously identified as a “MAHA Mom.” As voting results were streaming in Tuesday night, Hari posted a comment on social media that she had given Politico months earlier, saying: “Women don’t come out to vote for glyphosate and war,” referring to the pesticide Kennedy had embraced and the Iran war.
Midterm devastation
In the wake of the blue sweep, it’s clear that more than half of the 24 MAHA-endorsed candidates lost their races Tuesday. That includes Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Texas and Zach Lahn, who ran for governor of Iowa. Lahn in particular was considered a “dream MAHA candidate,” and his campaign was seen as a test of MAHA’s political influence. Kennedy himself headlined a political rally for Lahn last week, calling it “the most important election going on in this country.” Lahn lost to his Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, who flipped the seat with an 11-point spread, turning the office blue for the first time in 20 years.
Alex Clark Voetberg, who hosts a wellness podcast called Culture Apothecary for Turning Point USA, echoed Hari, pointing to the glyphosate betrayal as a reason for the defeats. “MAHA moms stayed home and it could’ve swayed some of these races that were unbearably close. Should’ve listened to our warnings on protecting glyphosate—but you needed Bayer for the war,” Clark Voetberg wrote on social media.
Otherwise, MAHA also lost allies, such as Senator Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who founded a MAHA caucus in the Senate. Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) lost his seat in the House despite reports that Kennedy allegedly intervened in the race to help him win. Meanwhile, critics of Kennedy notched wins, including Representative-elect Richard Pan, a physician from California; Senator-elect Annie Andrews, a pediatrician from South Carolina; and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist with a medical degree from Michigan.
Many congressional Democrats are already raring to hold Kennedy to account and remove him—and several of the newcomers are eager to help make it happen. In August, Andrews laid out her plans for health priorities to South Carolina Democrats, saying, “I believe we need to fully fund the CDC and the NIH, and I believe we need to impeach and remove RFK Jr.”
On Wednesday afternoon, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) wrote on social media: “The time is now. RFK Jr. must resign or be fired. End of discussion.”
MAHA and Kennedy
If Kennedy is removed from office, the outlook for MAHA in its current form seems even murkier. On the one hand, Kennedy’s removal may make it easier for those in the movement to shed the divisive, abhorrent aspects of his ideology and focus on broadly popular issues—healthy foods, environmental contaminants, and industry influence. Such a move may help MAHA cement itself as a sustainable political fixture. But some of the most vocal figures in the MAHA realm are doggedly loyal to Kennedy, throwing such a transition into doubt.
Zen Honeycutt, an anti-vaccine activist and founder of Moms Across America, is one of those Kennedy loyalists. Honeycutt drew attention before the election for reaching out to Democrats on common causes. Her group endorsed several blue candidates, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, and Rep. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire (all of them won their races).
“We expect Democrats and Republicans to work together,” Honeycutt told Politico earlier this month. “Health is not a political issue. You know, poison is not partisan. Cancer is not choosy.”
The sensible comment might suggest Honeycutt doesn’t care which party or politician follows through with MAHA’s goals, just as long as they’re achieved. But this is not actually Honeycutt’s position. Her intentions were made clear in exchanges on social media with Bowden, who harshly criticized Honeycutt for crossing party lines, particularly for talking with Ocasio-Cortez. “You understand she’s trying to use you?” Bowden wrote.
Honeycutt explained that she was working to smooth Kennedy’s path in Washington, not hand power to Democrats, who she said had been “fascist in mandating vaccines.” She instead turned the criticism to Bowden, saying the MAHA infighting and mudslinging was what was hurting the cause and handing Democrats wins.
On Wednesday, Honeycutt reaffirmed her allegiance to Kennedy, warning Democrats that impeaching him would be “extremely unwise.” She reposted a comment from one of her followers, writing: “I’m willing to give Dems a chance with their new power before I judge. I’m an independent. Kennedy is my red line. If they cross it I want them to get absolutely fucked in 2028.”
Still, there are some inklings that part of MAHA could be absorbed into blue platforms—whether the leaders of the movement in its current form like it or not.
Earlier this month, Brinda Adhikari, a journalist and co-host of the podcast Why Should I Trust You?, argued that MAHA wasn’t dying but remaking the Democratic Party to be more like its old self. In a Substack post titled How MAHA Is Making Democrats Democrats Again, Adhikari pointed to a health policy document from House Democrats with a section, led by Ocasio-Cortez, titled “Reclaiming MAHA and Protecting American Families.”
Adhikari wrote that some of the issues touted by MAHA are a natural fit for the Democratic Party. She stretched back to Rachel Carson’s seminal Silent Spring in 1962 and the progressive environmental activism that elevated issues of health, pesticides, toxic chemicals, and corporate influence over public health. “These were once bread-and-butter Democratic issues,” Adhikari wrote. “But somewhere along the way, Democrats lost some of their identity as the party leading these fights.”
Adhikari and Democrats credit Kennedy with redirecting attention to these issues, which have broad support among voters.
“Americans’ concerns about chronic disease and food safety, especially that which is linked to corporate influence over environmental regulation and public health, are legitimate and long overdue for a serious legislative response,” the House Democrat’s policy document reads. “The Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has galvanized a significant segment of the Republican Party and attracted many previously apolitical and non-traditional voters, yet many of the concerns raised by the movement are bipartisan in nature.”
A KFF poll in May found that 75 percent of Americans want stricter regulations on food additives—a prominent MAHA priority—and 64 percent want stricter regulation of pesticides in agriculture, another key MAHA agenda item.
But Kennedy and the Trump administration have not only failed to deliver on these issues, but they have also spoiled the movement, using “the legitimate concerns of American consumers about food safety to spread misinformation about vaccines, public health, and science,” the policy document reads. “Their rhetoric has systematically led to the erosion of trust in public health, the science community, and decreased vaccination rates, leading to fatal outbreaks in some cases.”
Possible political shift
Democrats intend to reclaim the popular health and environmental issues, free of Kennedy’s corrosive anti-science rhetoric. The document outlines plans to restore regulations that protect clean water and air damaged by the Trump administration, advance policies to keep toxic substances out of food, and further Food is Medicine policies, which provide produce prescriptions to American families to improve nutrition and health.
Adhikari predicts a political shift. “I increasingly think MAHA’s most unexpected legacy may be pushing Democrats back toward their own roots: challenging corporate power, fighting dangerous chemicals in our food supply, and holding toxic polluters accountable,” she wrote.
MAHA leaders tied to Kennedy and the anti-vaccine movement, like Bowden and Honeycutt, are unlikely to get behind such a shift. This could cause MAHA’s political power—however strong it actually is—to fracture. MAHA leaders have claimed repeatedly that their followers have the ability to sway elections. If MAHA hadn’t been betrayed or at least disappointed by Kennedy and Trump in the last two years, MAHA could have prevented Tuesday’s Republican wipeout, they have said.
But the polling data doesn’t support the idea that keeping MAHA in its current form maximizes its political power. While MAHA does have significant support among voters—41 percent of US adults say they support MAHA—that support is primarily tied to the health, environmental, and food safety issues, which are popular among non-MAHA supporters, too. Further, just 4 percent of MAHA supporters cited vaccines and medical choice—Kennedy’s key issues—as their reason for supporting the movement, the KFF poll revealed.
Beyond MAHA’s primary issues, both voters overall and MAHA supporters specifically said MAHA issues weren’t top of mind this election; instead, both groups named the cost of healthcare as a bigger issue than those prioritized by MAHA (the MAHA movement is not associated with the issue of health care reform). A separate KFF poll on election day found that 50 percent of voters thought that the Democratic Party was better able to handle healthcare, while only 30 percent of voters said the same of the Republican Party.
For now, it’s unclear exactly how—or if—MAHA will influence the political landscape going forward. It could break apart, live on through revamped Democratic policies, or try to form a new political party entirely. And, apparently, there’s also the possibility it will try to overthrow the GOP.
Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes.

Indian drug regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical Industries to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in its quality management system, documents reviewed by Reuters showed.
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the office of Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown on August 20 after a joint federal-state inspection of the facility identified lapses in the system meant to ensure product quality and safety, following Sun Pharma’s move in July to voluntarily recall about 11 eye-care brands.
India’s drug quality standards have come under increased scrutiny at home and overseas in recent years after locally made cough syrups were linked to the deaths of children in India and also in countries including Gambia and Uzbekistan.
The regulatory agencies’ move marks an escalation of the action against Sun Pharma, India’s biggest pharmaceutical firm, which will be unable to continue ophthalmic drug production at the Assam factory until it submits a satisfactory compliance report. Sun Pharma said previously the site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing hubs for sterile products in a business identified as a key global growth driver.
The regulator sought more information on the recall of 332 batches of ophthalmic suspension products — liquids used to treat eye conditions — the documents showed.
In an internal notice sent to stockists at the time, the company said it was withdrawing the products as a “precautionary measure.” It remains unclear whether all of the recalled products were contaminated.
Sun Pharma did not publicly disclose details of the recall.
The company has submitted a compliance report in response to the order, which is being reviewed by the regulator, an official familiar with the matter told Reuters on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
“We voluntarily initiated a temporary cessation of manufacturing activities and informed the regulators,” Sun Pharma said in a statement on Friday (October 30, 2026), adding that remedial measures have been put in place.
It did not respond to a request for comment on the recall. The company says on its website it follows a single global quality standard.
Recall could involve hundreds of thousands of bottles
Some of the recalled products included Lotepred 1% 5ml eye drops, Nepalact OD eye drops, Nepalact-Z, Brinzotim eye drops 5ml and Depopred 2ml. The eye drops are used to treat eye inflammation, infections and chronic eye diseases, according to doctors.
It is unclear whether these eye products were exported from India or whether any patients reported any adverse effects.
Reuters found that, based on the product packaging, most of the recalled products were manufactured at the Assam state facility in Kokjhar village. Reuters could not independently verify whether the 332 batches cited by regulators were related only to the 11 identified brands in the recall notice or included additional brands.
The affected batches could translate into hundreds of thousands of eye-drop bottles, according to industry experts, who declined to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
Ophthalmology contributes about 3% of Sun Pharma’s domestic revenue, according to its 2025-26 annual report. It is also one of its key areas for the U.S.
The company reported a drop in second-quarter profit on Friday (October 30) weighed down by a one-time charge related to its acquisition of U.S.-based Organon.
The eye product recall coincided with a patient-safety advisory issued in June by the All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS), an independent body of eye specialists, warning that certain batches of Predmet eye drops appeared to be contaminated.
“There were some adverse cases of infections reported in patients who used Predmet and we got sealed bottles investigated and found it was contaminated,” Santosh Honavar, a doctor and secretary of AIOS, told Reuters, adding that Sun Pharma had also recalled those Predmet drops.
Sun Pharma did not respond a request for comment on the AIOS advisory.
The regulators issued a show-cause notice to Sun Pharma on August 10, citing the quality management system failures, the documents showed.
Dissatisfied with the company’s response, the regulators ordered a halt to the manufacturing, sale and distribution of all ophthalmic products from the facility.
Indian regulators did not respond to requests for comment. The agency did not issue a public health alert after the recall.
It is not the first time Sun Pharma’s sterile manufacturing facilities have faced regulatory scrutiny. Last year, the U.S. FDA halted the company’s shipments from Gujarat’s Halol plant after inspectors cited shortcomings in contamination controls.

Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material
Thomas Wayne Markle was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida
WARNING: This article contains details of abuse.
The father of Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, was arrested Friday morning by U.S. federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material.
Thomas Wayne Markle, 82, of Lakeland, Fla., is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for Central District of California.
In a statement, it said Markle was arrested on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.
It says agents seized approximately 78 items, including two images that depict an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle — with a nude prepubescent girl.
"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," said FBI Director Kash Patel in a statement, indicating the FBI is still investigating this matter.
Patel also thanked FBI partners in Mexico, Manila and the Marshall Islands law enforcement attachés, who aided the investigation.
This image taken on Sunday shows the entrance to a storage facility where Mexican authorities seized a storage unit with belongings of Thomas Markle during a search for alleged child sexual abuse material, on the outskirts of Tijuana, Mexico. (Guillermo Arias/AFP/Getty Images)
Thomas Markle Jr. involvement
The statement from the U.S. Attorney's Office appears to confirm reports by the Sun, a British tabloid, that Meghan's half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father's home in the Philippines.
"According to an affidavit filed with the complaint, in October 2026, law enforcement learned that an individual signed an affidavit regarding their discovery of suspected [child sexual abuse material] among Markle's possessions in the Philippines," the statement said. "Information from the first individual later led agents to a second unit."
Philippine Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla told reporters on Friday that Thomas Markle Jr. is also being investigated.
"We have a witness saying that underage girls were being brought to his house and we're following it up. We are looking into whether the 60-year-old son, Thomas Markle Jr., was involved in the crime," said Remulla. "To accuse the father is only half the police work."
Thomas Markle Sr. was not at his daughter Meghan's wedding to Prince Harry in 2018. (Phil Noble/Reuters)
Meghan estranged from father
There was no immediate comment from Meghan's representatives on Friday.
Meghan Markle recently said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said of the letter.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama Suits, married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.
Thomas Markle is expected to appear in a Tampa court on Friday.
If convicted, he would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.
If you're in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a real incident of a girl being kidnapped while walking along a road in Bihar. In the video, a group of men travelling in a Bolero vehicle with a covered number plate is seen abducting the girl. She attempts to break free from their clutches, while a passing motorcyclist who records the incident can be seen trying to stop the kidnappers. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a real incident of a girl being kidnapped by men in a car while walking along a road in Bihar.
Fact: The video is scripted and does not show an actual kidnapping in Bihar. Muklesur Ali, who creates videos with Isa Stunt, confirmed to NewsChecker that the incident was scripted and that all the people seen in the video were members of his team. The Instagram and YouTube accounts associated with them also feature similar staged videos created for entertainment purposes. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an Instagram post uploaded by an account named ‘Isa Stunt’ on 11 October 2026, featuring the same video (archived). However, unlike the viral clip, this version had no audio and instead featured background music. Further, the accompanying caption provided no specific information about the incident.
Upon reviewing the Instagram account, we found several other videos similar to the viral clip. Many of these videos (here, here, and here) featured the same Bolero vehicle, motorcycle, and man seen in the video of the alleged kidnapping and scuffle. This suggests that the videos may be staged and do not depict actual incidents.
We also found a YouTube channel linked in the bio of the Instagram account ‘Isa Stunt’, which featured several videos similar to the viral clip, depicting incidents such as a girl’s kidnapping, a street assault, and a road accident. However, the video descriptions and the channel’s bio stated that the content was created for entertainment purposes.
We also noticed an Instagram account named ‘Muklesur Ali’, which was tagged in several videos (here, here, and here) posted on the ‘Isa Stunt’ account. Upon reviewing Muklesur Ali’s account, we found several videos similar to the viral clip, including a video depicting a similar staged kidnapping. We have previously debunked (here, here, and here) several videos created by Muklesur Ali that went viral on social media and were shared as depicting real incidents. This further suggests that the viral video is staged and was created for entertainment purposes rather than documenting an actual kidnapping.
NewsChecker reached out to Muklesur Ali, who told them that he and Isa create scripted videos as a team. He confirmed that the viral video depicting the girl’s kidnapping was also scripted and that all the people seen in it were members of his team.
To sum up, this viral video of a girl being kidnapped on a road in Bihar is scripted and does not show a real incident.

Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those investments replaced with shares of a thinly traded Chinese microcap. Nearly 30 investors say their portfolios were altered without consent on October 15. Their established US stock holdings were allegedly liquidated and the proceeds used to buy Nasdaq-listed Zhibao Technology shares. One investor told Moneycontrol that securities worth $3.1 Mn, or around ₹29 Cr, were sold within two minutes, followed by purchases of 30.5 Lakh Zhibao shares within 15 minutes. Another reported that holdings worth $335,768 were sold and 3 Lakh Zhibao shares purchased. Media reports put investor-reported losses above ₹100 Cr. Inc42 has not independently verified this aggregate or authenticated the investors’ account details and alleged transactions. An FIR has reportedly been registered in Bengaluru. The dispute now centres on how the accounts were accessed, whether safeguards failed, and who bears responsibility across Stockal, its parent Borderless Investing, and US brokerage partner DriveWealth. How The Trades Unfolded Founded in 2016 by Sitashwa Srivastava and Vinay Bharathwaj, Stockal enables Indians to invest overseas through US stocks, exchange-traded funds, and curated portfolios. It has raised over $15 Mn from investors like ScaleX Partners, Arc Ventures, July Ventures, HDFC Securities, and Cadenza Ventures. The startup partners with DriveWealth to facilitate US stock investments. Bharathwaj left Borderless in 2022 and is currently the founder and CEO of “AI-first money intelligence and advisory platform” Cruise Money, as per his LinkedIn profile. Investors allege the October 15 transactions replaced holdings in companies including Alphabet and AMD with Zhibao shares, leaving them exposed to a thinly traded microcap. Borderless said DriveWealth notified it on October 16, India time, of suspicious trading across 13 accounts. Its assessment indicated an unauthorised third party had accessed 26 accounts using valid login credentials. In 13 accounts, large-cap US equities were liquidated to acquire thinly traded microcap securities. Borderless said it restricted access shortly after receiving the notification. An investor told Moneycontrol that Borderless contacted him on October 18, acknowledged suspicious activity, and said DriveWealth had restricted transactions in his account. Zhibao’s subsequent decline deepened investors’ reported losses. Against an average purchase price of around $1.05 cited in investor accounts, the shares closed at $0.42 on October 23 — a fall of approximately 60%. Differing Accounts Of Access In an October 30 letter to an investor, DriveWealth reportedly said the unauthorised access occurred through the Stockal interface and attributed responsibility for associated security lapses to Stockal. It reportedly said it froze the account on Stockal’s instructions. Responding to Inc42’s questions, DriveWealth said, “The Stockal incident is unrelated to DriveWealth’s systems. It occurred on Stockal’s app, not our platform. DriveWealth does not have a customer-facing app through which trades are placed, and our systems and client data were not affected by this incident.” Borderless’s public statement offered a possible explanation – social engineering involving information exposed in another company’s data breach several weeks earlier. It stressed that this connection remained unverified and under investigation. Borderless said its investigation found no evidence of a breach or compromise of its platform, interface, infrastructure, or internal systems. It also said no funds were withdrawn from affected accounts, based on findings available so far. This distinction leaves the disputed trades themselves central to investors’ concerns – their allegation concerns changes to their holdings without consent, irrespective of whether money left the accounts. Safeguards Under The Spotlight The precise access method remains under investigation. However, the incident raises questions about whether possession of valid credentials could have been sufficient to execute the disputed trades. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of cybersecurity firm Security Brigade, told Inc42 that stolen credentials are a common entry point, but platforms cannot shift responsibility entirely to customers when compromised passwords enable financial transactions. He said layered safeguards should include two-factor authentication, SIM binding, device and geographical checks, and separate transaction-level authentication. Behavioural monitoring is also critical. Multiple accounts accessed from one IP address, or similar trading patterns across accounts within a short period, should trigger scrutiny, he said. Such monitoring could explain DriveWealth’s detection of suspicious activity, Kadakia suggested, although the actual detection mechanism remains unclear. He added that implementation and enforcement remain challenges despite stronger SEBI cybersecurity requirements for regulated entities. Borderless Sets Out Its Position Borderless said it had engaged independent cybersecurity specialists, introduced additional authentication and account-protection measures, and found no evidence of a wider threat to its platform, products, or other customer accounts. It maintained that unauthorised trading identified so far was restricted to 13 accounts. The company said it had been engaging affected customers and working with DriveWealth to reconstruct events, examine disputed transactions, and explore avenues for a fair resolution. However, it said assistance should not be construed as an admission of liability, negligence, wrongdoing, or responsibility. It said it was cooperating with authorities and regulators. Borderless also maintained it had provided substantive responses to media enquiries before publication and cautioned that its public account could change as the investigation progressed. Inc42 has separately sought answers on the transactions, investigation, and investor concerns. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Who Bears The Responsibility? The controversy has also drawn attention to Stockal’s former partnership with HDFC Securities. Launched in 2019 through globalinvesting.in, their operational association ended in July 2024. HDFC Securities has clarified that it is not named among the accused in the FIR and said it would cooperate with regulators and law enforcement authorities. While HDFC Securities has clarified its position, questions about the disputed trades remain unresolved. How were the accounts accessed, why were the transactions not intercepted, and what recourse do affected investors have to restore their holdings or recover losses? Cross-border investing divides responsibilities across the customer interface, trade execution, and custody of securities. Establishing each intermediary’s obligations and the safeguards applied will be central to determining accountability. For affected investors, the immediate issue remains whether the investigation will explain the disputed trades and deliver a resolution. For now, neither the source of the alleged compromise nor responsibility for the claimed losses has been conclusively established. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

If the vote to impeach Hegseth passes in the House, the Senate must then vote to either acquit or convict Hegseth on the articles of impeachment. Under the Constitution, convicting and removing a public official from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
Shortly after Election Day, a rumor spread that U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., planned to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in response to the Democrats' outsize victories in the 2026 midterms — which were widely seen as a rebuke of President Donald Trump's policies, particularly his war in Iran.
The rumor circulated on X and Facebook. Snopes readers searched the website for information on a possible Hegseth impeachment trial.
In short, the claim is true. It originated with a CNN article titled "Republicans quickly turn against Pete Hegseth after midterms rout." Here's what the story said about Massie (emphasis ours): 
House Republicans are expected to vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the famously anti-Trump GOP lawmaker, told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week — and multiple GOP sources said they expect it to pass.
Massie then referenced CNN's reporting in a Nov. 4 X post (archived) that confirmed he planned to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth. (Massie previously forced a vote on impeaching Hegseth in September, which failed.)
"There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said on his official X account, which has a gray checkmark badge verifying that it authentically represents a government official.
Snopes has not independently verified CNN's report that at least some Republicans believe Massie's impeachment articles against Hegseth will pass.
The House passes impeachment articles through a simple majority. The Senate must then vote on whether to convict Hegseth on those articles of impeachment before he would be removed from office — and the Constitution requires a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate to convict.
Congress has never successfully removed a Cabinet member from office under the impeachment process.
After several news outlets reported that Hegseth did not intend to step down and that Trump was showing support for him — at least publicly — Massie said in a Nov. 5 X post that his impeachment resolution was a "much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress."
(While Democrats won majorities in both congressional chambers, they won't actually take control of the Senate and House of Representatives until the new members are sworn in in January.)
Following Massie's Nov. 5 post, Hegseth shared a video that same day calling Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" who, alongside Democratic allies, "dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly" (at 4:12).
In the video, Hegseth compared the impeachment efforts against him to lawmakers' previous attempts to impeach Trump.
"It's all about the politics of personal destruction," he said. "Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."

In 1904, two scientists, Henry Wheeler and Treat Johnson, synthesised a variant of cytosine, one of the building blocks of DNA, in the laboratory.
The variant they synthesised contained a chemical tag called a methyl group (-CH3) attached to cytosine, so they called it 5-methylcytosine. Their motivation for doing so was based on the observation that two other building blocks of DNA and its chemical cousin RNA, called thymine and uracil, differed only by the presence of a methyl group.
So Wheeler and Johnson figured that a methylated version of cytosine might also exist in nature.
In 1925, Johnson, while working with another scientist named Robert Coghill, finally discovered 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Two more decades later, Rollin Hotchkiss found 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of cows. Soon, scientists found that it existed in nearly all animals.
However, nobody knew why it existed — or why some of the cytosines in DNA were methylated while others were not.
Genes on and off
That insight came in 1975, when Robin Holliday and John Pugh proposed that the methylation of the cytosine could be a way for the body to use the information stored in DNA.
DNA is segmented into genes, and each gene contains the information necessary to make a particular protein. These proteins perform their specific functions in the cells. Since every cell in the body has two copies — one from each parent — of all human DNA, all cells technically have the blueprint to make a whole organism.
However, cells also have specialised functions. A brain cell will not need the genes for the proteins used to digest food. So Holliday and Pugh suggested that chemical modifications such as the methylation of cytosine could help establish and activate genes that a cell wants while silencing those it does not.
This idea, that cells could use chemical tags on DNA to control which genes were active, has come to be called epigenetics. (The British biologist Conrad Waddington had actually coined the term in 1942 itself.) Soon, scientists found enzymes that could add and remove these chemical tags to and from DNA.
Today, we know that cells use many other chemical tags, not only on DNA itself but also on the proteins around which DNA is wrapped like a vine around a stick.
Together, all these chemical marks help control which genes are switched on or off. Problems in this system can lead to changes in gene activity, which in turn can lead to diseases like cancers.
Functional cure
Now, according to a paper that appeared in Nature Biomedical Engineering on September 21, scientists have used this epigenetic control to treat a hepatitis B infection.
This is a remarkable development because, instead of targeting the virus directly, the work silenced the viral DNA. This is promising because current treatments rarely eliminate the DNA, which allows the virus to rebound. By silencing this residue, the treatment could offer a path to a lasting functional cure for hepatitis B.
The hepatitis B virus mainly infects liver cells. After entering a cell, the virus’s DNA serves as the template to make new viral particles. In many people, the immune system clears the infection, but if it does not, the viral DNA can persist for years or even decades in the host’s liver.
In this time, the virus can remain silent, meaning the viral DNA is still present in the cell but its genes are not active to produce new viruses. This allows the virus to ‘hide’ from the immune system. Then, at a later point, the virus can activate again and produce new virus particles.
And studies have shown that one of the mechanisms by which the virus stays silent is by methylating the cytosines.
Locator and effector
The authors of the new study have reported a new experimental therapy called CRMA-1001, which, they have claimed, can silence the DNA of the hepatitis B virus by selectively adding methylation marks to the viral genome.
The study is innovative because it uses several different technologies to overcome three major challenges. To epigenetically silence viral DNA, scientists first need to be able to target the virus’s DNA without methylating any of the cytosines in the host’s DNA. Then, the silencing mechanism must switch off the virus’s DNA effectively. Finally, all of this should happen without causing any unwanted side-effects to the host.
The study authors solved the first two problems by combining two substances called a ‘locator’ and an ‘effector’. The locator used the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool to find and bind to a specific DNA sequence: in this case, that was a sequence within the viral DNA. This allowed the CRISPR system to take the ‘effector’, the methylation machinery, to the correct location. The effector had proteins that could add methyl groups to nearby cytosines in the viral DNA and proteins that help switch off genes.
Finally, the researchers packed the entire system and delivered it on an mRNA platform (similar to the mRNA vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic). This made the system transient: once a cell had read the instructions to make the required proteins, it degraded them, stopping the production of those proteins too.
Novel therapy
The researchers gave mice infected with hepatitis B virus either a single dose of CRMA-1001 or three doses, one month apart, and regularly tested them for six months for the signs of infection. They reported that after one dose, the levels of several hepatitis B virus markers, including the viral DNA and two viral proteins called HBsAg and HBeAg, dropped significantly. When they tested the viral DNA, they found new methyl groups, suggesting that the treatment was working as intended. The effect was even stronger after three doses: six months after the first dose, as many as 90% of the animals had less viral DNA than could be detected.
CRMA-1001 is not a cure in the traditional sense of the word. The hepatitis B virus DNA is still present in the liver cells. Instead, the study demonstrated a functional cure: when the virus is not necessarily eliminated but is kept so thoroughly suppressed that, for all intents and purposes, the patient has no active signs of disease.
In this study, the team followed up with the mice for six months after treatment, and the researchers found sustained suppression of the virus in that period. However, the study did not establish whether the virus could eventually become active again after those six months, since the viral DNA was still present.
Further studies are needed to examine the long-term effects of CRMA-1001, including whether the silencing effect can persist over many years and whether the virus can ever become active again after treatment. An ongoing phase I/II clinical trial includes these among other questions.
If CRMA-1001 is eventually approved as a therapy for the market, it will represent a novel way to tackle a viral infection: where instead of fighting the threat, the cell ignores it.
Arun Panchapakesan is an assistant professor at the Y.R. Gaitonde Centre for AIDS Research and Education, Chennai.

Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguay's lower house voted unanimously Thursday to impeach President Santiago Peña just minutes after he announced his resignation, as the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings, sent protesters surging into the streets and turned his own party against him.
The 78-0 vote marked a stunning repudiation of Peña by lawmakers from his long-ruling Colorado Party, who joined the opposition in backing his impeachment after three days of demonstrations rocked the capital, Asunción. The vote sends the charges to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is required to convict the president and formally remove him from office.
The impeachment came as thousands protested for a third day, as they attempt to recoup lost savings, wages and pensions from Ueno Bank, a major digital lender.
Peña, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."
The president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis that has plunged a South American nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.
"I also want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
The extraordinary turn of events set the stage for a transfer of power later Thursday. Congress was expected to formally accept Peña's resignation at 5 p.m., clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in as president an hour later. Alliana would serve out Peña's term through August 2028, with lawmakers expected to choose a new vice president.
From star lender to seized bank
Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.
Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno's holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.
The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."
Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.
Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.
As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.
Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
Long lines outside branches but customers are locked out
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.
Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left.
Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Peña's request.
Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud. Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.
Protesters in the streets
Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez, the bank's parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank. A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asunción, the capital.
"We want your head, Peña!" they shouted. Their signs demanded Peña's impeachment, called him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.
Many demonstrators saw Ueno's collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.
"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said protester Belarmino Balbuena.
At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.

Every year, as Indians celebrate Dhanteras, many throng to jewellery stores to buy gold, silver, and other valuables. However, others make their way to a local shop or a vendor near the jewellery store to purchase a broom (jhaadu). Have you ever wondered why? This seemingly ordinary household item holds a special place in Dhanteras traditions. Many believe that bringing a new broom home on the occasion invites Goddess Lakshmi's blessings, drives away negative energy, and paves the way for prosperity. But where does this belief come from, and what is the significance of buying a broom on Dhanteras? Many of us have often been warned against touching a broom with our feet or even stepping over it. Further, kicking it accidentally is considered inauspicious, with many people immediately touching it and then their forehead as a way of seeking forgiveness, similar to what they would do if they accidentally stepped on a book. Quick answers to key questions A new broom is seen as a symbol of sweeping away negativity and past misfortunes. The tradition is also believed to help make the home ready to welcome prosperity. Traditional beliefs say Goddess Lakshmi stays in clean, well-maintained homes. Since a broom removes dust and dirt, it is symbolically linked to preparing the home for her blessings. Yes. Buying a broom is a Dhanteras tradition and is an affordable way to take part in the occasion, regardless of how much you can spend. Dhanteras 2026 falls on Friday, November 6. The article says devotees can buy a broom after Trayodashi begins, around 10:30 am, and traditionally bring it home before the evening puja. Yes. The tradition described in the article is to offer prayers to the new broom before using it to sweep away negativity. If the elders in families are to be believed, these customs are deeply rooted in the belief that Goddess Lakshmi stays where homes are clean, well-maintained, and lit. Since the broom or jhaadu is used to remove dust and dirt from our homes, it is symbolically associated with keeping the house ready to welcome Lakshmi, who is a symbol of abundance, good fortune, prosperity, and wealth. The belief is also linked to Lakshmi's elder sister, Alakshmi, who is associated with misfortune and poverty. Also known as Jyeshtha, she is believed to reside in places marked by filth, discord and negativity. Cleaning the house with a broom is therefore seen as a way of driving away Alakshmi and making room for Goddess Lakshmi and prosperity, The Times of India reported. Since Dhanteras is the day when Lakshmi is formally welcomed into a home, purchasing a new broom on this occasion fits right in. The tradition of purchasing a broom is considered a symbolic gesture of sweeping away past misfortunes and negativity while making room for wealth and prosperity. Another reason why this practice has never faded is its affordability. A broom may cost around ₹50 or ₹100, making it accessible to people across income groups. From a daily-wage worker to a factory owner, anyone can participate in the tradition, regardless of how much they can spend on Dhanteras. This year, Dhanteras, also known as Dhantrayodashi, is being celebrated on Friday, November 6. The festival marks the onset of the five-day Diwali celebrations. It is considered an auspicious occasion for offering prayers for health, prosperity, and wealth. Devotees can purchase a broom after Trayodashi begins, at around 10:30 am, and are traditionally advised to bring it home before the evening puja. Further, one must remember that before using the new broom to sweep away negativity, one has to offer prayers to it.
