India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
- Published
India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.
Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.
One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.
Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.
Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.
Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).
The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG, which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.
The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.
But the critical response so far has been mixed.
Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it, external three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".
Rishabh Suri of the Hindustan Times newspaper was more enthusiastic, awarding it four stars.
"I am happy to report, all that money shows on screen," he wrote, praising the performances and visual effects, though he found the first half sluggish and the music underwhelming.
Shubhra Gupta, external of The Indian Express, who gave the film three stars, confessed to initial misgivings about its extravagant scale but found herself gradually won over, calling it the "perfect epic".
There was "enough sorcery and thrills and adventure" to sustain the spectacle, she wrote, and the filmmakers had managed to tell a sprawling story without being swallowed by it.
Internationally, too, the film drew contrasting reactions.
Writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw called it a "thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama". He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Rama into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita. Its sweeping landscapes and fantastical imagery reminded him of The Lord of the Rings and The Lion King.
"It's a rather amazing adventure," he wrote, external, giving it four stars.
Others were less impressed. Siddhant Adlakha of IGN scored the film four out of 10, describing its action as "clunky" and its computer-generated imagery as an "eye-sore".
Giovanni Lago of Next Best Picture, who gave it, external five out of 10, praised Yash's magnetic Ravana and the score by Rahman and Zimmer. But he felt the film's vast narrative might have been better served by a Game of Thrones-style series.
The use of AI to adjust actors' lip movements for the English-language version also drew criticism. While Tiwari said it was intended to make the film more accessible to international audiences, Adlakha likened the result to "exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches".
In India, the film has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, particularly Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, which captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint.
When the series first aired in 1987, Sunday mornings across India took on an almost devotional stillness.
Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship.
Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs.
Broadcast on the state-run Doordarshan network, some of the most popular parts of the 78-episode series drew an estimated 80-100 million viewers, astonishing numbers at a time when owning a TV was a luxury in India.
The actors, too, became objects of reverence. Arun Govil, who played Ram, has recalled people weeping at the sight of him and touching his feet. Now, in a casting choice brimming with nostalgia, Govil returns in Tiwari's film as Dasharatha, Ram's father.
Other adaptations found their own ways to reimagine the epic. The 1992 Indo-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama brought the tale to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation.
Tiwari's Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined - but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters.
It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity - over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.
The 2023 film Adipurush, another big-budget retelling of Ramayana, sparked backlash on several fronts.
Hindu groups called for a ban, accusing it of disrespecting religious figures, while some critics questioned its depiction of Ravana, which they said drew on Mughal imagery and reinforced stereotypes about Muslims. The film was also criticised for its dialogue and visual effects.
For the actors portraying these characters in the latest film, that burden was deeply felt.
"I was filled with fear," Kapoor told the BBC Asian Network's Haroon Rashid. "I knew that maybe I'm too old for this. I won't be able to do justice to it."
He called the role "an opportunity of a lifetime", but said playing a figure worshipped by millions left little room for the creative freedom he had enjoyed in other films.
Sai Pallavi, who plays Sita, said the experience was as much spiritual as artistic. Raised in a religious household, she said she approached the part not just as a performance, but as an opportunity for personal growth.
How the film is being received will become clearer soon, as audiences head to cinemas.
But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale.

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.
The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.
Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.
Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are in Gauteng, South Africa’s most populous and densely populated province and its economic engine. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance is leading the polls in all three metros but has not been polling above 40%.
The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs with a combination of the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters and the populist Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA across the province’s three metros.
In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to controversial past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.
The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.
In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma is polling above 40%. The 84-year-old Zuma, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.
South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
- Published
Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured.
"We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC.
On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded.
Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing.
He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.
Earlier this week, Lissu went on a hunger strike as he was not being allowed access to his lawyers - an allegation the prison authorities denied.
His lawyer Dickson Matata told the BBC on Wednesday he had now been granted a meeting and would be eating again.
In its statement, Amnesty said it had documented how over the past year security agencies had committed human rights violations with impunity against government critics, opposition supporters, media organisations and dissenting members of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party.
"Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters," said Tigere Chagutah, the group's regional director for East and southern Africa
"In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear."
The authorities in the East African nation have repeatedly denied accusations of widespread abuses and say the government is committed to respecting human rights.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her.
Last year, the BBC verified multiple videos of police shooting towards protesters. Footage posted online showed demonstrators being confronted by heavily armed units blocking their progress and firing tear gas to disperse crowds.
The BBC has since spoken to families of some of the victims of the electoral violence, who are still seeking answers.
Many, like Mwajuma Hamisi, have been left destitute. Her husband George Kisivani was shot in the northern city of Arusha on 29 October 2025, the day of the vote, and died two days later.
"I lost my husband, upon whom we, a family with five children, depended. We now have no other source of support. I am left to fight for the family on my own. We have no other assistance," the 32-year-old told the BBC.
She now sells vegetables at a nearby market to support the family - and would like help from the government.
Sane, who shot in the leg in Arusha, has been suffering physically and financially.
The father of three says he has undergone more than five major operations to deal with the gunshot wound. He still needs further surgery but says he can no longer afford treatment.
"We have done everything within our means, but we have reached our limit," the 33-year-old told the BBC.
"The government should look into the situation of those of us who have suffered these tragedies, so that we can receive medical treatment, as some of us are still very sick."
He explained how in the wake of the violence hospitals initially refused to treat injured people.
In the intervening months, his relatives have sought help from local officials and the district commissioner, but he says they were told the government had not allocated a budget for victims of the violence.
The BBC has not independently verified his account of those conversations.
A commission of inquiry's report into the violence was handed to President Samia in April, officially recording 518 deaths.
But Amnesty has criticised the fact that the full report has not yet been made public, saying it "entrenches a culture of secrecy".
The president has since set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
"It is imperative that this new commission comprehensively address the role of security forces in the election-related crackdown," Chagutah said.
The rights group says that between 3 and 17 September 2026, it interviewed 17 people who gave details of a continuing crackdown by the authorities.
Some of them were targeted after demonstrations were called for 7 July to demand democratic reforms and justice for those killed last year.
These marches were banned by the authorities. A 26-year-old man who had expressed support told Amnesty how he was arrested on 24 July in Dar es Salaam and held without charge for 47 days.
He said he was blindfolded by his interrogators who wanted to know who was funding the protests and threatened to kill him.
"On the first day, they didn't give me food. When I asked for water, they urinated on my blindfolded face and said, 'That is the price for those of you opening your mouths to make noise'," he said.
"On the second day, I was taken to Gogoni police station where they beat your legs until they get numb but then insist that you must stand."
The right groups also cites other "acts that may amount to torture... arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances and abductions".
The authorities did not respond to the BBC's or Amnesty's request for comment.
Many of those who lost relatives a year ago want the government to acknowledge their suffering and address their questions about justice, like 40-year-old Neema Munuo.
She says her grief over the death of her 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami, who had gone out to buy phone credit in Arusha when she was shot, has often left her too distraught to leave the house.
"It is a date I will never forget for the rest of my life, because whenever I recall it, I feel as though I am burning inside," Munuo told the BBC.
This feeling resonates with farmer Juma Nasibu, who lives near the city of Mwanza on the shores of Lake Victoria.
He has not seen his 25-year-old nephew Juma Shabani since the unrest.
The young man had been at a cinema hall in the evening when his uncle later heard unconfirmed reports that he was amongst people rounded up and shot. His family have fruitlessly searched for him at hospitals, police stations and prisons.
"To date, what still pains me is that we were never able to recover the body," Nasibu told the BBC.

Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan.
So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.
For the fourth time in October, parts of Greece are at risk of flooding. In the early part of this week, low pressure will bring severe thunderstorms and longer spells of heavy rain to much of the country, and this will be followed by a deep area of low pressure passing across southern areas.
The national meteorological agency issued warnings for Monday, with 30mm-60mm of rain forecast in a 12-hour period across central areas, and50mm-80mm in the north-east Aegean Islands. Forecast models indicate the potential for similar totals in a 12-hour period between Wednesday and Thursday, making further flooding possible.
A low-pressure system developed into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal this weekend. Cyclone Arnab is expected to move towards the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coast by Wednesday. The India meteorological department has alerts in place for extreme heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong surface winds across the eastern side of the country.
Models are forecasting gusts of up to 85mph, and six-hourly rainfall totals of up to 100mm, as the storm makes landfall, currently expected on Wednesday. From then, the system is set to drift to the north before gradually dying out over north-east India at the end of the week.

Three social media content creators from West Bengal — Akash Sarkar, Surajit Shee and Srimoyee Chakraborty — were recently arrested after making posts which questioned the ruling BJP government and its policies.
While Sarkar was granted bail on October 29 after spending three days in police custody, Chatterjee was released from detention on a personal bond on October 26. Shee was first sent to judicial custody and held at Medinipur Central Jail. At present, he is in police custody till November 6.
An FIR was lodged against Shee under Sections 152, 197 and 353 of the BNS, pertaining to acts endangering integrity of India, assertions threatening national integration, and statements amounting to public mischief, respectively.
In the FIR registered against Sarkar, the police invoked Sections 356(1), 353(1)(2) and 299(1) of the BNS, pertaining to criminal defamation, spreading false information/hate speech, and intentionally outraging religious feelings, respectively.
Surajit Shee: Posts on Durga Puja Stampede
Surajit Shee, hailing from Dantan village of West Midnapore district, runs a Facebook page called ‘Core Bangla-Janakantha’, which has over 2,52,000 followers. Shee shares posts on a range of social, political and scientific issues. The two last posts on his page were made on October 19. In one, he is seen appreciating the BJP government for banning DJs and loudspeakers during processions in the state, and in the other post, he talks about allegations that followed the Chorbagan stampede which killed 19 people in Kolkata at a Durga Puja.
Another post by Shee from October 18 caried a video that has been restricted in India. The caption reads, translated from Bengali, “What is the actual truth behind the Chorebagan incident? Which version is correct? The official government figures or the claims made by the public? The government itself is abusing the law. Those in power are misusing their authority to silence the voices of ordinary citizens.”
Shee is a member of ‘Bharatiya Biggyan o Juktibadi Samity’ — an organization which aims to promote scientific temperament in the society.
Alt News spoke with Dipak Roy, a key member of the outfit. Roy mentioned that beside discussing political issues, Shee was vocal about various scientific and social issues.
“Surajit had been telling us that for almost a year that a section of local BJP-RSS workers had been harassing him over his social media content. The intensity of the harassment increased after May 4 (as BJP came to power in the state). On either October 17 or 18, Shee told me that his house had been attacked by the same group, who claimed that he was posting anti-national content. I suggested that he take shelter elsewhere. He then went to a friend’s house in Contai. The police arrested him from there on October 24,” alleged Roy.
Although Shee was detained by police on October 24, he was shown as arrested on October 25, Sunday, from his residence in Dantan, instead of Contai.
According to Roy, the group that attacked Shee’s house claimed that a complaint had been lodged against him at Dantan police station over his alleged ‘anti-national’ activities. Roy told Alt News that when Shee’s father and father-in-law went to the police station to enquire about the alleged complaints, the police could not produce any complaint lodged against him. Police allegedly told them that the chief minister had ordered Shee’s arrest and that it “would be better if he surrendered” or else they would “make an example out of him”.
During the arrest, Roy alleged that only three to four police personnel were present while nearly 20 RSS-BJP workers rounded him up. “Around 15-20 RSS-BJP workers surrounded the house of his friend in Contai. These people assaulted him before handing him over to the police, who then took him away in a car,” alleged Roy. “We thought Contai police had arrested him and arranged for a lawyer to represent him at the Contai sub-divisional court. However, later we realised that Shee had been arrested by Dantan police and was produced before the Dantan court.”
Roy further alleged that Shee’s family could access the legal documents related to the case two days after his arrest. Police have also allegedly seized Shee’s mobile phone, but no seizure list has been provided to his family.
Alt News’ attempts to contact both Dantan and Contain police were unsuccessful till publication time.
Alt News spoke to Tapan Jana, Shee’s maternal uncle, who said, “Surajit was produced in Dantan court on November 2, and police sought seven days of custody. However, the judge allowed only four days.”
“After he was remanded to police custody, an officer from Dantan police station verbally abused us when we went to meet him. The officer said that Surajit had insulted Sanatan Dharma, the state and central governments, and was inciting the public through his Facebook posts. He told us to make sure that Surajit reveals during questioning who had instructed him to make those posts,” Jana said.
“The officer further said that unless Shee confessed, he would make it difficult for him to get bail,” Jana added.
Akash Sarkar: Posts on Stampede and Suvendu Adhikari
Akash Sarkar (30) was arrested from his home in Nagerbazar on October 25, produced before the Barrackpore court on October 26, which ordered three days of police custody. He was released on bail on October 29.
Sarkar told Alt News that during interrogation, police pointed to three aspects of his posts which they claimed led to his arrest — his reference to Suvendu Adhikari’s ‘bhaipo’ (nephew) in connection with the Chorbagan stampede, his comments about the government’s handling of the situation following the stampede, and his use of the term ‘teen bati’ (three bowls) to refer to Adhikari.
Sarkar said, “In one of my Facebook posts, I had mentioned that Suvendu’s nephew was the chief patron of Chorbagan Sarbojonin, the puja where 19 people were trampled, and that he should take responsibility for the tragedy. I had also flagged the manner in which the Durga idol, with its hands tied, was taken away by the police for immersion.”
“I had written in my Facebook post that, according to the BJP, previous governments in West Bengal were not Sanatani. But even those governments did not treat the goddess in the way the Sanatani government treated her. The police flagged my post as religiously inflammatory and kept me in custody for three days,” added Sarkar.
According to Sarkar, in another post, he had addressed chief minister as ‘teen bati’ — a political jab aimed at Adhikari.
“The ‘teen bati’ jab was popularised by Ali Aftab Chand, a lawyer at the Calcutta high court who identifies himself as a ‘Rashtravadi Muslim’. He was not arrested. Is it because he is close to the BJP?” asked Sarkar.
According to the FIR, a person named Soumen Das had lodged a complaint against Sarkar, alleging that Sarkar “has been using his Facebook profile to publish false, defamatory, religiously inflammatory and provocative posts concerning the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Sri Narendra Modi and Hon’ble Chief Minister of India, Sri Suvendu Adhikari.”
“While I was in the lock-up, I heard from a few police personnel that our local MLA, Tarunjyoti Tiwari, had visited the police station and taken a personal interest in my case. Police hinted that although the charges against me were flimsy, orders from higher-ups were forcing them to keep me in custody,” he alleged, adding that the police was yet to return his phone.
Srimoyee Chakroborty: Posts Critical of State Government
Chakraborty had posted an update on her Facebook profile on October 26, mentioning that she had been held at the Bidhannagar East police station. She was later released the same day on a bond of Rs 2,000.
On October 26, she announced on Facebook that she was detained, while vowing to continue her fight. Her posts on Facebook reflect a similar pattern of posts critical of the BJP-led state and central government and its policies. However, it is not clear which particular post led to the administrative action.
A scroll through her Facebook timeline shows her vocal support for the Left.
Similar to Shee and Sarkar, Chakraborty had also made a series of posts critical of the government’s management of the Chorbagan stampede and the immersion process. On October 21, she shared the chief minister’s video where he announced that only people who follow Sanatana Dharma would participate in the Durga idol immersion process. In the caption, she referred to Adhikari as ‘teen bati’.

The cow, the flea and the genome: One Health and the statecraft of prevention
A cattle virus at home and a plague scare abroad make the same argument this World One Health Day: life is epidemiologically indivisible, and the institutions that govern and study it must learn to be so too
About three-quarters of emerging human infections originate in animals. India, with 1.4 billion people, some 536 million livestock and the world’s largest milk output, sits at the centre of this arithmetic. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.

High-profile attorney Alex Spiro said artificial intelligence could strip much of the "fat in the middle" out of the legal industry, pushing more cases toward either quicker settlements or all-out trials.
Spiro, a partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan's New York office and Elon Musk's go-to attorney, said during a Thursday appearance on the tech talk show TBPN that AI tools could help make it easier for lawyers to decide whether a case is worth taking to trial.
"I think AI will eliminate a layer of a lot of things, including my day job. And by eliminating that layer, it allows you to get to the truth and synthesize it faster," Spiro said. "If you can do that, then I think you can make quicker decisions on, this is something to resolve or this is something to go all the way on."
Spiro, who has represented actor Alec Baldwin, rapper Jay-Z, New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, and ex-New York City Mayor Eric Adams, said this could mean fewer cases languishing in costly, drawn-out litigation.
"Maybe the way it'll work is a lot of the fat in the middle is going to be cut out," Spiro said. "Cases will settle quickly or go to trial, and there won't be as much in-between litigation that is pointless and sort of ebbing between the two."
Ultimately, the use of the technology could lead to more trials by helping attorneys analyze cases more quickly and identify which cases are worth fighting.
"Maybe there are more trials, frankly, because people just say, 'Okay we just did an analysis of these 10 cases. These nine should settle. This one shouldn't. We're going all the way,'" Spiro said. "And then people don't get that nervousness that they get where some companies they'll think in their mind, 'Okay, these three are going to have to be tried,' but then they end up caving because they're too risk averse."
Still, Spiro said AI would not change his strategy.
"I haven't changed my approach to trying cases or how to present in front of a jury in 20 years," said Spiro, adding, "There are argumentative techniques that work and some that don't."
Jurors, he said, "are not changing based on AI."
"So I'm going to talk to them exactly the same way," Spiro said. "It just may be that the people that get me the information that I distill into my arguments, there needs to be fewer of them, or they have a simpler, more linear path in getting me that information because they have technological tools that make it faster, sleeker."
Asked whether AI could make clients overly confident in their own legal judgment, Spiro quipped that he was already familiar with that dynamic.
"I represent almost exclusively clients that think that they know more about the law," said Spiro. "It's my specialty."

A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the State's first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced on Monday (November 2, 2026).
The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles (150 kilometres) north of Syracuse, Governor Kathy Hochul said.
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
Ms. Hochul, a Democrat, said the child's death is “a devastating reminder of what's at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but State health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
Ms. Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighbouring States and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

The Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections saw major gains for Democrats both in the House and Senate, including key Senate victories in Michigan, South Carolina and Texas. News media outlets reported the results as a sweeping rebuke of President Donald Trump's administration, with vote tallies exhibiting sizable differences from his second-term victory in 2024.
In the hours after the election results began coming in, some people began claiming a screen-recorded video showed that tech entrepreneur Elon Musk — who reportedly contributed $474 million to support Republicans in the midterms — had deleted his post from Election Day that read, "Vote red today!"
For example, one X user's popular post featured the screen recording showing the post still loaded on the person's device but not properly displaying after refreshing Musk's feed. That clip appeared to originate from a different user, with many (archived) others (archived) reposting (archived) the content.
Others shared (archived) a screenshot with a message reading, "The post you are trying to reply to has been deleted or is not visible to you."
(@PollTracker2024 via X)
In sum, Musk, or another person who manages his X account, truly deleted the post reading, "Vote red today!"
While knowledgeable users can create fake screenshots and videos, we found definitive proof that the post once existed. Someone archived the post prior to its removal. As of that archiving, the post had nearly 12 million views.
Attempts to access the original post displayed the message, "Hmm...this page doesn't exist. Try searching for something else."
We also confirmed firsthand that DuckDuckGo search results still displayed a link to the deleted post, which we further archived.
(DuckDuckGo)
The DuckDuckGo search results displayed the time 14:35:34, appearing to correspond to GMT. That timing aligned with the post first appearing just after another one visible in the screen recording, in which Musk answered "Yes" in a quote repost of another user's post (archived) about how to properly use artificial intelligence.
Snopes emailed an apparent media relations email address for X to ask whether Musk wished to comment about this matter. In the past, journalists' correspondence sent via a similar email address did not result in receiving answers to questions. We will update this article if we receive more information.
For further reading, we previously investigated whether Musk paid Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan to endorse GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

New Delhi, Nov 6: The CBSE class 10 and 12 examinations will begin on February 16, 2027, the board announced on Friday.
The class 10 exams will conclude on March 9, while those for class 12 will end on April 9.
"In class 10, students will appear in 83 subjects and in class 12, students will appear in 121 subjects. The date sheets are being released 101 days in advance of the commencement of examinations," CBSE Examination Controller Sanyam Bhardwaj said.
Adequate gaps have been provided between examinations of subjects commonly offered together by students in both class 10 and 12, he said.
"The tentative schedules of major entrance examinations for class 12 students have been taken into account. Every effort has been made to complete the board examinations well before the commencement of such entrance examinations, enabling students to manage their preparation effectively," he added.
A total of over 19.8 lakh students in class 12 and over 26.5 lakh students in class 10 have registered for the 2027 board examinations.
Class 10 and class 12 students will appear for their Painting and Physics exams on the same day, on February 16.

The State government on Friday (October 30) told the Karnataka High Court that it would not insist, for now, on the implementation of the circular which mandates that all hospital pharmacies disclose the landing base/purchase price and maximum retail price (MRP) of medicines, medical devices and consumables on bills.
An undertaking in this regard was given to the court on behalf of the State’s Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) during the hearing of a petition filed by Private Hospitals and Nursing Homes Association, Bengaluru, and a private hospital. The petitioners have challenged the legality of the October 1 circular.
Justice C.M. Pooncha, before whom the petition came up for hearing, has adjourned further hearing on the petition till November 12 after recording the undertaking given by an Additional Advocate General on instruction from the officials of the FSDA.
Having a re-look
The government also informed the court that “the officials concerned are in the process of having a re-look at the circular dated October 1, 2026, and will not enforce the mandate of the circular till November 12, the next date of hearing on the petition”.
The undertaking was given while requesting the court not to stay the circular to allow the government to re-examine the issues raised by the petitioners.
It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the FSDAhad no statutory power to impose such conditions for disclosure of purchase price, which is a commercial agreement between the sellers and buyers that vary depending on suppliers, purchase quantity, discounts, credit arrangements and other factors.
Sans consultation
Mandating disclosure of purchase price would result in exposing confidential commercial arrangements between the suppliers and health establishments, it has been contented in the petition, while pointing out that the circular was issued sans adequate consultations with the stakeholders, even though the circular has direct implications on their finance.

The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) morning, while many parts of the city reeled under “severe” level of air pollution, according to official data.
Many parts of the city, including ITO, Dwarka, Rohini, Punjabi Bagh, Alipur, Bawana, and Jahangirpuri witnessed “severe” level air pollution.
Other cities and towns in north India, including Noida, Gurugram, and Panipat also witnessed “very poor” air quality, on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) morning.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi was 379 (very poor) at 9 a.m. on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), as per Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
“Severe” level air pollution affects healthy people and seriously impacts those with existing diseases, as per the CPCB.
The overall air quality of Delhi is likely to be in the “very poor” category for three days, as per the Central government’s ‘Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi’.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 350 (very poor) at 4 p.m. on Tuesday, up from 324 (very poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI.
A higher AQI means worsening of air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.
The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.
But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.
The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.
Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.
The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships.
 
“Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

Bengaluru airport-bound road to see disruptions for 1.5 years starting tomorrow as elevated corridor work begins
The movement of KSRTC and private buses, along with all goods vehicles, has been prohibited on the stretch.
Traffic on Bengaluru's Kempegowda International Airport (KIA) Road is set to be affected for 18 months from November 6, with the BDA beginning work on a four-lane elevated corridor along Ballari Road.
The movement of KSRTC and private buses, along with all goods vehicles, has been prohibited on the stretch, the Bengaluru Traffic Police announced on Thursday.
The elevated corridor is being built between UAS Staff Quarters and Mekhri Circle, under the jurisdiction of Sadashivanagar and Sanjaynagar traffic police stations.
The restrictions have been imposed to ease congestion and ensure smoother traffic movement during the construction work.
Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards KIA and Bengaluru city, including emergency vehicles, have been advised to take alternative routes.
Alternative routes for vehicles heading towards Bengaluru airport
Via Cantonment railway station: Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards KIA can take the route via Old High Grounds Junction, Kalpana Junction, Old Udaya TV Junction, Cantonment Railway Station, Tannery Road and Nagawara Road before proceeding towards the airport.
Via BEL circle: Vehicles travelling from Yeshwanthpur towards KIA should take Mattikere Road, turn right at BEL Circle and continue via Ring Road towards the airport.
Alternative routes for vehicles heading towards Bengaluru city
Via Nagawara Junction: Vehicles travelling from KIA towards central Bengaluru can take a left turn at Hebbal, proceed towards Nagawara Junction, take a right turn and continue via Bamboo Bazaar and Queens Road towards the city.
Via Goraguntepalya: Alternatively, vehicles travelling from KIA towards central Bengaluru can take a right turn at Hebbal and proceed via Hebbal Ring Road and Kuvempu Circle towards Goraguntepalya Junction. They should take a left turn at the junction and continue via Dr Rajkumar Road towards the city.
Via Margosa Road: Vehicles travelling from Yeshwanthpur towards central Bengaluru should proceed via BHEL Junction, take a right turn near Maramma Circle and continue via Margosa Road towards the city.
Via CBI Junction: Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards Bengaluru city should enter the service road in front of Baptist Hospital after descending the Hebbal Flyover and continue along it up to CBI Junction. They can then proceed towards the city via Ballari Main Road.
Via Anand Nagar main road: Vehicles travelling from Hebbal towards Anand Nagar and RT Nagar should enter the service road in front of Baptist Hospital and proceed towards Anand Nagar Cross. They should take a left turn at CBI Junction to join Anand Nagar Main Road and continue towards RT Nagar and Jayamahal Road.
The Bengaluru traffic police have requested commuters to cooperate and follow the alternative routes during the construction period.

Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.
The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.
One connection, works every time, needs no retries
There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
When all the conditions are met, the consequences are high.
“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,” Alpine maintainers said Thursday. “It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.”
When logging into a passwordless account, the attacker can gain access by inputting more than 256 characters in the password field.
Security firm Checkpoint said that the use of the SHA256 or SHA512 functions “matters because sshd borrows that account’s salt. Without it, the attack fails.” Company researchers said their testing also showed that the account must be active, not just hold a hash. Checkpoint further reported that root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit password setting, though reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still become root.

Keralam court rejects plea to cancel bail of judge’s minor son ran over man in Kochi
The Ernakulam Sessions Court rejected appeals by the State and the victim’s family against bail granted to the 17-year-old in the fatal Kochi crash.
A Keralam court on Thursday rejected appeals seeking cancellation of bail granted to a 17-year-old boy accused of driving a luxury car into a scooter, killing a 55-year-old street food vendor in Kochi last month.
The Ernakulam Sessions Court upheld the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB)’s decision to grant bail to the teenager, whose father is an additional district judge.
The court was hearing appeals filed by the State and the victim’s family challenging a JJB ruling granting bail to the teenager.
A Mercedes-Benz driven by the judge’s minor son hit the two-wheeler near Cheranalloor at around 2.30am on October 25. Jayabalakrishnan, a resident of Manjali who ran a street food cart in the Chittor area, was thrown into the air and died on the spot.
The teenager was immediately caught and handed over to the police. He was later produced before the JJB, which granted him bail citing the absence of any prior criminal record.
Bhadrakeerthy, daughter of Jayabalakrishnan, told reporters that she and her family were losing faith in the judiciary. “We expected a verdict in our favour. But there was so much drama and so many twists inside the court. I am losing trust in the judiciary. There have been lapses on the part of the police and the judiciary. We will speak to our lawyers and reassess,” she said.
A detailed copy of the court order is awaited.
The father of the minor, an additional district judge presiding over the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal in Keralam, was granted anticipatory bail by the high court on Thursday. The court orally told the prosecution that he is a judicial officer who has been cooperating with the investigation.
He was booked on additional charges of attempting to destroy evidence on Monday, police said. The judge was earlier booked on charges of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, along with rash and negligent driving, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act.
According to Cheranalloor police, the family of the victim, Jayabalakrishnan, lodged a fresh complaint on Sunday, alleging that the minor’s father spent a lot of time at the accident site in a bid to destroy evidence in the case. The complaint also alleged that the judge visited Cheranalloor police station after the accident and forced an officer to delete a photograph of his son that had been clicked by a member of the victim’s family.
The judge had earlier been granted interim protection from arrest by the Kerala High Court. He told the court that he was asleep at the time of the incident and was not aware that his son had taken the vehicle from the house.

Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
- Published
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing sceptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".
In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

For the first time in a dozen years, a leading OB-GYN group has updated its guidance on managing hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and other disruptive symptoms that often come with menopause.
Doctors stressed the importance of hormone therapies, which many women are considering again after the removal of federal safety warnings. On Friday, federal officials said the Food and Drug Administration has been taking steps to ensure there's an adequate supply.
Doctors also described various nonhormonal options in the new advice released this month by the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, or ACOG.
“We would love our patients to go to their OB-GYNs regarding questions about menopause and really advocate for getting the treatment that they need,” said Camille Clare, the group’s president.
Menopause occurs when a woman has gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. In the U.S., it usually happens around age 50. The time leading up to it is called perimenopause, during which the body’s production of the hormones estrogen and progesterone declines sharply.
Problems commonly arise. More than half of women in menopause report having “vasomotor” issues such as hot flashes and night sweats, said ACOG. As many as two-thirds report menopause-related sleep disruption. And more than a third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women worldwide report depressive symptoms.
In the past, doctors said, many women quietly suffered.
There's growing consensus that "these symptoms should be treated,” said JoAnn Manson, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. “This should help to empower women to discuss their symptoms with their healthcare provider.”
Manson said ACOG’s new guidelines are similar to those put out by other medical organizations.
"Moderate to severe or bothersome menopausal symptoms should be treated with hormone therapy as the first line of treatment,” she said. While it's not appropriate for all women, she added, it’s a good option for many.
But some have been wary.
In 2002, a landmark study in women taking a pill-based combination of estrogen and progestin was stopped early because of links to breast cancer, blood clots and other serious issues. Concerns lingered even though later studies showed the benefits of today’s hormone therapies outweigh the risks for many women. For more than 22 years, all hormone-based menopause treatments carried a government warning, which Manson said discouraged patients and doctors from using them.
But last year, the FDA announced it would remove the boxed warning from more than 20 pills, patches and creams containing the hormones estrogen and progestin. On Friday, the FDA approved updated labeling for three additional estrogen-based patches.
Removing the boxed warning has helped revive interest in and demand for the treatments.
Since the FDA labeling change, some women have reported difficulty obtaining estrogen patches in certain doses and formulations.
FDA officials said Friday that despite such reports, they are unaware of “an imminent risk of a nationwide shortage.” Officials also noted that drug manufacturers have doubled their output of the products over the last year by adding extra manufacturing shifts and production capacity.
Stephanie Faubion, medical director at The Menopause Society, said she’s glad to see ACOG’s guidelines stress the importance of these treatments. “It’s undisputed that hormone therapy is the first line and most effective therapy for hot flashes,” she said.
ACOG reviews the latest evidence on hormone therapy and includes detailed information about the various types. Whole-body therapies, which come in pills, patches, sprays, gels and a vaginal ring, deliver doses of hormones into the bloodstream at levels high enough to have significant effects on symptoms like hot flashes. Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy is applied directly with very little circulating in the blood. It’s often prescribed to women whose biggest complaint is vaginal dryness.
ACOG recommends that decisions about hormone therapy should be made jointly by doctors and patients, and take into account the benefits and risks given a patient's age and medical history. If it’s appropriate, the group advises starting it before age 60, or within 10 years of menopause.
Some patients choose not to take full-body hormonal medications or are advised by their doctors to avoid them because of their medical histories or conditions.
For them, doctors pointed to different medicines. One is fezolinetant, which works in the area of the brain that controls body temperature and blocks a source of hot flashes and night sweats. Another is elinzanetant, which works similarly.
Doctors also said certain antidepressants can help manage symptoms like hot flashes and depression in patients with either or both of these problems.
There’s also evidence supporting some non-drug treatments for hot flashes, night sweats and sleep or mood problems, ACOG said. These include cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, exercise, clinical hypnosis and acupuncture. Such approaches can be used alone or alongside medications.
Clare said women may see misinformation and disinformation about menopause treatments online, and urged patients to come to their doctors with any questions. ACOG offers advice on sorting out truth from false claims as well as overall information on menopause.
“Women have options. They have lots of options, hormonal and nonhormonal,” Faubion said. “They shouldn’t be told that nothing can be done about their symptoms. Because again, we have evidence for many different things that can help.”

Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
- Published
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.
A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.
But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.
Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.
The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.
"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.
Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.
"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.
He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.
He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.
Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.
President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.
Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.
- Tundu Lissu - the great survivor of Tanzanian politics 
  - Published24 April 2025
The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".
Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.
They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.
But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.
He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.
Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:
- Electoral commissioners should be independently appointed (not by the president)
- Police should allow all parties to campaign free of intimidation
- Government-appointed district chiefs should no longer act as returning officers
- Party agents should be able to observe counting without harassment
- It should be possible to challenge presidential election results in court.
During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.
These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.
His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.
Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.
Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.
The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.
He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.
In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.
He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.
The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years outside Tanzania.
He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.
Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.
His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.
But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.
Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.
His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.
Last week, rights group Amnesty International accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.
Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
- Published
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."
The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.
Peña has rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation comes after Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.
In his video message posted on X, Peña said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.
Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.
It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.
The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.
A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.
Peña won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.

Australia recruit Hussey for Ashes build-up
- Published
Australia have recruited Michael Hussey as a long-term batting consultant to help them prepare for the 2027 Ashes and 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
The 51-year-old former batter has been added to the national staff as Australia look to improve their form in the longest format, having drawn 1-1 at home to Bangladesh and then lost 2-1 in South Africa in their last two series.
Hussey, who has served as a short-term batting consultant for Australia on a number of occasions in recent years, will start work with the national side when they face England in a five-game T20 series from 21 November.
In the T20 format he will help his country prepare for the first Olympic cricket competition in 128 years and the 2028 World Cup, which will be held in Australia and New Zealand in October and November of the same year.
"I am extremely excited about being a part of the team in a more formal and meaningful role in the coming years," Hussey said in a statement.
"This team has achieved so much in recent times, to which I hope I can add value to the coaching and playing groups ahead of what will be an exciting and challenging period."
Australia have suffered a number of poor red-ball batting performances in the last year, starting when two of last winter's Ashes Tests lasted just two days.
They were bowled out for 198 in August as Bangladesh won their first ever Test in Australia, and were dismissed for 99 and 111 in defeats in the second and third Tests against South Africa.
Following the final England T20 on 2 December, they will start a heavy pre-Ashes Test schedule where they will play New Zealand in home for four matches then travel to India for a five-game series.
They then face England in a one-off Test at the Melbourne Cricket Ground from 11 March, celebrating 150 years of Test cricket, and could conceivably reach the World Test Championship final at the Oval on 9 June.
The five-match Ashes series runs from 18 June to 2 August, while Hussey will also work with Australia at the ODI World Cup in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe in October and November 2027.
Hussey did not play Test cricket until he was a 30-year-old, breaking into the Australia side after the 2005 Ashes and becoming an all-format regular until his international retirement in early 2013.
He played 79 Tests for his country, averaging 51.52 with the bat, and featured in 185 ODIs and 38 T20s, winning the 2007 50-over World Cup and the 2006 and 2009 Champions Trophies.
He is the current head coach of Welsh Fire in the men's Hundred and has worked in the Indian Premier League with Chennai Super Kings, where he served under new England Test coach Stephen Fleming.
Hussey served as a batting consultant for England in 2022, helping them win the T20 World Cup in Australia.
"Mike has been a highly valued part of our staff in the past and brings a considerable skill set which is complementary to the coaches and players," Australia coach Andrew McDonald said.
"Not only is his expertise as a player and coach across multiple formats, competitions, countries invaluable, so are his qualities as a person."

California governor commutes death sentences for all 548 people on death row
- Published
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
Most of Newsom's action on Thursday will need court approval, CalMatters reported. For the commutations of the nearly 400 prisoners convicted of multiple felonies, at least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court have to sign off.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.

A Bengaluru cab driver allegedly killed his wife and six of her relatives and dumped some of the bodies across Karnataka while his 11-year-old nephew, whose parents were among the dead, travelled with him believing they were on a holiday, police said on Friday.
Indusekar alias Sekar, who also runs a Kannada-English monthly tabloid, allegedly confessed during interrogation, Bengaluru police commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh said. The victims were his wife Sunita, his mother-in-law Rupavathi, his brothers-in-law Shankar and Shivakumar, their wives Nalini and Divya, and Shivakumar and Divya’s seven-year-old son. Shankar and Nalini were the boy’s parents.

“The accused claimed to have committed the murders over 15 to 20 days, a timeline that is still being verified,” Singh said. “He is giving a version that he called them one by one, murdered them, and disposed of the bodies in places he has indicated.”

He switched off her phone and told neighbours she had gone on a trip. The next day, he allegedly invited both brothers-in-law and their families to his house for a party and killed the two men, and then Divya, Nalini, Rupavathi and Puneeth. Police have seized the grinding stone and the car, and are still investigating how the others were killed. He allegedly used chemicals to clean bloodstains from his house in Rajajinagar.
Police suspect Indusekar kept the boy with him to answer calls and send messages to relatives to make it seem the family was travelling. NASA has announced a new experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, that will supposedly feature reconfigurable flight-control technology and a modular design for swapping in different payloads. But much remains unknown about the aircraft’s design and development timeline, even as NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the X-plane could take flight within two years.
The mystery surrounding NASA’s newest X-plane was exemplified by the agency’s press release, including an apparently AI-generated image of the X-70, showing a dark silhouette vaguely resembling a military fighter jet obscured by smoke. The news was announced by Isaacman during the UP.Summit held at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 4.
“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” Isaacman said. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next.”
NASA’s press release described the X-70 as a crewed aircraft designed to cruise at Mach 0.75 while reaching a maximum altitude of up to 45,000 feet, and having an operational range beyond 1,726 miles (2,778 kilometers). The article did not mention a specific aircraft manufacturer that might be helping the agency develop the X-plane.
The X-70 would also have a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds (4,536 kilograms) and a design capable of accommodating up to 2,000 pounds (907 kilograms) of experimental payloads both internally and externally. Ars has reached out to NASA for more details.
Return of the Blackbird?
Another X-plane is also expected to be announced at the UP.Summit on November 6, according to Aviation Week. That would coincide with a scheduled announcement from President Donald Trump at the event.

Psoriasis is an autoimmune condition that causes thick, scaly patches on the skin. However, it often remains unidentified and undiagnosed because it does not look the same on all parts of the body: it could be mistaken, for instance, for dandruff on the scalp, persistent eczema on the palms, or a fungal infection. You can’t always judge psoriasis by looking only at visible parts of the skin.
Why does this happen? Our skin isn’t the same everywhere. The thickness of the skin can vary considerably depending on the diversity of the environmental conditions that it is exposed to and the kind of treatment given to it. These factors can contribute to how psoriasis appears and feels.
