Why rugby league needs Tonga-Samoa World Cup final
- Published
With blow out wins and a convoluted format, the men's group stage at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup did little to dissuade cynics about the unhealthy state of the international game.
From Group A, Australia and New Zealand came through as expected and are widely tipped to face off in the final on 15 November.
But from the strange lands of Group B-C, two beacons of hope have emerged. Tonga will face New Zealand after winning all three group matches, before Samoa face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final.
And if either goes all the way, it would be good for international rugby league, shaking up the game in the same way Wakefield's Grand Final win has for the Super League – proving there is still room for surprises in rugby league.
"Could this be a dress rehearsal for the final? I hope so," former Bradford Bulls head coach Matthew Elliott told BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra after Tonga and Samoa's riveting Group B-C match, won 20-18 by the Tongans. "I shouldn't say that out loud as an Aussie but I hope so."
History suggests this scenario is unlikely, but not impossible.
The first semi-final, New Zealand v Tonga, is a match with a dramatic recent history. Tonga beat New Zealand 25-14 in an epic Pacific Championships match two years ago to reach their first-ever elite tournament final.
Last year, their meeting was overshadowed by a head injury to Tonga back-rower Eli Katoa, who needed emergency brain surgery after receiving three separate concussions and has not played since.
Tonga were semi-finalists in 2017, winning their group after stunning New Zealand 28-22 in the group stage. In the last four they were only narrowly defeated by England, 20-18, scoring three tries in the final seven minutes to give the English a huge fright in their best previous World Cup effort.
'It was an absolute cracker'
Samoa have gone one further of course and were surprise runners-up four years ago having not previously gone beyond the quarter-finals since first appearing at the World Cup in 1995.
They were beaten 60-6 by England in their opener but fought through to the semi-finals, where they stunned the hosts 27-26 in a golden point win at Emirates Stadium.
At Old Trafford they were overpowered by Australia but not overawed, losing 30-10. In doing so Samoa became only the sixth different team to reach a men's final after Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain, England and France, in 16 editions.
Australia have won 10 of the last 11 World Cups, including the last three, with New Zealand winning the other.
Such dominance at the supposed peak of the sport, in a tournament reduced from 16 to 10 teams this year, indicates a gap growing between haves and have nots.
Of the outsiders, Samoa and Tonga can shake that up.
The teams met at the quarter-final stage of the last Rugby League World Cup, with Samoa winning a classic 20-18 in Warrington. Tonga won by the same scoreline three days ago, in similarly exhilarating fashion.
"The occasion was unbelievable," Samoa head coach Ben Gardiner said after the game. "I looked down at the start of the game and I've never seen so many people on the sidelines at a footy match in my life.
"It was a sensational occasion, and international rugby league is about that. It's about fanfare and it's about creating opportunities for our fans to come and watch our nations play. It was an absolute cracker."
'Five or 10 levels above NRL'
Not only are the Pacific islands bringing the colour and passion of their nations to the world stage, they are also bringing world-class quality.
Nine players featuring in the group game squads played some part in this year's State of Origin, an annual series between New South Wales and Queensland representative teams regarded as one of the pinnacles of world rugby league.
"I think that was about five or 10 levels above NRL tonight," Tonga half-back Isaiya Katoa told Premier Sports of the group match. "Every tackle felt like the first of the game. There are going to be some sore bodies out there.
"Something that goes so unnoticed is the impact Woolfy [Kristian Woolf] has as the coach. He cares about every single one of us. The reason you've got Jojo Fifita and Rob Toia [two of the State of Origin players] wanting to play for Tonga is because of the coach."
Both nations have Australians in charge. Gardiner has been in post since 2023, while Woolf has led Tonga since 2014 and overseen their remarkable rise in rugby league prominence.
Both have experience coaching in the NRL, and have brought the quality and professionalism of the world's best domestic league to bear fruit on their respective islands – with both talking about working on "emotional regulation" in big games.
They have also both been helped by an international eligibility system which is much more forgiving to smaller nations than in many other sports.
Since 2016, the IRL introduced a tier system for member nations: Australia, New Zealand and England are in tier one; all other full members are in tier two.
Under this system, players can elect to represent both a tier one and two nation but are permitted to represent only one nation in a calendar year or at a Rugby League World Cup.
This flexibility has allowed members of diaspora populations to represent their family heritage and national identities – particularly those with ancestors from Pacific islands, who may have had to move away in the past.
These connections mean that when those with Tongan and Samoan heritage do represent their historic countries, they do so with gusto.
'This is the pinnacle'
"I can't put it into words," Tonga prop Addin Fonua-Blake told BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra. "This is the pinnacle for me. Representing my people is something special.
"I just want to thank from the bottom of my heart all the supporters. You could feel it this whole week, the amount of support that we had, that both teams had. And it's only going to keep growing. What the supporters have done for this game, it's unheard of.
"A few years ago, we wouldn't even sell out a game out of Campbelltown and now we're sitting here on one of the biggest stages selling out, and it's only going to get bigger."
Both countries have also benefited from generous financial deals the likes of which English rugby league supporters want introduced for their team.
Australia's government in July announced, external it was committing A$250m (£130m) over 10 years to the Pacific Rugby League Partnership, designed to help create opportunities in Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Samoa and Fiji, and is being led by the Australian Rugby League Commission.
It is the kind of diversification rugby league badly needs, after a reduced and unbalanced World Cup which at times has struggled to live up to its name.
"The branding of the World Cup, I think that's wrong," former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is, it's a festival of the sport.
"I'm not saying Rugby League could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but certainly more than 10. It's meant to be a festival and showcasing to everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play, get it out there.
"I'll talk about Italy in 2013. Italy don't play Rugby League too much. They managed to get a team full of people who love their heritage, based in the NRL, a lot of Australians, and they managed to beat England in a warm-up game. So don't tell me there's no countries out there, such as Italy, who cannot live up to displaying well in the World Cup and putting on an event."
If rugby league is to grow and the World Cup is to survive, it needs new blood to thrive. A world title for Tonga and Samoa would certainly help.

The round was led by Goyal, who invested a little over ₹100 Cr, with participation from Steadview Capital, Peak XV Partners, Vy Capital, Info Edge Ventures, among others. In July 2026, it acquired London-based longevity medicine practice Longevous for an undisclosed amount, bringing clinical and scientific expertise into the business.

India's cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has issued a critical warning to entities in the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector over an escalating campaign of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting payment and disbursement APIs. In an advisory dated November 4, 2026, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) identified the threat actor behind the campaign as 'CRAFTY FALCON', describing it as an AI-assisted financial threat actor that uses machine intelligence to identify targets, execute attacks at machine speed and exploit victims' own payment and disbursement APIs to initiate unauthorised fund transfers. Banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), fintech companies and other financial services entities have been warned of the growing threat. CERT-In's Computer Security Incident Response Team-Finance (CSIRT-Fin) said the campaign has witnessed a significant escalation, with successful attacks continuing to be reported across the financial services ecosystem. The agency has urged all BFSI entities to treat the campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. Repeat Attacks Despite Remediation A key concern highlighted in the advisory is the threat actor's continued targeting of financial entities that had already received earlier restricted advisories and undertaken remediation measures. According to CERT-In, some of these organisations have been deliberately targeted again, including cases where remediation was incomplete. The attacks have also been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other periods of reduced monitoring, potentially delaying detection and response. CERT-In's analysis identified the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools in the campaign. These include the ARTEX family of large language model (LLM)-based tools, PentAGI, an autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system, and the Cairn attack search engine, alongside the CyberStrikeAI framework. These tools can execute complete attack chains autonomously, generate and refine large volumes of customised attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on responses from targeted systems. The supporting attack infrastructure also changes frequently, with IP addresses rotating within hours to days. CERT-In said infrastructure fingerprints and detailed detection rules have been shared with affected entities through restricted advisories. AI Agents Pose Growing Cybersecurity Risks The latest advisory follows another critical warning issued by CERT-In in October, when the agency flagged attackers using publicly available agentic AI tools to conduct financially motivated intrusions into Indian organisations. The watchdog warned that autonomous AI agents, ostensibly deployed for research and evaluation, had accessed live systems without authorisation, reading business records containing personal data and confidential information. Meanwhile, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has also warned banks, NBFCs and fintech startups about the growing use of AI agents by cybercriminals to perpetrate financial fraud. The agency said it had uncovered multiple individual cases in which malicious agentic AI systems exploited compromised financial systems to execute unauthorised transactions involving amounts running into crores of rupees. CERT-In Flags Vulnerabilities In Tata Motors' Connected Vehicle Apps Separately, CERT-In has flagged multiple vulnerabilities in select versions of Tata Motors' iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev connected vehicle applications, which could allow attackers to access sensitive credentials and vehicle-related information. The agency identified four vulnerabilities, including hardcoded service account credentials, API keys and authorisation tokens within the applications; inadequate validation of URLs and origins loaded through the apps' WebView component; authentication tokens being recorded in application logs; and improper implementation of SSL certificate pinning in the network security configuration. CERT-In has urged users to update their applications to the latest versions of iRA 2.0 (version 26.8.2) and iRA.ev (version 26.9.1). The applications provide access to connected vehicle functionalities, including vehicle status updates, health monitoring, trip details and remote vehicle commands.

Color us nostalgic.
Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player.
Originally called the “MDR-3L2,” the first Walkman headphones were known for their sleek, adjustable gray plastic headband, which extended via metal sliders and ended in signature orange, circular ear cushions. The lightweight, on-ear headphones are a contrast to the bulky headsets that are popular these days, which use wide, cushioned headbands for long-term comfort and large earcups that can support big drivers and are often heavily padded for noise isolation.
The new MDR-3R (note the slightly different name) headphones look just like the originals and come with orange and blue ear cushions.
New headphones are often wireless these days, but the MDR-3R continues the wired tradition of the MDR-3, with an essential twist: a USB-C connector.
“The MDR-3R has been redesigned for modern use while preserving the experience value of freely taking music out into the world, which the original MDR-3 helped popularize,” Sony’s announcement says.

The New York Times Company is reportedly trying to buy Letterboxd for $330 million
Letterboxd would reportedly continue operations as a standalone site.
The company that owns The New York Times is in "exclusive negotiations" to purchase the cinephile online platform Letterboxd, anonymous sources told... The New York Times. The price being discussed is reportedly around $330 million, significantly more than the $250 million figure that was bandied around earlier this year. Discussions are ongoing and could still break down, the report states.
Letterboxd would reportedly continue operations as a standalone site for the "foreseeable future," the NYT reported. However, the Times Company could introduce its own advertising technology into Letterboxd's systems. (The New York Times Company declined to confirm the New York Times' reporting.)
With its "social film discovery" tagline, Letterboxd allows members to create curated lists, diaries, logs, ratings and reviews of movies, while following other members' activities — a Goodreads for movies, if you will. Though relatively small with 30 million members, Letterboxd is an influential online film site with a dedicated and active community that includes notable figures like Martin Scorsese. The site is projected to have $15 million in revenue for 2026.
The Canadian investment group Tiny purchased 60 percent of Letterboxd in 2023, but reportedly started seeking a sale in July this year at a valuation of around $250 million. The list of potential suitors at the time was a who's who of Hollywood, with Netflix, Paramount and Sony Pictures all reportedly interested.
The New York Times Company is now in the mix at a higher price, and is arguably a better buyer because it wouldn't pose a conflict of interest like those Hollywood studios. The Times Company also has a similar business model with a mix of ad and subscription revenue.
The NYT website currently has 13.8 million subscribers, with a goal to hit 15 million by the end of next year. Much of the site's traffic is driven by its puzzle games like Wordle, along with recipes and its sports site, The Athletic. Letterboxd could fit neatly into that mix, offering readers a new way to discover and explore films.

India successfully test-fires indigenously developed quasi-ballistic missile Pralay | Watch
Pralay, developed by the DRDO, is a short-range surface-to-surface missile with a payload capacity of 500-1,000 kg.
India on Thursday successfully test-fired quasi-ballistic missile Pralay from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island off the coast of Odisha. The missile, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), is capable of carrying conventional warheads, the defence ministry said in a statement.
Pralay is a short-range surface-to-surface missile with a payload capacity of 500-1,000 kg. "With this successful test, the induction of the system has become imminent," the ministry said.
Defence minister Rajnath Singh also complimented DRDO, Defence Forces and industry partners on the successful flight-test and said the missile equipped with advanced technologies will further enhance the technological capabilities and operational preparedness of the military against emerging threats.
“The test was conducted as part of user evaluation trials and successfully met all the stipulated objectives, as validated by data captured through various range instruments. This successful trial marks another significant milestone in strengthening India’s indigenous defence capabilities,” Singh wrote in a post on X.
The defence ministry said that all the test objectives were fully met as confirmed by the test data captured by various range instruments deployed by Integrated Test Range, Chandipur.
Research Centre Imarat, Hyderabad, along with other DRDO laboratories, indigenously developed the missile, it said.
Bharat Dynamics Limited, one of the development-cum-production-partners, has produced the system.
The flight-test was conducted in the presence of senior officials from DRDO, representatives from the industry and the defence forces, as part of user evaluation trials, the ministry said in a statement.

Pakistan says willing to grant visa to Bhagwant Mann if he wishes to visit
Pakistan said it would consider issuing Bhagwant Mann a visa for a Lahore conference. His proposed visit remains subject to permission from the Indian government.
Pakistan on Friday said it was willing to consider issuing a visa to Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann if he wished to visit the country, following his announcement that he had been invited to attend the World Punjabi Conference in Lahore later this month.
Pakistan Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan made the statement during his weekly media briefing while responding to a question about the possibility of Mann travelling to Pakistan.
The Pakistani government would "consider issuing him a visa if he wished to visit the country", Khan said. However, he clarified that whether the Indian government would allow the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leader to travel across the border was a separate matter.
On October 23, Mann had revealed that he had received an invitation to attend the World Punjabi Conference scheduled to be held in Lahore on November 27. However, he expressed uncertainty over whether he would be permitted to visit Pakistan.
"Our culture is the same. Many poets from here will go there," Mann had said.
The Punjab Chief Minister had also expressed a desire to take all members of the state legislative assembly to Kartarpur Sahib in Pakistan if the Kartarpur Corridor reopened.
KARTARPUR CORRIDOR REMAINS SHUT SINCE MAY 2025
The Kartarpur Corridor connects Dera Baba Nanak in India's Punjab with Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, Pakistan, a shrine associated with Guru Nanak Dev, the founder of Sikhism. The visa-free arrangement allows Indian pilgrims to visit the gurdwara and return on the same day, subject to applicable travel arrangements.
However, the corridor has remained closed to pilgrim movement from the Indian side since May 7, 2025, when India launched strikes on nine terror targets in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir under Operation Sindoor, following the Pahalgam terror attack.
Pakistan's Foreign Office spokesperson said Islamabad remained willing to facilitate religious pilgrims once the restrictions were lifted, reiterating that the country welcomed visitors of all faiths to its religious sites.
Khan said Pakistan issued more than 9,000 visas to Indian religious pilgrims in 2025, including Sikh and Hindu devotees. It also granted over 4,000 additional visas to Sikh pilgrims during the first half of this year.
"Pakistan looks forward to welcoming a large number of Sikh pilgrims at Nankana Sahib later this month to mark the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji," he said.
Khan also highlighted the Kartarpur Corridor as a special initiative to facilitate Sikh pilgrims, saying it had enabled more than 5,000 devotees to visit the shrine daily and return on the same day.
He referred to the 1974 Protocol on Visits to Religious Shrines between India and Pakistan, which provides a framework for facilitating religious pilgrimages between the two countries.
The spokesperson further said Pakistan was taking steps to preserve Buddhist heritage sites, including those in Taxila and Takht-i-Bahi, and had established a special task force for their protection.

Manufacturing corporate sector’s GVA grows 9.28% in FY25: Govt survey
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh emerged as the five largest contributors to manufacturing GVA
The gross value added (GVA) of India’s manufacturing corporate sector grew 9.28% in 2024-25, while the number of factories in operation and total employment increased by 3.45% and 7.57%, respectively, according to the latest Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) released by the ministry of statistics and programme implementation on Wednesday.
The manufacturing corporate sector accounted for more than 89% of the total GVA during the financial year, underlining its dominant contribution to the country’s registered industrial output.
The survey also recorded a 7.25% increase in the gross value of plant and machinery in the registered manufacturing sector over the previous year. Net value added per factory in operation rose 6.59%, while GVA per person engaged increased by 2.25%.
Also Read | India’s manufacturing growth momentum eases in Oct
The ministry released Volume I and the Summary Results of Factory Sector of ASI 2024-25, along with unit-level data and metadata, providing a detailed picture of the performance, investment patterns, employment and output of India’s registered manufacturing sector.
The five leading industries — food products, textiles, basic metals, motor vehicles and wearing apparel — together accounted for more than 41% of total manufacturing employment during 2024-25.
Geographically, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh emerged as the five largest contributors to manufacturing GVA, collectively accounting for more than 54% of the national total.
The survey highlighted a significant concentration of capital and production among larger factories. Units with investment of ₹10 crore or more in plant and machinery constituted 15.84% of operational factories but accounted for 87.42% of total fixed capital, 59.66% of employment, 76.82% of gross output and 78.07% of net value added.
Also Read | Solving Make in India’s aluminium conundrum
In contrast, factories with investment of up to ₹5 crore represented 78.69% of operational units. However, their contribution to fixed capital was 10.55%, while they accounted for 34.32% of persons engaged, 19.24% of total output and 17.61% of net value added.
A similar concentration was evident when factories were classified by output. Units producing more than ₹10 crore worth of output accounted for 47.63% of operational factories but contributed 98.10% of total output and 97.87% of net value added. They also accounted for 95.55% of fixed capital and 88.78% of employment.
The ASI is the principal source of industrial statistics on the organised manufacturing sector and provides information on capital formation, employment, wages, input costs, output and value addition. Its findings are also used in compiling national and state-level national accounts statistics.
Also Read | Indian manufacturing is learning to produce better, not just more
The detailed publications supplement the factsheet released on September 30, 2026, and provide results at the national, state and industry levels. Volume I contains detailed factory-sector statistics classified according to the National Industrial Classification (NIC), 2008, while the summary publication presents key indicators of industrial performance across states and Union territories.
The survey covers registered factories, certain bidi and cigar manufacturing establishments, electricity undertakings and eligible establishments with 100 or more employees. Data are collected electronically through a dedicated web portal.

The measure, which may face legal challenges, requires girls who want to play in girls' sports to produce documentation from a healthcare provider who has verified "the student's biological sex" relying on the student's reproductive anatomy — in other words, a genital exam — genetic makeup or their natural testosterone levels. Due to how expensive genetic and testosterone testing can be, the genital exams are the most accessible option.
In the aftermath of Election Day, social media users circulated a rumor that Washington voters passed an anti-trans measure that would allegedly subject girls who want to play school sports in the state to genital inspections. 
The rumor spread on X, Threads and Bluesky. Some posts shared additional alleged context, claiming that the ballot measure would subject children who want to play in girls' sports to genital inspections. Others dismissed these claims as a "fantasy."
Washington voters did, in fact, pass a measure called Initiative 26-638 aimed at banning trans girls from playing in girls' sports. The act requires medical providers to "verify" a student's biological sex using reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels.
In theory, the law does not explicitly require genital exams for anyone because it provides three options for sex verification. In practice, due to how expensive genetic and testosterone testing can be, the genital exams are the most accessible option, according to child advocacy groups and medical providers who oppose the provision.
It is worth noting these tests cannot necessarily definitively determine a person's biological sex, which scientists say is a complex category.
The measure subjects every girl who wishes to play in girls' school sports to sex verification, but does not subject students who wish to participate in boys' sports to the same scrutiny. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association reportedly said earlier this year that it was aware of 10 trans student athletes total in the state; it's unclear how many of these athletes are trans boys, as opposed to trans girls. 
While the Washington secretary of state website indicates that there are still ballots left to count, as of this writing, support for the measure has a 13-point lead over opposition. Furthermore, The Associated Press called the race, stating that the "Yes" vote won.
Snopes, like many credible media publications, relies on AP calls for elections. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
(Some posts stated that the measure was "winning" or had won before AP called the race; ultimately, those posts turned out to be true, even if they called the race early.)
It's worth noting that the act may face legal challenges.
"Many have said that I-638 is likely unconstitutional and we understand there are legal groups and organizations considering litigation," said No Hate in WA State, the main coalition opposing the measure. The American Civil Liberties Union-Washington said in its own statement that it was "exploring all potential next steps to uphold the rights of transgender girls and their access to school sports."
I-638's text, examined
The complete text for I-638 is available on the Washington secretary of state's website. Here's the relevant section (emphasis ours):
NEW SECTION. Sec. 3. A new section is added to chapter 28A.600 RCW to read as follows:
(1) Policies, procedures, rules, and other requirements adopted in accordance with RCW 28A.600.200 by a school district board of directors or a voluntary nonprofit entity must prohibit biologically male students from competing with and against female students in athletic activities with separate classifications for male and female students if the athletic activity is:
(a) Intended for female students only; and
(b) An individual or team competition activity.
(2) A student who elects to participate in individual or team competition activities intended for female students only governed under subsection (1) of this section shall provide, as part of the required routine sports physical examination, a health examination and consent form or other statement signed by the student's personal health care provider that verifies the student's biological sex, relying only on one or more of the following: The student's reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.
As opponents to I-638 have noted, a birth certificate would not be an acceptable form of sex verification under I-638. About 28% of K-12 school-age girls in Washington do not have a personal doctor or nurse, meaning that it's likely many families would not be able to rely on an established medical history with a health care provider.
The nonpartisan Washington State Parent Teacher Association, the largest volunteer and child advocacy organization in the state, opposed I-638 on the grounds that it would likely require many girls to either undergo an intimate, embarrassing and medically unnecessary genital examination or forgo playing in girls' sports. Here's what the organization said (emphasis ours):
Two of the three permitted methods, genetic testing and testosterone measurement, are expensive and unlikely to be covered by insurance for this purpose, since neither is clinically indicated. That makes an examination of reproductive anatomy the most accessible pathway for most families.
The burden falls hardest on rural, uninsured, and lower-income families, and on families without an established relationship with a healthcare provider — who face the added problem that the measure never says what qualifies someone as a student's "personal health care provider."
Doctors and medical professionals opposing the initiative shared similar warnings and noted that major medical organizations advise against pelvic exams for adolescent girls, with some citing psychological harms and potential future avoidance of medical care. The Washington Academy of Family Physicians and the Washington State Nurses Association opposed the measure.
The Seattle Times reported that doctors may interpret the measure differently, given that it's vague and, in some views, "poorly written."

Southern Railway is waiting for clearance from the Research Designs and Standards Organisation (RDSO) for rectifying the gap between the train and the platform at the newly constructed Adambakkam station in the extended portion of the Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS).
The MRTS extension project from Velachery to St. Thomas Mount was cleared and new services to Beach were launched in March 14 this year. However, these trains have not been permitted to stop at Adambakkam station because of safety concerns flagged by the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety (CCRS) Janak Kumar Garg.
After inspecting Puzhithivakkam and Adambakkam stations on the extension line, the CCRS gave clearance for commercial operation of MRTS services, while prescribing speed restrictions and disallowing stoppages at Adambakkam station. A senior official of Southern Railway said a software simulation has determined the changes that could be made to the platform at Adambakkam to rectify the gap between the train and the platform, caused by a sharp curve, which could be unsafe for passengers while boarding and alighting.
These simulations were submitted to theCommissioner of Railway Safety (CRS), Southern Circle, Bengaluru, who directed that the results be sent to the RDSO for scrutiny and comments. The Southern Railway officials are awaiting the RDSO’s response.
Social activist V. Rama Rao urged railway officials to speed up the rectification work at Adambakkam station, as hundreds of commuters from Nanganallur are forced to go to Puzhuthivakkam to use the MRTS services.

India’s anaemia burden is not in doubt. The fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) found that more than half of women and about two-thirds of young children are anaemic. In this context, double-fortified salt (DFS) — fortified with iodine and iron — is often proposed as a potentially transformative solution. However, the case for DFS rests on convenience: everyone consumes salt, so why not add iron to it? But convenience is not efficacy, and a policy that asks the country to continue consuming salt to deliver iron deserves closer scrutiny.
Iron fortification of salt is a vehicle that cuts against public health. Indians consume, by most estimates, roughly twice the five grams of salt a day recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). About one in three adults has hypertension, and India’s own non-communicable disease (NCD) action plan commits to a 30% relative reduction in salt intake.

Insurtech Go Digit reported a 31.1% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) to ₹142.4 Cr from ₹206.8 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. The insurtech major's profit also declined 62.4% sequentially from ₹378.61 Cr in the June quarter. The decline in profitability came despite a marginal increase in insurance revenue, which rose 1.7% to ₹2,720.5 Cr during the quarter from ₹2,674.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. Sequentially, insurance revenue increased 2.1% from ₹2,665.6 Cr. Segment-wise, Motor Third Party (TP) insurance remained Go Digit's largest business, contributing ₹1,066.1 Cr to insurance revenue in Q2 FY27, up 8.3% YoY. Motor Own Damage (OD) insurance revenue grew at a faster pace of 11.4% YoY to ₹640.64 Cr. The company's gross written premium for the quarter dipped by 3.6% YoY to ₹2,571 Cr while gross direct premium, dipped 1.2% to ₹2,351 Cr. However, the company's insurance service result, which reflects the profitability of its insurance operations before investment and other financial income, sunk 73.4% YoY to ₹43 Cr from ₹161.98 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The figure also fell 62.3% sequentially from ₹114 Cr. The deterioration in the insurance service result came as insurance service expenses increased 22.4% YoY to ₹2,607.73 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹2,130.85 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Incurred claims rose 9.2% to ₹1,968.03 Cr from ₹1,802.96 Cr, while employee benefit expenses increased 4.3% to ₹95.48 Cr. Commission expenses, on the other hand, declined 2.6% YoY to ₹781.88 Cr from ₹803.10 Cr. Other insurance service expenses increased 1.7% to ₹94.52 Cr. On the investment front, Go Digit reported a 20.6% YoY increase in investment income to ₹368.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹305.5 Cr in the year-ago period. However, investment income declined 39.2% sequentially from ₹606.47 Cr. The company's net finance result, which includes investment income and insurance finance income or expenses, increased 28.6% YoY to ₹196.94 Cr. Consequently, Go Digit's profit before tax (PBT) declined 31.2% YoY to ₹190.18 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹276.30 Cr in Q2 FY26. The figure was also down 62.4% sequentially from ₹505.96 Cr in Q1 FY27. Total tax expense stood at ₹47.79 Cr during the quarter, comprising current tax of ₹3.93 Cr and deferred tax of ₹43.86 Cr. This compared with a total tax expense of ₹69.51 Cr in Q2 FY26. For the first half of FY27 (H1 FY27), Go Digit reported a 3.2% YoY decline in net profit to ₹521 Cr from ₹538.23 Cr in H1 FY26. Insurance revenue increased 4.5% YoY to ₹5,386.09 Cr during the six-month period. Shares of Go Digit ended today’s trading session 1.05% higher at ₹260.30.

The claim referred to a segment from an extended interview with El-Sayed on "60 Minutes," available to view on YouTube. In it, El-Sayed was asked about parental control over education and the interviewer cited one example being the debate over transgender kids playing sports. In response, El-Sayed made the argument that rather than try to shield kids from things they may not understand, it is a parent’s job to guide them through it. There was no mention of locker rooms or male genitalia, nor was there evidence El-Sayed ever made such a statement.
Rumors that Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed allegedly said it was OK for girls or young women to see male genitals in their locker rooms because they could see them just as easily on the internet are circulating.
People on X shared a purported clip of an interview with El-Sayed, with one person claiming, "Abdul El Sayed just embroiled himself in national scandal by saying we should let girls see men in their locker room because they can SEE IT ANYWAY on the internet."
The claim, including different versions of supposed direct quotes from El-Sayed on the matter, circulated online in anticipation of the 2026 midterm elections, in which El-Sayed opposed Republican Mike Rogers.
Can someone please check his hard drive? 😳 "Your daughters are going to see male g***tals anyway…so who cares if they see it in their locker room…" -Abdul El Sayed
— Liz Churchill (@liz_churchill10) November 2, 2026
The clip shared with the claim was authentic, but the alleged quotes on the subject attributed to El-Sayed were fabricated. We reached out to El-Sayed to ask if the alleged quotes accurately reflected his views and will update this article if we hear back.
Neither the clip itself nor the full-length version of the same interview showed El-Sayed made the statement, and there was no evidence he ever made such a statement publicly.
Rather, those sharing the claim were hyperbolizing one of El-Sayed's responses during an interview on "60 Minutes."
On Nov. 1, "60 Minutes" aired a segment about the contentious Michigan Senate race between El-Sayed and Rogers that featured interviews with both candidates. The segment is available to watch on the "60 Minutes" YouTube channel, and a transcript of the segment that aired is available to read on CBS News.
"60 Minutes" also posted extended interviews with the candidates to the show's YouTube page.
Social media users twisted El-Sayed's response to the question at the 44:30 mark of his extended interview into the version of the claim that circulated on social media.
The response came during a conversation about the protection of rights, including rights to religious and sexual preferences, that some individuals might not understand.
Interviewer Ross Douthat asked El-Sayed:
What about the rights of parents to control over their children's education? Because a lot of places where there's tension between Islam and Muslim voters and what I'm calling cultural liberalism are around issues like what is taught in school, what happens with transgender kids on sports teams, and so on, right? These are places where rights are in conflict. What do you think happens there?
El-Sayed did not immediately address the transgender kids in sports specifically. Instead, he explained a broader approach to his thinking behind the issue:
You have a phone in your pocket. You can get access to anything and everything in the whole world. All the world's information in your pocket. The notion, somehow, that you are going to prevent your child from being exposed to something that you may find disagreeable, and that that is going to be because of school, is so profoundly outdated.
Because of course, you have all the information and they have all the information. So here's the thing about it. I think it's really important for us to recognize that the free flow of information is actually a beautiful thing. It's really important. And the most important thing you can do is not try to protect a person from seeing a thing, it's about trying to make sure that as you coach your kids through the world, that you are engaging with them and saying, "Here's what I believe. Here's what you may see in the world."
You get to make your choices about who you're going to be in the world, but that's going to require us to make do with the fact that the internet is a real thing and this debate about "what's taught in a classroom," I think, has been made intro a cultural flashpoint because a lot of the folks who want to make this a topic of conversation don't want to be talking about the real issues that we face in our lives.
It was this part of his response that critics on social media latched onto, turning it from a hypothetical conversation about fundamental rights to a made-up example about male genitals in girls' locker rooms, presumably in an attempt to extend his line of reasoning to that specific scenario despite him not doing so himself.
Regarding transgender kids in sports specifically, El-Sayed said:
A lot of the culture war issues that get fought right now are about trying to distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas, can't afford our groceries, can't see a doctor, are worried about whether or not our kids are going to have a good life. And instead, we're out here talking about who gets to play what sport. Which should be a question for the people who govern sports. I'm not running to govern sports.
My interest is in making sure people have the ability to live a good life, that they can get the healthcare that they need. That they can breathe clean air, drink clean water. That they've got good schools are well-funded in the first place.
A comprehensive search of Bing, Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo about El-Sayed saying a statement such as the one in the claim yielded no credible results.
Given the tumultuous nature of the Michigan Senate race and the national attention it drew, had El-Sayed actually said the statement or one like it, major media outlets would have reported on it.
El-Sayed won election in Michigan on Nov. 3 and said during his victory speech of his opponent, "You chose hate and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again."

A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.
“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”
The bill sacrifices caution for speed
The sea change in Congress following the midterm elections could put the bill in an even more precarious position, giving Democrats a better shot at pushing for their priorities in the bill and potentially triggering a fight with President Donald Trump. Should it come up for a vote during the current lame-duck session or get kicked to next year, the bill will test whether Democrats and Republicans can actually get something done to address some of the biggest issues voters carried with them to the polls: rising energy costs and data centers encroaching on their communities.
“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge.
Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.
The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.
The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.
“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”
If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.
Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”
The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.
The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.
The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.
Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action.
“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”
They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.
“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”
Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release.
“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.
Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.
“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.
Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.
BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.
Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.
One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.
The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.
Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.
Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.
The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

Keralam Health Minister K. Muraleedharan on Friday said the government would take further action after receiving a report from an expert committee probing the allegations that expired doses of Remdesivir were administered to Nipah patients in previous years.
However, critical care specialist Dr A S Anoop Kumar, who treated several Nipah patients at a private hospital, said that patients who died due to Nipah were not administered doses of Remdesivir.
Former Health Minister Veena George said that allegations raised by Mr. Muraleedharan are suspicious as the medicine has an expiry period of 2.5 to 5 years.
In a reply to a submission by Congress MLA Mathew Kuzhalnadan in the Assembly on Thursday, Mr. Muraleedharan said that Remdesivir procured in 2021 had an expiry date of May 2023 but might have been administered to patients admitted to Kozhikode Medical College till 2025.
Speaking to reporters in Kozhikode, Mr. Muraleedharan said the information presented to the Assembly was based on reports from responsible officials of the Health Department and that he would not make further comments until the expert committee submitted its findings.
The government would investigate whether the deaths of Nipah patients were linked to the administration of expired medicine and whether other patients who received the drug had suffered any adverse effects, Mr Muraleedharan said.
“There are several doubts regarding the medicine, including whether it was administered after its expiry date. We will investigate and take a decision,” he said.
The Minister clarified that there were no concerns about the quality or efficacy of Remdesivir itself and that the issue under investigation was whether expired doses had been administered to patients.
Recalling the procurement of the drug during the Nipah outbreak after the UDF government came to power, he said efforts to source it from different parts of the country had failed as the available stocks in Mumbai had expired.
Subsequently, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) informed the government that the medicine was available in Bahrain, following which it was procured within 48 hours, he said.
He said patients who received the medicine within its validity period had recovered and asserted that the controversy concerned its expiry date rather than the drug’s efficacy.
Mr. Muraleedharan said the expert committee headed by Dr R Aravind, head of the Infectious Diseases department at Thiruvananthapuram Medical College, would conduct an impartial examination without any preconceived conclusions.
The probe would also examine how the medicine was procured and supplied, the role of intermediaries and the functioning of KMSCL.
The government would investigate whether any agents were involved in the procurement process, he said.
The Minister also said the Kozhikode Medical College superintendent had informed him that the packaging of the Remdesivir medicine listed an expiry date but did not mention its manufacturing date. Both details are normally required on medicine packaging, and the discrepancy would be examined, he said.
“Further decisions on the issues would be taken after receiving the expert committee’s findings,” he said.

AI models are increasingly being built to do more than answer questions. Some are now designed to make specific decisions, such as whether a customer query should go to a sales or support team, whether a document needs further review, or whether an AI agent has completed a task correctly. In India, Kerala-based ConvAI Innovations was one of the first to explore this category with Laya, an open-weight decision model intended to run locally on devices such as laptops and phones. Hyderabad-based PurpleTalk’s research lab, Sthānika AI, has also developed Sieve, a family of decision models that returns probabilities for a fixed set of possible answers. Both startups are betting that specialised models can make these decisions faster and more efficiently than general-purpose AI systems. The space has now attracted Sarvam AI, one of India’s prominent homegrown AI model developers. The company introduced Prism, a decision model built on its 105B-parameter foundation model. Sarvam says Prism combines high accuracy with low response times, while allowing enterprises to customise and run it on their own infrastructure. The launch raises a bigger question for India’s AI ecosystem, especially given the implications on cost, reliability and speed: Are decision models the opportunity for Indian AI startups to compete with global players, rather than trying to match them across every general-purpose AI capability? What Are Decision Models, And Why Now? Most large language models (LLMs) are designed to generate text. Even when asked to make a simple choice, they typically produce a response that another software system must interpret. This can add processing time, increase costs and introduce inconsistencies. Decision models approach the problem differently. They receive information, a question and a defined set of possible answers, then return a score or probability for each option. Instead of generating a paragraph explaining which department should handle a customer complaint, for instance, the model can assign probabilities to sales, support and billing. This makes them useful for repetitive tasks performed at scale, including customer-support routing, content moderation, fraud checks, security screening and evaluating the actions of AI agents. General-purpose models can perform these tasks too, but a specialised decision model may be faster and easier to integrate into workflows that require predictable outputs. The category gained visibility with Jev, the first public model from TypeSafe AI. Global companies, including Microsoft and Perplexity, have since introduced their own decision-model offerings. Indian startups are also developing alternatives, with different priorities around local deployment, openness and enterprise use. How Sarvam Is Positioning Prism Prism is built on Sarvam 105B, the company’s large language model, but is fine-tuned specifically for making decisions. Rather than generating a sequence of words to arrive at an answer, it evaluates the available options in a single processing pass and returns a probability for each. According to Sarvam, Prism recorded an average score of 71.8 across three evaluation indices, with a median response time of 44 milliseconds on an Nvidia B200 GPU. The company said this was the highest average score among the 25 decision models it tested that responded in under 100 milliseconds. Sarvam also tested whether the order of available options would change the model’s decision. It reported that Prism produced consistent results across 2,000 questions after applying a fixed ordering mechanism before scoring. The company further said that Prism’s observed error rates were lower than its predicted error rates across the confidence thresholds it tested, including in Indian languages. These are company-reported results, and independent testing across comparable workloads will be important to establish how they translate into production performance. Sarvam is releasing Prism’s weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. This allows developers to access the model’s trained parameters, adapt them and deploy the model on their own infrastructure, subject to the licence terms. It is also available through an API. The company is targeting applications such as customer-support routing, document intelligence, security checks, prompt-injection detection and evaluation of AI-agent activity. Its positioning is not simply about offering another language model, but about adding a specialised decision-making component to the broader AI stack. India’s Decision Model Race Heats Up Laya, Sieve and Prism reflect different approaches to decision models in India. Laya prioritises small models that can run locally, while PurpleTalk’s research lab Sthānika AI focuses on open-weight Sieve models, with an emphasis on evaluation and tasks such as intent detection and AI-agent tool selection. Sarvam’s Prism builds on its foundation-model capabilities, with speed, confidence calibration, Indian-language performance and open-weight deployment among its key selling points. Articul8, an enterprise AI company, is also developing the category through Bivia, its multimodal decision model designed for domain-specific, evidence-backed decisions across text, images, documents, audio and video. Ananthanarayanan S, managing director for India at Articul8, said Sarvam’s launch adds to the growing range of general-purpose models, while positioning Bivia around a different enterprise need. He said Articul8 benchmarks Bivia against models such as Jev and evaluates it through a broader enterprise lens, including its ability to abstain when evidence is insufficient. He believes that the competition, however, will extend beyond benchmark scores and response times. Enterprises need models that can handle unfamiliar situations reliably and integrate with existing systems through domain grounding, orchestration and execution frameworks. Prism has also drawn scrutiny from developers and independent evaluators. Sandipan Kundu, a developer relations and AI engineer focused on fine-tuning and inference, and the builder of Tensorant, a platform for fine-tuning, evaluating and deploying open models, said on X that the model appeared capable but questioned whether its 44-millisecond median latency claim reflected real-world performance. He cited a p95 latency of 420 milliseconds in his testing. He also flagged the cost of self-hosting a model of its size. Separately, Faizan Shaik, a software engineer at Atlan, an enterprise data and metadata management platform, shared results from the company’s Decision Bench, where Prism scored 91.5% across 1,071 decisions on 36 public datasets, placing it 12th among 22 models. His evaluation reported a median latency of 65 milliseconds on a B200 GPU. These assessments suggest that Prism is competitive, but also underline the need to examine performance across different benchmarks and deployment conditions. For Indian builders, the opportunity lies in proving that specialised decision models can deliver measurable gains in cost, latency and reliability across real-world workflows.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

Some images of the Paris landmark shared on social media were authentic but miscaptioned. Others displayed evidence of AI generation. The Eiffel Tower has a well-documented history of being lit blue for various occasions, but there was no evidence that this happened in celebration of Democratic victories in the 2026 U.S. midterms.
A rumor that the Eiffel Tower was illuminated with blue lights to celebrate Democrats' victory in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections circulated in early November.
Following the election, people on social media shared purported images of the world-famous Paris landmark lit blue, with one post claiming this signified France stood "in solidarity with the new leadership in the House and Senate."
The claim gained popularity as the national conversation focused on the results of the midterms, in which Democrats, typically represented by the color blue, landed a decisive victory. The claim's popularity led Snopes readers to ask that we look into it.
There was no evidence France illuminated the Eiffel Tower blue to celebrate the results of the U.S. midterms.
Rather, some of the images shared in the posts were authentic, but taken during previous instances of the landmark being illuminated blue. Others displayed evidence of AI generation and were therefore fake. As such, we've rated this claim false.
For instance, one Facebook user shared a photo of the Eiffel Tower illuminated blue with the text, "They gave us the Statue of Liberty and now they lit up the Eiffel Tower in blue to celebrate with America." But that image shows the landmark illuminated blue with the 12 stars of the European Union, which was done in both 2008 and 2022 to celebrate French leadership of the EU. The Facebook user who shared the image also pointed out that some users were "attaching erroneous meaning to an unrelated photo."
Similar images to the one shared in the post from both 2008 and 2022 are available to view on the Getty Images repository, but our searches returned none from 2026.
Other images shared in some versions of the claim appeared to be generated using artificial intelligence.
The artificial intelligence detector Pangram said it was highly likely this particular image, used in the most-popular instances of the rumor, was generated with AI, though it should be noted that such platforms are not always reliable.
However, both OpenAI's Verify tool and Google's Gemini SynthID scan also confirmed the presence of a SynthID, which Google describes as "a technology developed by Google DeepMind that adds imperceptible digital watermarks to AI-generated content."
(OpenAI Verify)
(Pangram)
(Google)
A search of the Eiffel Tower's location tag on Instagram revealed dozens of posts that included photos of the landmark the week of the U.S. midterm elections, many of them at night, that clearly shows the landmark lit in its usual golden color.
Further, searches of Bing, Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo revealed no credible or relevant results about France illuminating the Eiffel Tower in blue as a result of the midterm elections, which would have been widely reported as international news. 
The official Eiffel Tower website has an entire page dedicated to the Eiffel Tower's blue illuminations, which states that "over the years, the monument has been bathed in blue to mark major events and support symbolic causes," naming "Europe, autism awareness, children's rights, tributes, or the colors of the French and Ukrainian flags," specifically.
According to the website, the first day the landmark was illuminated blue was May 9, 2006, in celebration of the 20th anniversary of Europe Day.
The site included other instances of the tower going fully blue in 2008, 2012, 2019 and 2021, as well as other instances of the blue lights being part of an overall display to convey the colors of the French and Ukrainian flags on the landmark.
There are other examples of the landmark's blue hue over the years available online. Photographer Peter Talke posted a photo of the Eiffel Tower illuminated in blue to his blog on Aug. 31, 2009. In September 2026, an Instagram user posted a blue-tinged Eiffel Tower among other photographs from Paris.
We reached out to the Eiffel Tower Operating Co. for further comment and will update this article if we hear back.
For further reading, we investigated a similar claim about Canada lighting Niagara Falls blue to celebrate Democrats' midterm wins.

The Large Hadron Collider has been slamming protons together for years. But recently, a proton collision produced an improbable result that is the first step toward exploring the so-called “zeptoverse”—a scale of reality many, many times smaller than an atom. This would be the smallest scale of the physical world ever explored and may defy our expectations of how physics works.
While crashing protons together at nearly the speed of light, scientists at CERN found evidence of one of the most improbable decays of matter—so unlikely that it’s a phenomenon physicists have been hoping to observe for more than four decades. The collision produced numerous particles, including some known as neutral B mesons, and scientists found signals indicating that one of these had decayed into a muon and an antimuon.
Mesons decay all the time. These tiny particles, smaller than atoms, arise from collisions between other particles and exist only briefly before transforming into other particles. Muons, on the other hand, are similar to the electrons found in atoms, but about 200 times heavier. Scientists study these particles and their decays to test the predictions of current physics and search for clues to unknown particles.
The standard model—the sort of bible of particle physics—predicts that for every 10 billion decays of neutral B mesons, this transformation will occur once. In other words, even if scientists were to observe 10 billion of these particles decaying, they would expect to find, on average, only a single muon and antimuon. This discovery is the first time an experiment has obtained evidence of this phenomenon, the details of which the researchers have made available in a preprint on arXiv.
“Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than 40 years,” Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team, said in a press release from CERN. “Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.”
The extraordinary rarity of this process explains why it’s taken decades of research to arrive at this discovery. But upgrades to the Large Hadron Collider in 2024 also made observing this phenomenon possible. The revamp enabled faster data collection, and new machine-learning techniques allowed researchers “to suppress the vast background of processes that would have otherwise swamped the signals from these rare beauty-particle decays,” as CERN described it in its statement.
This decay opens a new avenue for investigating the limits of what scientists have been able to observe. For now, the results are consistent with current physics predictions, but future measurements could reveal phenomena unique to the zeptoverse, which describes the scale where distances are measured in zeptometers (equivalent to one quadrillionth of a meter). To put this unit into perspective, a typical atom is about 100,000 million zeptometers in diameter. That’s also about the difference in size between you and one of your skin cells.
Beyond the zeptoverse lie even smaller scales, such as the Planck length, which is about 60 trillion times smaller than a zeptometer and the smallest theoretically possible unit in physics. Scientists still don’t know whether anything truly exists at that level, but it’s generally believed that physics as we know it completely breaks down on that scale. However, if scientists could gain access to this micro world, it could help us understand the first infinitesimal fraction of a second after the Big Bang, when the whole universe was such a size.
But, for now, much of what might happen there remains in the realm of speculation.

A BioWare documentary is set to arrive next year
Massive Effect: The BioWare Story started filming two years before EA shut down the studio.
BioWare is no more after Electronic Arts shut down the storied studio last month. As it turns out, a film crew documented the studio's final act. A documentary called Massive Effect: The BioWare Story is in the works, as Deadline reported, and it's expected to arrive next year. Filming started two years before BioWare shut down.
The documentary — which Canada's Super Channel commissioned — will cover "the story of how a group of underdogs from the Alberta prairies built one of the most beloved studios in gaming, told by the people who were there," producer Shane Fennessey said in a statement on X. "Now, with the shocking news of the studio's closure, we carry the responsibility of telling how the story ends."
Massive Effect: The BioWare Storyhttps://t.co/ye1n5oEkBC pic.twitter.com/7IYLjOYywk
— Shane Fennessey (@ShaneFen) November 5, 2026
The movie will cover the 31-year history of BioWare, with founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip all making appearances. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect director Casey Hudson will feature, along with FemShep voice actor Jennifer Hale, former EA CEO John Riccitiello, several BioWare developers and other figures from the gaming world.
BioWare fans have a chance to feature in the film, as the team behind it has set up a website where they can share photos, videos, cosplay, fan art and other memories about the studio. Fans have also been campaigning to save Mass Effect, including by petitioning the Canadian government to help former BioWare workers buy the studio.
EA, which is now owned primarily by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, shuttered BioWare after its last few games failed to meet the company's sales expectations. The studio, which had around 50 workers after previous cuts, was in the early stages of making the next Mass Effect game — a trailer for which leaked after EA announced BioWare's demise. Bloomberg reported that, rather than fund the full development of Mass Effect 5, EA opted to put its resources into making Star Wars Battlefront 3, which has not been formally revealed.
