What to know about the presidential wiretapping scandal rocking Indonesia
- Published
Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations might have been spied on.
Several senior figures of Prabowo's administration have been embroiled in the wiretapping scandal, including his chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - who is not related to the president despite his name.
It is unfolding against what many have interpreted as a widening rift between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo - otherwise know as Jokowi - who had thrown his support behind Prabowo's 2024 presidential campaign.
"Listyo's position, as we know, is actually very close to Jokowi," Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told BBC Indonesian.
"So now it's practically said that they're going their separate ways."
What happened?
Listyo Sigit Prabowo, the president's chief of staff, was arrested on Tuesday along with two senior police officers for allegedly wiretapping President Prabowo.
The three men are suspected of keying phone numbers, including Prabowo's, into the police's official electronic surveillance system - which allows authorities to intercept communications - without following proper procedures, such as obtaining an investigation warrant or case report.
Authorities say the operation was discovered last week after a tip-off from a police officer. But they believe the alleged wiretapping stretches back to 2025, when Listyo was serving as the national police chief.
This could amount to treason, as it involved "sensitive information" that could "endanger the interests and sovereignty of the nation", a spokesperson for the president told reporters on Wednesday.
In Indonesia, treason is punishable by life imprisonment or even the death penalty - though the country has not executed anyone in a decade.
The spokesperson said the motive behind the alleged wiretapping remained unclear.
It was not just President Prabowo who was targeted in the alleged wiretapping operation, either. Other targets included politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople, authorities said.
On Thursday evening, police named a fourth suspect: Slamet Uliandi, from the national police criminal investigation unit. But he was not detained due to his ill health after suffering a stroke, according to authorities.
Listyo, who was appointed the president's chief of staff last month, was sacked from his new position shortly after his arrest.
This is not the first wiretapping scandal to have involved Indonesia's leaders. In 2014, several wiretapping devices were discovered at Jokowi's official residence when he was the governor of Jakarta. Former president Megawati Soekarnoputri claimed in 2024 that she had avoided using her personal mobile phone number because she was the target of wiretapping.
Indonesia's police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters on Thursday that the probe into wiretapping was "purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else".
But many see it as the latest blow in a disintegrating alliance between President Prabowo and former president Jokowi, who led the country from 2014 to 2024.
Prabowo vs Jokowi
Jokowi had thrown his support behind Prabowo in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, as part of an alliance that ultimately propelled Prabowo to become Indonesia's next leader.
Riding to victory with him was Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Jokowi's eldest son, who became Indonesia's vice president.
Two years on, that alliance appears to be fracturing - even if neither party has confirmed the rift.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many of Jokowi's allies into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Meanwhile, uncertainty also looms over Gibran, Jokowi's son, who is mired in a growing controversy over the validity of his high school credentials, a pre-requisite to run for vice presidency. He now faces calls to be disqualified from his job, on the grounds that he should not have been eligible as a candidate.
The wiretapping scandal and subsequent arrest of Listyo - who rose to the top of the police force in Jokowi's administration, and is seen as one of the ex-president's longtime allies - is now adding to the tensions between Prabowo and Jokowi.
When asked about the wiretapping incident after the court session on Thursday, Jokowi told reporters that "we should all respect the ongoing legal process".
This latest scandal comes during a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. His flagship free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
Experts, meanwhile, say all this has distracted from the more pressing challenges that Indonesians are facing on the ground - from economic uncertainties to environmental pollution.
In recent months, protesters have taken to the streets to pressure the government on a range of issues such as toxic wildfire haze, corruption, and cost-of-living woes.
"It's like we're living in a country on autopilot," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia, told BBC Indonesian.
"Because the way the government operates proves that it's not the people's interests that are being pursued, but rather the interests of individual groups."

Google is ditching Firebase Studio soon, and it wants you to use its newer AI tools instead
The company is going all-in on Antigravity and Google AI Studio.
In March, Google announced it was "sunsetting" Firebase Studio, its online integrated development environment (IDE), in favor of coding tools that put AI at the center. The company's preference for Antigravity and Google AI Studio serves its broader push around Gemini, but it also leaves anyone who liked Firebase Studio's approach in the lurch.
The ability to create new workspaces and sign up to use Firebase Studio ended on June 22, and developers have until March 22, 2027 to export their work to another IDE before it's shut down completely and all remaining data is deleted. Until then, Firebase Studio is in limbo, and deciding on an alternative largely comes down to how developers want AI to be incorporated into their development process.
Retiring Firebase Studio streamlines Google's development workflow
Google conceived of Firebase Studio as a coding tool that could connect directly to Firebase, backend services it provides to developers that cover everything from databases to web hosting. From the launch of the IDE in 2025, Google has imagined that AI agents would play a role in development. What's changed since then is how central AI has become. Firebase Studio offers an AI chatbot experience that can prototype and tweak apps and handle other development tasks, but the bulk of Firebase Studio is still devoted to editing code. In 2026, a growing number of coding projects start with a prompt, and thanks to the popularity of vibe coding, some users never even deal with the raw code.
Both of Google's newer coding tools, Antigravity and Google AI Studio, are designed for that reality, and since Firebase itself is sticking around and either tool can connect to it, a separate Firebase-focused IDE isn't essential. Google more or less framed its decision that way when it announced it was retiring the tool. "To streamline your workflow and make it clearer where you should start building, we're beginning the process of sunsetting Firebase Studio," the company wrote in March.
Firebase Studio alternatives
If you'd prefer to stay in Google's ecosystem, you can either switch to Google AI Studio or Antigravity. Google AI Studio is "the fastest path from prompt to full-stack production app," according to Google, which means its interface prioritizes prompts and chatting with AI. Like Firebase Studio, it's also web-based, so you can access it from any browser. In comparison, Antigravity is a desktop app that's meant to run locally on your computer. Its interface is designed for users to directly interact with their code, while also directing multiple AI agents that can work on their own. Notably, it also supports AI models other than Google's own.
Most other coding tools tend to follow a similar logic, where the coder is a team leader for agents that handle the first pass. Cursor, now owned by SpaceX, is a popular option. Both Anthropic and OpenAI also have their own AI-focused coding tools in Claude Code and Codex, respectively. Using AI in projects can come with associated costs, either in the form of subscriptions, paying for tokens, or both. Which tools developers migrate to after Firebase Studio shuts down will likely be determined as much by price as by the interface and each tool's future.

Kalshi is having a bad week in the federal court system. Two circuit appeals courts rejected the prediction market’s latest attempts to block state gambling laws in Connecticut, New York, and Nevada. Kalshi is separately facing a new lawsuit filed by the Arkansas attorney general.
In all cases involving Kalshi and state governments around the US, the main issue is whether state gambling laws apply to prediction markets despite Kalshi’s claim that its platform offers “swaps” that can only be regulated by the US Commodity Futures Exchange (CFTC). The Trump administration is on Kalshi’s side, with Donald Trump Jr. serving as an advisor to Kalshi in exchange for a generous equity deal.
“Kalshi insists that its products are not gambling,” but “Arkansas law is concerned with substance, not semantics,” Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said yesterday when announcing his lawsuit against Kalshi. Kalshi’s prediction market lets customers “wager money on the outcome of just about anything” despite the fact that “gambling on an unregulated platform is squarely prohibited by Arkansas law,” he said.
Griffin’s lawsuit was filed in an Arkansas state court. Kalshi violated state law by offering gambling to people as young as 18 and by failing to pay taxes or comply with other restrictions, Griffin said. Arkansas law permits gambling within certain limits, such as an age minimum of 21 years old for electronic wagering accounts.
“Instead of obtaining the licenses, submitting to the oversight, complying with the restrictions, and paying the taxes required of lawful gambling operators in Arkansas, Kalshi opened its platforms to Arkansas consumers, including individuals as young as 18 years old, encouraged them to wager real money on sporting and entertainment events, and profited from those wagers,” Griffin said.

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
- Published
The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.
Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.
It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.
"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."
Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.
But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.
Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.
In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".
There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.
"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.
"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."
A diplomatic dilemma
Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.
Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.
Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.
Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".
The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent détente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.
As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.
One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.
"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.
"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.
To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.
But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.
"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.
"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."
Waiting for winds to change
In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.
Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".
For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.
It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.
But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.
The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.
"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."
In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.
Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.
Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.
In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.
"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.
And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.
For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.
"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people.
 
John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999.
 
Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008).
 
Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum. The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage. Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation. The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services. What Changes For Operators? The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships. For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation. In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage. However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation. The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years. Connecting Phones To Satellites TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators. For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India. For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity. However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use. TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them. TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee. Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator. Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz. For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue. The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market.

A small chit on the dressing-room wall carried Tripura’s bowling plans — the areas to target, the lines to bowl and how to approach individual batters.
Satrajit Lahiri had spent hours studying Saurashtra. Now, he wanted his bowlers to execute the plans.
They did. After three successive defeats, Tripura stunned former champion Saurashtra at home, with 23-year-old off-spinner Sandip Sarkar claiming eight wickets to lead the revival.
Former Bengal cricketer Lahiri, who joined Tripura as coach this season, had closely studied videos of individual Saurashtra players before drawing up specific plans for his bowlers.
“I watched videos of the players, studied each and every one of them from different angles, and planned accordingly. We showed the bowlers what they needed to do and which areas to target. We even put a chit on the dressing-room wall with the plans. The players saw it and executed everything to perfection,” Lahiri told Sportstar from Agartala.
Sarkar was the standout performer. Lahiri was particularly impressed with the youngster’s control and classical off-spin.
“Sandip was terrific. He is a classical off-spinner and should play for the East Zone immediately,” he said.
The attack had clearly defined roles. Sarkar was encouraged to attack, Parvez Sultan was asked to contain the batters and build pressure, while Abhijit Sarkar was used in spells to provide breakthroughs.
India international Mandeep Singh, whose experience has been valuable in guiding the younger players, also helped Sarkar fine-tune his bowling.
“When we played on rank turners, I advised him to occasionally bowl fast, mixing it up with slower deliveries and cross-seam variations. He grasped that quickly and implemented it. He was very impressive and is a quick learner,” Mandeep told this publication.
For Sarkar, the victory was as much about the team’s recovery as his own performance. Tripura had struggled to find its feet early in the season, but the improvement in its collective effort was beginning to show.
“Cricket is a team game, and I have always believed in playing as a unit. We did not have the best start, losing our first three matches, but we have made a strong comeback since then. I feel we have gained a lot of confidence,” he said.
“In the last three matches, our team bonding and understanding have improved. I have always tried to play for the team, and everyone has contributed. We are winning because of our collective effort. I feel good about the way things are going and am confident that we will continue to do well in the coming matches.”
There is a shared geography to the stories of Tripura’s two important contributors. Sarkar and Ridam Paul, who scored 86 and 50 to shore up the batting, both hail from Bamutia in Mohanpur sub-division.
Sarkar began playing at a coaching centre near his home. Cricket was a childhood passion rather than an immediate career ambition. With little family support, he continued playing with friends. Eventually, he went on to captaining Tripura’s Under-25 side for a couple of years and before earning his Ranji Trophy opportunity.
His inspiration has always been Ravichandran Ashwin. The two met during a match in Tamil Nadu last year, when Ashwin watched him bowl, appreciated his efforts and encouraged him to keep practising.
Paul’s contribution was equally important. Tripura’s batting had been a concern, with Mandeep struggling for runs.
Hanuma Vihari, another India international, featured in only one match before deciding to miss the remainder of the season. The BCCI has not granted Tripura a replacement.
“The wicket was difficult to bat on, but the plan was to stay at the crease. We knew things could be difficult early on, and as the conditions eased, I could take control. That is exactly what I tried to do,” Paul said.
He also acknowledged the impact of Vihari’s absence.
“Vihari bhai’s absence was felt. We played a couple of games on rank turners, but we did not lose hope. It is a positive for me as well, from a batting perspective,” he added.
Mandeep sees considerable promise in the youngster.
“Ridam is a huge talent. You will see him setting the stage on fire in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy. He is a solid player,” he said.
He also credited Bikram Kumar Das for taking the shine off the ball in challenging conditions and praised Parvez and Abhijit for their contributions.
Captain Manisankar Murasingh, meanwhile, made effective use of his bowling resources, with his shorter spells keeping Saurashtra guessing.
“Mura is very proactive as captain. He used shorter spells, which left the opposition confused. He has led from the front and is the perfect man to lead this team,” Mandeep said.
Tripura still has work to do, particularly with the bat. But the win against Saurashtra has given the side the belief it badly needed.

Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is “not cool anymore” and so much of the internet has been compromised.
“I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC,” Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair.
Ohanian has a complicated relationship with the internet. He resigned from Reddit in 2020, following the killing of George Floyd, to make room for a Black board member and to pressure the company to reform its content moderation policies. The social site had been notorious for hosting violent and harmful rhetoric. Ohanian reflects on recently learning someone with a Reddit tattoo—once a sign of the site’s success to Ohanian—had since covered it up: “I don’t blame him.”
He now runs venture capital firm Seven Seven Six, which has over $1.3 billion in assets under management. He focuses on sports, where he finds real-life communities “in the age of AI slop” and a “manipulated” internet.
Ohanian is a proponent of the “Dead Internet Theory”—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. “The internet that I grew up on … that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away,” said Ohanian, “because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people.”
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. “Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs,” Ohanian said.
But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google’s AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialisation of these conversations means they are full of “bullshit.” “The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so,” he said.
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, “there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy.”
An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. “There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure,” he said. “I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better.”

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up
- Published
It may be a surprise to some but Jobe Bellingham's call-up to the England senior side has been a long time coming.
The 21-year-old's career path has been very similar to that of his 23-year-old brother Jude - England's star player at the World Cup and one of Real Madrid's best players. Both were stars of the Birmingham City academy before big-money moves to the German Bundesliga and England call-ups.
Jobe's debut for Birmingham came at the age of 16 years and 107 days - 69 days older than Jude when he made his first appearance for the Blues' senior side.
The central midfielder then moved to Sunderland and helped them win promotion to the Premier League before joining German side Borussia Dortmund at the age of 19 in a deal worth up to £31m.
Jude also moved to Dortmund when he was 17, before developing into one of the world's best players and joining Real Madrid.
Having one of the best midfielders in the world as your older brother comes with challenges and Jobe has consistently been compared to his sibling.
But the former Sunderland midfielder is his own player, wearing 'Jobe' on the back of his shirt instead of his family name. He said it was suggested to him by a former coach because "it shows that I'm going my own way".
England manager Thomas Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live it is "a beautiful story".
"They are both good for each other," he added. "My understanding is they are very close.
"It makes life easier for Jobe to come into camp and know his brother is one of the key players in our team. So, that will hopefully help him, but don't forget he is here on his own merits, and he is not here because of his brother."
Jobe is a different type of player to Jude, sitting deeper in the midfield, but is as physically imposing while still being good on the ball.
He is the current captain of the England Under-21 side, and Tuchel said Young Lions head coach Lee Carsley had been pushing for some time for the younger Bellingham to get senior recognition.
"He's the standout player," said Tuchel. "He's the captain, so the door should always be open for the pathway, always be open for special performances over a long period of time.
"That's what Jobe has done on top of it. He found his way, he found his rhythm with Dortmund. He's had an excellent start to his season, is a regular starter and influential."
England host Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November before travelling to Madrid to take on Spain on 15 November in this next international break.
With Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended for the first game, and Bournemouth's Alex Scott out injured after shining on his debut in last month's 7-0 win over Croatia, Tuchel said a natural "opportunity" for Jobe had opened up.
"He deserves to make an impression for us," said the German in his news conference after naming the squad.
"It's an incredible achievement for the family and for the brothers. I saw his excitement straight away and his smile.
"He has an open and calm personality. He's one of five players for the central midfield.
"He's a more defensive player than Jude. So strong on the ball, good physique, a big body, a very physical player and can keep possession.
"It's now up to him, but he's excited and happy and eager to impress, and that's the best foundation to have a good camp for him."
Which other brothers have played for England?
If they get on the pitch together, Jude and Jobe won't be the first brothers to represent the Three Lions.
It has been 19 years since Gary and Phil Neville, who both played for Manchester United, last played together for England, and 30 years since they started.
They first played together for England in 1996 against China, becoming the first siblings to do so since Bobby and Jack Charlton 26 years earlier.
Jack and Bobby were both part of England's 1966 World Cup-winning squad.
Bobby was the younger of the two, but made his Three Lions debut first. He went on to win 106 international caps.
Jack, who was not called into the England team until days before his 30th birthday, won 35 caps.
More recently, brothers Nathaniel and Trevoh Chalobah have both played for England, but never alongside each other.
Nathaniel made his solitary appearance as an injury-time substitute in a 3-2 away win against Spain in a 2018 Nations League game.
His younger brother Trevoh, currently a Como defender, made the first of his three international appearances against Senegal in June 2025 and was in England's 2026 World Cup squad.
1 of 3
'Jobe has shown remarkable progress'
Jobe has shown remarkable progress since last winter. In the first couple of months, following his move from Sunderland to Borussia Dortmund, he seemed timid, as if he was just trying to avoid making any mistakes. His passes rarely, if ever, caused trouble for opposing defences.
Even Dortmund manager Niko Kovac said at one point that he was surprised how long it might take him to get comfortable in the Bundesliga. But hard work in the gym to build up muscle mass in order to become more explosive and the fact that he received plenty of chances in Dortmund's line-up has helped his development.
In the latter stages of last season, his decision-making was much faster and his intensity seemed higher. Still, Dortmund decided to sign Dutch midfielder Joey Veerman, a specialist at making line-breaking passes, in August.
It meant Jobe's place in the starting XI was far from secure at the beginning of this season.
In recent games, Kovac has employed Bellingham in a more advanced role, as one of the two number 10s behind the striker. In this role, Bellingham drove into the final third with pace and showed intensity during pressing sequences.
His performance in the 2-2 draw against Bayern Munich in the Bundesliga last Saturday was arguably his best since his arrival in Germany.

Quick Answer
Windows 11 is testing eight upgrades in Insider builds to reduce daily friction. Key updates include flexible taskbar positioning, faster Windows Search with inline actions, a Battery Status widget, phone-to-PC integration, per-app privacy controls, smarter Windows Hello, anti-glare tools, and enhanced File Explorer previews.
I can’t count how many times I’ve had to drag the window to full size, squint at a bright screen, or open Settings just to turn on dark mode. Each one takes a few seconds, but you repeat them all day. Thankfully, Windows 11 is about to trim a lot of that. Microsoft seems to have noticed, and over the past few months, it has been stacking up small but genuinely useful changes for Windows 11. The best part is that all these features are coming with future updates.
With new optimized features, Windows now feels up to 20% more responsive, with the gains showing up in Start, File Explorer, Search, and more. With the latest Windows Insider release notes, you are in for a eight-feature treat you should know about. One heads-up before we start: not everything is available to everyone yet. Many of these are still being tested in the Windows Insider Experimental channel, so I’ll tell you where each one stands.
Table of Contents
Taskbar customization
For years, the Windows 11 taskbar has been stuck to the bottom of the screen. There was no way to change its position. That is finally changing. Microsoft’s Windows Insider blog confirms that, with the current insider update, users can now park the taskbar on the top, bottom, left, or right edge. Here’s what you can do:
- You can choose icon alignment for every position. On the sides, icons can be top-aligned or centered. On the top or bottom, they can be left-aligned or centered.
- Start, Search, and other flyouts follow the taskbar. Meaning, if you put the taskbar at the top, Start opens from the top.
- On a vertical taskbar, when you choose “Never combine” and turn on labels, every app window gets its own labeled button, so you can see all your windows at a glance.
Moving the taskbar to the side can give you vertical space, handy for developers who want to see more code. To tweak the taskbar, you need to navigate to Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors. You can also choose to make the taskbar smaller, optimal for small screens. Simply choose the “Show smaller taskbar” option to Always, and you get smaller icons and a shorter bar. No restart or sign-out needed.
Things may not work perfectly, though. Auto-hide and the tablet-optimized taskbar don’t work in the new positions, touch gestures are still in progress, and the search box shows up as a plain search icon for now. Aside from this, the Recommended section is getting renamed to Recent, and you can hide your name and profile picture. There are also separate toggles to show or hide Pinned, Recent, and All.
Smarter Windows Search
This one might be the biggest everyday upgrade. Microsoft has confirmed that a new search built on WinUI 3 is incoming and says it makes it faster and lighter on resources. Windows Search also understands you better. Typos and synonyms are matched more intelligently, so a sloppy query is more likely to give you the right result.
The main highlight is inline actions. So, instead of finding a setting and then opening Settings to change it, you can enable/disable a setting from search. This means you’ll be able to:
- Switch to dark mode, turn on night light, or turn on Bluetooth
- Dim your screen or mute your PC
- Minimize all your windows or arrange windows on screen
Phone actions are coming soon too, allowing you to quickly do things like sending a text through a Phone Link-connected device. Search is soon expected to get inline previews of files, richer file details, web answers (think weather or “how tall is the Eiffel Tower”) and filters. This new experience is also expected to arrive for the Start menu, but only next year. Other features are expected for broader availability later this year.
Battery status widget
This is not a big update, per se, but if you want to know what the battery level is on your wireless mouse? Your headphones? Your laptop? Or any other connected device, usually you’d have to hunt through different menus for each answer.
With the Windows 11 26340.9616 release, Microsoft introduced a Battery Status widget that shows the battery levels of your PC and your peripheral devices in one view. To get it, you need to open the Widgets board > Add widgets > Battery Status. It is rolling out to Insiders on newer builds. Widgets are also getting lighter. Microsoft says on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets now load only when you open them. This helps free up more than 200 MB for your apps.
Phone to PC continuity
Microsoft seems to be making sure that your phone and PC act like one setup. With the upcoming updates, Windows 11 could allow users to reply to messages, answer calls, and open phone apps without picking up their phone. Here are all the features, reportedly available in the insider build:
- Messages and notifications: You will be able to preview them from your Android phone or iPhone right in Start. When you want to reply, you can open a window focused on that chat.
- Quick Settings: Put your phone in silent mode or ring a misplaced phone right from your PC.
- Phone apps on your desktop: Supported Android phones can open phone apps in separate, resizable windows.
- Files: You will be able to browse your phone’s files in File Explorer.
- Photos: You can snap a picture on your phone, and your PC shows a notification that you can open with one click.
- Resume: Pick up supported activities where you left off when you switch devices.
One thing to note is that this requires a compatible Android phone or iPhone, and features vary by platform. The rollout date, similar to other features, isn’t confirmed, but it may arrive by next year.
Better privacy controls
Until now, regular desktop apps were controlled by a single device-wide switch for things like your camera, microphone, and location. That was not something one would want, especially when you want to have granular controls. According to the 28120.3302 release notes, Insiders can now allow or deny access for each desktop app individually. For that, you need to head to Settings > Privacy & security, then open Camera, Microphone, or Location.
The rollout is gentle on your existing setup. All the apps that were granted access will continue to keep it, and apps that were denied stay denied. Nothing will reset. Apps that haven’t asked yet will prompt you the first time they request access.
Smarter Windows Hello
According to Microsoft, with the latest insider builds, it has introduced faster Windows Hello sign-ins, made them easier, and more reliable, with improvements to both face and fingerprint recognition. There’s also a very practical new trick for face sign-in. If you’ve ever tried to unlock your laptop in a dim room, you know the struggle. You have to turn on the light so that your face is detected correctly.
The 26340.9750 release notes say Windows Hello facial recognition can temporarily brighten your screen to help you sign in when the lighting is poor. To use it, go to Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Facial recognition (Windows Hello) and turn on Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition. This one is currently in the Experimental channel.
Anti-glare mode
Although Microsoft doesn’t use the name “anti-glare mode,” that’s exactly what the newly added option does. Notably, it’s a contrast theme toggle inside Magnifier, as mentioned in the 28120.3302 release notes. While many people use Night light or color inversion to calm a bright screen, but the downside of using is that it flips everything, including photos, charts, and videos.
With the new toggle, it will recolor the interface only. This way, your images keep their real colors. The dark theme is the default, and you can pick a different contrast theme under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. You still get the “Color inversion” option, and it isn’t going anywhere if you prefer it.
Magnifier also learned some multi-monitor tricks:
- Zoom per display: With your monitors set to Extend, each screen can have its own zoom level. So, one screen where you are writing can sit at 300% while your reference screen stays at 150%.
- View locking: Press Ctrl + Windows + K while pointing at a screen to hold its view in place, then press Windows + Esc to release all locks.
If you just want a softer tint, Windows 11 is also testing a “Screen Tint,” which lets you pick a color overlay and adjust its strength.
File Explorer previews
You might already be using third-party software for file previews inside File Explorer, but wait. Microsoft is also cooking the same feature, and it may arrive very soon for Windows 11. A couple of preview-related changes are incoming:
- Thumbnails in the Recommended section on File Explorer’s Home page are sharper, so they’re crisper and easier to read without needing you to open them.
- You can now preview and install fonts from File Explorer and desktop right-click menus.
If you work with fonts, that second one saves a few steps. For everyone else, it’s a polish update, and it’s good to see File Explorer getting some attention.
Can everyone try these features?
Unfortunately, these features aren’t available for everyone, for now. Most of the features above live in Windows Insider builds. If you’re comfortable with a few bugs, you can join through Settings > Windows Update > Windows Insider Program. You will see most features in builds 26340.9616, 26340.9750 and 28120.3302 in the Experimental channels.
These builds can be unstable, and features in them might change, be removed, or never ship. Many are also rolled out gradually to a subset of Insiders first, so you may not see everything right away. For those who are using Windows 11 on their primary device, you should probably wait.

Jordan has cancelled next week’s international against Indonesia at the request of the Indonesian FA (PSSI) but said a friendly with Australia in Amman will go ahead despite the security situation in the Middle East.
The Jordanian FA announced the cancellation of next Friday’s match against Indonesia late on Thursday, saying PSSI had apologised for not fulfilling the fixture.
“We decided to cancel it primarily due to security considerations,” a PSSI official told Reuters on Friday.
“We know that the situation in the Middle East is currently not good, so we took into account concerns that it could affect the psychological well-being of the players and the team. Based on that, I communicated with the coach and PSSI chief that we had to be brave enough to take a stance,” they added.
The official said PSSI might look to arrange another fixture in the November international window, but that was unlikely given the limited time available.
The friendlies were originally planned to help all three teams prepare for the Asian Cup , but that was postponed on Tuesday until December next year following attacks on host nation Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
The Jordanian FA said in its statement that the November 17 friendly against Australia at Amman International Stadium was “still scheduled to take place, without any changes”.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported on Friday that Football Australia had delayed the announcement of the squad for the Jordan friendly and one against Qatar next Friday because some players were unhappy about making the trip to Amman.

Jordan launched airstrikes on what it said were Islamic State militants in neighbouring Syria late last month in response to an attack on a church that killed 9 people and injured 40.
Attacks such as the church shooting are rare in the country, a relatively stable US ally, but a security officer was killed and another wounded in a stabbing attack in Amman on Thursday.
Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is advising its citizens to “reconsider” the need “to travel to Jordan due to the unpredictable security situation in Jordan and the region, and the threat of terrorism”.
Australians are advised to “exercise a high degree of caution” when visiting Qatar after the alert level was lowered last month.

KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla.—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.
With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP.Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.
Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.
A new Northstar
The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts, 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.
Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine, and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.
“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”
The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.
Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.

Mugabe's son faces assault charges linked to luxury car smuggling case
The son of the late Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe faces assault charges after allegedly attacking an anti-corruption official
HARARE, Zimbabwe -- A son of the late Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe appeared in a court in Harare on Thursday accused of assaulting an anti-corruption agency official during an operation linked to the alleged smuggling of two luxury vehicles into the country.
Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe arrived at the Harare Magistrates Court with four other men who were arrested with him at a lodge.
Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said Bellarmine, 29, and the four others were arrested Tuesday and face assault charges.
An anti-corruption commission spokesperson told state media Wednesday that officers had gone to the lodge to seize a Lamborghini and a Mercedes-Benz when one of the officials was assaulted. The spokesperson said the vehicles were in the country illegally.
Neither vehicle has been linked to Bellarmine, who is Mugabe’s youngest child with his second wife, Grace.
The arrest is the latest in a series of legal troubles involving members of the former president’s family in Zimbabwe and neighboring South Africa.
Bellarmine appeared in a Harare court in October on drug possession charges, but prosecutors withdrew them after his co-accused accepted responsibility for possessing cannabis.
Other cases involving Bellarmine and his older brother, Robert Jr., in recent years have largely centered on allegations of cannabis possession, assault and property damage.
In April, Bellarmine was deported from South Africa after pleading guilty to brandishing an object “likely to lead a person to believe it is a firearm” and being in the country illegally. He was ordered to pay fines totaling about $36,000 or serve two years in prison. A magistrate also ordered his immediate deportation as part of a plea deal.
Their mother, Grace Mugabe, became embroiled in a high-profile legal dispute in South Africa in 2017 after allegedly assaulting a young model she found in the company of her sons at a Johannesburg hotel. South African authorities initially granted Grace diplomatic immunity, but the country’s High Court overturned that decision in 2018 following a legal challenge.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being ousted in a military-backed coup in 2017. He died in 2019 at age 95.

European air traffic targeted by new threats in at least 3 incidents
Officials across Europe report more bomb threats against flights, following a series of hoaxes causing diversions this week
BERLIN -- Officials across Europe reported a fresh slew of bomb threats against multiple flights on Friday, following a string of hoaxes that have caused flight diversions this week. Two broadcasters also received security threats.
No suspicious items were found and no one was injured, but the threats have raised concern because they came as Europe digests other recent disruptions — including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.
In Hungary, the defense minister said military fighter jets escorted three separate passenger planes across the country's airspace within an hour after each received bomb threats. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said they were flights from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Cyprus and Romania.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said Friday that “four new bomb threats were made today against aircraft flying over French territory.” The planes landed safely at Paris’ Orly Airport and bomb disposal experts were conducting inspections. The office didn’t give details of the flights affected.
Other incidents included threats against a Prague to Bucharest flight operated by Romanian carrier Tarom, and a Ryanair flight traveling from Lisbon to Rome. Security inspections were carried out and no explosives were found.
A WizzAir flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice after a bomb alert, and passengers were evacuated after the aircraft landed. Air traffic at the airport was briefly suspended, but police searches turned up nothing.
At Prague's Vaclav Havel Airport, spokesperson Denisa Hejtmánková said a total of nine flights were threatened, including arriving flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and Britain. Czech police said security measures were taken that had “a minimal impact on the normal operations at the airport.”
In the Danish capital, Copenhagen, police said Friday they went to the airport for a second consecutive day “in connection with threats directed at air traffic” as a precautionary measure. They said they assessed that there had been no danger to passengers or to others at the airport.
More than two dozen flights were affected by threats earlier in the week, with some diverted as authorities scrambled to rule out any danger.
Fake bomb threats are relatively common but it is unusual to see so many in such a short period.
It remains unclear who is behind the wave of airline hoaxes, which come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe.
Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government. An email containing the threat sent Thursday to airport authorities in Rome and reviewed by The Associated Press purported to come from a group describing itself as anti-feminist and claiming it was targeting a “feminist regime.” Another European airport received a threat with similar wording, but it was unclear if it came from the same sender.
Bomb threats are on pilots’ minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice president of the European Cockpit Association. Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.
Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes “totally unacceptable.”
In Ireland, the Dublin headquarters of national broadcaster RTE was evacuated Friday after a bomb threat, and live broadcasts were replaced with pre-recorded programs.
Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána, said it was ”aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe.” It said that it has been liaising with Irish media organizations and the threat will be investigated.
U.K.-based broadcaster Sky said it had also received a “security threat.” In a statement reported by its Sky News channel, it said that “we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure.” Sky News remained on air.
It's not clear if the incidents were linked.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the threats to RTE and others “just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause fear and anxiety.”
He said there would be a “very significant security operation” in place next week when Dublin hosts meetings of the European Political Community and European Union leaders.

Srinagar, Nov 06: The Counter Intelligence Kashmir (CIK) wing of Jammu and Kashmir Police on Friday searches at six locations across Kashmir in connection with a terror recruitment case, officials said.
An official said that CIK teams carried out searches at residential houses in Budgam, Srinagar, Bijbehara and Mattan, Anantnag areas of south Kashmir, besides a village in Pulwama district.
He said the searches were conducted in coordination with local police and revenue officials in the presence of executive magistrates.
“The case, registered under FIR No. 07/2023 at Police Station CIK Srinagar, pertains to an alleged terror recruitment module that was operating through social media platforms to radicalise and recruit youth into proscribed terrorist organisations,” the official said.
He said the investigation was initiated following inputs that individuals based in Pakistan, allegedly in connivance with handlers of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and other banned outfits, were using social media platforms to lure Kashmiri youth and instigate them against the sovereignty and integrity of the country.
Further details regarding any recoveries or detentions are awaited.—(KNO)

A video featuring Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is being circulated on social media. In the video, Lavrov allegedly describes India as merely a trading partner, stating that India is neither a Russian ally nor a superpower and has no right to interfere in or advise Russia on its foreign policy decisions concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States, or other countries (here, here, here). Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated that India is neither a Russian ally nor a superpower and has no right to interfere in or advise Russia on its foreign policy decisions concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States, or other countries.
Fact: The viral clip has been digitally manipulated by altering the original footage and adding fabricated statements about India’s relations with Russia. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A keyword search related to the viral claim led to no credible reports confirming that Sergey Lavrov made such statements.
Further, we conducted a search using the ‘M World’ logo visible at the top of the viral clip. This led us to the M World News Instagram page, where we found the original video featuring Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. The video was posted with the caption, “Lavrov Fires Back Over Claims Putin Refuses to Meet Zelensky.”
Based on this clue, we found in the original footage that Lavrov dismisses claims that Russian President Vladimir Putin is refusing to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He emphasises that any potential negotiations must address the underlying issues. During the briefing, he discussed US-Russia relations, possible peace talks on Ukraine, and international diplomatic responses (here, here).
Upon closer examination of the video, we noticed certain inconsistencies, particularly that Lavrov’s lip movements do not appear to be properly synchronised with the audio.
To further verify the video’s authenticity, we analysed it using multiple AI detection tools. Hive Moderation’s AI-generated content detector gave an aggregate score of 99.4%, indicating that the media likely contained AI-generated or deepfake content. Similarly, NVIDIA’s Synthetic Video Detector classified the footage as synthetic media.
To sum up, this Video of Sergey Lavrov making derogatory remarks about India is digitally manipulated.

CAPFs debated merit, ex-Agniveer postings before Union Cabinet’s Agnipath overhaul approval
The Cabinet approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial service an option to remain in service
The central armed police forces (CAPFs) debated how to assess Agniveer merit for induction and where to post these highly trained soldiers to ensure smooth integration with existing personnel without friction, before all of the short-term military recruits were given a retention option.
Seventy-five per cent of the first Agniveer batch were set to be released under the Agnipath scheme before the Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial four-year service an option to remain in service for two more years. Agniveers were offered a route to enrol as regular soldiers at the end of the extended period.
In March 2023, the government announced a 10% Agniveer quota in CAPFs and exemption from the Physical Efficiency Test when the scheme was first notified. They had to take the written test, and ex-Agniveers could join as constables (general duty), the junior-most functional rank. “The quota increased from 10 to 50% in CAPFs, a substantial increase. More than that, the issue concerned 50% of former soldiers being inducted directly while the other 50% had to clear all tests. It was a challenge to ensure this would not affect the morale of those who had to clear all tests to get inducted,” said an officer.
Deep Dive
The CAPFs were awaiting clarity on how merit was to be established for the 50% ex-Agniveers because there was to be no test, written or physical, during their induction until the Union Cabinet’s retention approval.
Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani, who on Wednesday announced the Cabinet’s decision, said there would be no reservation for ex-Agniveers. “The reservation in the paramilitary forces and states was announced when 75% of soldiers were to be released back into society.”
He said the defence forces are offering all 75% Agniveers a chance to join back and also enrol as regular soldiers after completing their tenure. “This is why, after this, no reservation, whether in paramilitary forces or state government, will exist because the Indian defence forces are providing them all an opportunity to rejoin for a second engagement period of two years and after that to become regular soldiers in the armed forces.”
Merit assessment and integration within CAPFs gained urgency after the government made changes to the Agnipath scheme over the last year. The first two Agniveer batches from the Navy and Air Force were due to complete their tenure in November and December, making them eligible for reemployment in the CAPFs.
People aware of the matter said Union home ministry officials held meetings on how to decide merit among the Agniveers and avoid friction between regular CAPF personnel, who have to pass three tests.
In November 2025, the government exempted ex-Agniveers from all written, physical efficiency, or physical standard tests for enrolment in the CAPFs.
Officials said the ministry also formed an ex-Agniveer cell this year. The cell was taking feedback and inputs from all CAPFs regarding the induction and career progression of the ex-Agniveers.
The Central Reserve Police Force was appointed the nodal agency for their induction and career progression across all CAPFs.
A second officer said all CAPF chiefs were holding internal discussions with their senior officers on ways to induct the former soldiers into the force in the weeks leading up to Wednesday’s announcement. “This looked like an easy transition, but it is a challenging one. Soldiers are highly trained and motivated.”
The second officer said the Agniveer job is proactive, while it is reactive in CAPFs, barring counter-insurgency or counter-militancy operations. “All chiefs were taking inputs to find the best place to post highly trained soldiers and reorient them. ...this would not have been the first time such a transition happened. There are hundreds and thousands of cases, especially in the early years of BSF [Border Security Force] when the force took army personnel on deputation.”
The officer added that many officers enjoyed the work culture and decided to continue their service in the CAPFs. “There are also many cases of army officers joining state police forces too.”
Brigadier (Retd) Rohit Nautiyal joined the CRPF as a deputy inspector general and was posted in Srinagar in 2022 after serving the Army for 32 years. He retired from the CRPF last week after a three-year tenure post-reemployment.
Decorated Colonel (retired) Nectar Sanjebam of the 21 Para Special Forces, who led the 2015 surgical strikes in Myanmar, was inducted into the Manipur Police as a senior superintendent (combat).

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

A new British startup believes that artificial intelligence is the key to speedrunning the slow and temperamental process of drug design.
Potential Sciences plans to build large-scale chemical datasets by using basic principles of physics to simulate interactions between atoms, then small molecules, then complex amino acids and proteins. With that data, it’s betting it can train AI models and prediction systems capable of identifying highly targeted drugs for specific diseases, bypassing costly and time-consuming lab experimentation.
“We want molecules that are never going to work in the clinic to fail fast,” Hatem Helal, Potential Sciences founder and CEO, tells WIRED. “That means having better predictors of how they will behave as they interact with human biology.”
The startup, which launched on November 5, says it has seed funding in the tens of millions of dollars from SovAI—the UK government’s AI venture capital fund—and Twin Path Ventures, among other investors. The founders declined to disclose the precise figure or valuation.
If things pan out as Potential Sciences hopes, it could pave the way for the accelerated development of new treatments for all sorts of diseases. By reducing the cost of experimentation, Helal says, the company’s approach could also make it economical for pharmaceutical companies to pursue drugs for rare conditions that have previously gone untreated.
“We want to make it possible to have more bespoke treatments for diseases—this idea that medicines can be one-off molecular combinations that are tailored to your unique human biology,” he says.
The question is whether Potential Sciences will be able to predict how well drug candidates will bind to disease-related proteins as accurately as it hopes, which would require a marked leap forward.
“I’m sure it will be an improvement,” says Peter Wolynes, a professor of chemistry at Rice University. But currently, “the engineering is at the level of the Romans, not of the Renaissance, in terms of how protein engineering is done,” he says.
Industry luminaries like Demis Hassabis, who won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for his work at Google DeepMind, have long said that advances in AI will eventually lead to momentous scientific breakthroughs, in the same way the technology has recently carved up mathematics. The hope among startups like Potential Sciences is that drug discovery will be one of the first scientific frontiers to be transformed by the technology.
At the moment, a large proportion of AI drug discovery labs are developing models on top of a single public database of 3D atomic structures—the Protein Data Bank—which researchers have expanded over decades with the results of new experiments. The problem, according to Helal, is that the dataset remains too small to train AI models advanced enough to reliably accelerate the search for viable drug candidates.
“Of all the atoms in the universe, there’s around 1060 ways that you could assemble them into molecules that you could potentially give to a human,” says Helal. “Think of drug discovery as a search problem; it’s about how fast you can navigate and prune that space into promising molecules for a particular disease.”
To address that issue, Potential Sciences is trying to construct far larger datasets made up of synthetic data, produced by simulating interactions between different chemical compounds. From far larger pools of data, the theory goes, the startup will be able to train far more advanced AI models and prediction systems.
Academics see the potential in the simulation-based approach that Potential Sciences has adopted. “If we could calculate accurately the interactions between all molecules in the cell and the fluctuations in their structure we could predict where molecules would bind and that would indeed revolutionize drug development,” says Alan Fersht, an emeritus professor of chemistry at the University of Cambridge who specializes in protein engineering. “I am optimistic that this will eventually happen.”
In receiving investment from SovAI, Potential Sciences joins fellow AI drug discovery companies Basecamp Research and Isomorphic Labs, and materials discovery startup CuspAI.
The UK government established SovAI earlier this year with a mandate to invest in British startups capable of becoming indispensable components of the global AI supply chain, affording the country vital geopolitical leverage. The fund has at its disposal roughly $800 million and the ability to offer its portfolio companies access to the UK’s national AI supercomputer.
“Coming at drug discovery from a physics angle—the physics of chemistry—sets [Potential Sciences] apart from other companies,” says Joséphine Kant, head of ventures at SovAI, who has joined the startup’s board as part of the investment. “Giving them access to computing resources, they can do this work at a scale that would be very difficult otherwise for a small startup.”
However, AI drug discovery is a crowded market. Even with a leg up from the UK government, Potential Sciences will face steep competition from a multitude of entrepreneurs and academics racing to solve the same bottlenecks from varying angles of approach.
Nor does the ability to more quickly identify promising drug candidates eliminate the cost and time required to test their safety and efficacy, meaning new treatments will continue to take a long time to come to market, regardless of advances in AI. “The cost of designing a drug is nothing compared to figuring out what it will do to mice; to really sick patients; to normal people,” says Wolynes. “In some sense, it’s not the rate-limiting phenomenon.”
As the field progresses, startups like Potential Sciences will also have to contend with the prospect that technologies able to identify effective treatments could be abused to develop highly dangerous chemicals, too. “If we can design tools that perfectly minimize toxicity, it’s a bit flip to maximize it as well,” Helal says.
Potential Sciences doesn’t yet have all the answers. The startup hasn’t settled on a way to generate revenue from the various technologies it’s developing nor decided whether to make its models freely available, given the potential for misuse. But Helal is convinced that there are few more worthwhile problems to try to remedy with AI.
“There have been many waves of promising breakthroughs that don’t quite have an impact in drug discovery,” says Helal. “It’s a fundamental, high-impact problem for us to try and solve.”
